Millions of particles: GPU simulation and sorting

Millions of particles: GPU simulation and sorting

A 100 000-element particle system is not “many objects” but a dense array of data. On the GPU it is updated by a single dispatch and drawn with a single instanced call. The bottleneck is not the simulation but the sorting for transparency.

particlesbitonic sortindirect drawGPU particles
01 Essence

The CPU approach (a particle pool, a loop over it, sorting for alpha blending) hits three walls: updating the state, sorting, and issuing the draw. The GPU approach takes the first two off the CPU: the state lives in a buffer, a compute shader updates it, and the render reads the same buffer as instance attributes (position, colour, size). Sorting remains.

Sorting is only needed for correct alpha blending (back to front). On the GPU you use a bitonic sort: a merge sort that is parallel by nature, O(n·log²n). The standard trick is to sort 32-bit keys, where the high bits are the sort value (say depth) and the low bits are the particle index; the keys are sorted along with the data, then the data is permuted by the index. For 200 000 particles that is tens of milliseconds on the CPU — and milliseconds on the GPU.

Alternatives to sorting: (1) additive blending, where the order does not matter but correct transparency is lost; (2) weighted blended OIT, an approximate order-independent transparency that is the modern standard for sparks and smoke; (3) a two-pass render: opaque first, then transparent with depth fade. The conclusion: sort only where it actually changes the picture, otherwise use OIT.

the mathematical model
bitonic sort: O(n log²n) comparisons, particle_cost = sim + sort + draw
For 2^k elements: k(k+1)/2 passes. With 262 144 particles (2^18) that is 171 passes. Dropping to 2^16 removes a third of the sorting time.
02 How to build it
  1. Set the budget: how many particles fit into 1 ms of GPU. Start at 10 000 and measure.
  2. Keep the state in a single buffer (pos, vel, colour, life) in SoA or a dense struct layout.
  3. Update it with a compute shader: one dispatch per frame, no readback.
  4. If correct transparency is needed, sort keys (depth << 16 | index) with a bitonic sort.
  5. Draw with a single instanced call, reading the positions from the buffer instead of CPU structs.
  6. Cap overdraw: a million particles across the whole screen is a fill-rate problem, not a compute problem.
03 Working code
GLSL 
#version 450
// Draw the particles from a GPU buffer with one instanced call.

layout(location = 0) in vec2 corner;   // quad of 4 vertices
layout(location = 1) in vec2 offset;   // per-instance position
layout(location = 2) in vec4 color;    // per-instance colour and size

layout(std430, binding = 0) readonly buffer Particles {
    vec4 pos_size[];   // xy - position, z - size, w - alpha
    vec4 color[];
};

out vec4 v_color;

void main() {
    uint i = gl_InstanceID;
    vec4 ps = pos_size[i];
    vec2 world = ps.xy + corner * ps.z;
    gl_Position = vec4(world, 0.0, 1.0);
    v_color = color[i];
}

// One draw call for all particles:
// glDrawArraysInstanced(GL_TRIANGLE_STRIP, 0, 4, particleCount);
// the triangles are not sorted - for sparks use additive blending.
04 Computational complexity
Time
Simulation O(N); sorting O(N log²N); drawing O(N)
Memory
O(N) on the GPU
In practice
The real limit is overdraw and bandwidth, not the particle count.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Assuming a million particles is “a lot for the GPU”: with heavy overdraw that is 10 ms of fill alone.
  • Reading particle positions back to the CPU every frame: readback is synchronisation and latency (topic 61).
  • Always sorting transparent particles: for smoke and sparks, additive/OIT is cheaper and looks better.
  • Growing the buffer “just in case”: GPU memory is expensive, size it for the worst case.
  • Ignoring spawn and death: free slots have to be recycled or the buffer inflates.

GPU-driven pipeline: GPU-side culling and command building

GPU-driven pipeline: GPU-side culling and command building

The classic frame: the CPU decides what is visible and issues a draw per group, the GPU draws. A GPU-driven pipeline flips the scheme: the GPU picks the visible objects and builds the command list, while the CPU issues a single call.

indirect drawGPU cullingHi-Zbindlesscompute pipeline
01 Essence

The problem with the classic scheme is that the CPU does not know what the GPU will finish in a frame, so planning is guesswork and the frame is bounded by the CPU. A GPU-driven pipeline solves it: the scene lives in permanent GPU buffers (positions, radii, mesh and material indices), a compute shader does the frustum culling and writes the surviving list into a buffer, and `drawElementsIndirect` / `drawIndirect` reads that buffer as the draw arguments.

Occlusion is done with a Hi-Z hierarchy: the previous frame's depth buffer is reduced into a pyramid (max-depth reduction), and an object's visibility is tested by sampling its AABB in the pyramid. The same buffer can be built before the main pass (depth prepass) to cull against the current depth.

The consequences and the price. Upside: the CPU barely participates in building the list, the frame becomes predictable, culling is more accurate. Downside: debugging is much harder, “draw calls” disappear from the profiler, and you have to think about synchronisation and about how to debug content. A separate problem is support: APIs like WebGPU expose the needed primitives, while WebGL2's indirect draw is only available through extensions.

the mathematical model
visible_list = cull(frustum, hzb) → count + instance_ids → drawIndirect(count)
One indirect draw per (mesh, material) instead of thousands of normal draws. CPU cost: 1 dispatch + 1 indirect draw per material group.
02 How to build it
  1. Move the scene into permanent GPU buffers: positions, radii, mesh and material indices.
  2. Write the culling compute shader: frustum test on the AABB, Hi-Z check, write the surviving indices.
  3. Group the visible objects by key (mesh + material) — that gives the counts for the indirect draws.
  4. Use drawIndirect / multi-draw with the counts from the GPU buffer.
  5. Drop per-draw state binding through bindless or texture arrays — otherwise every material still needs its own call.
  6. Add a debug mode: visualise the culled objects and the counters, or there is nothing to debug.
03 Working code
GLSL 
#version 450
// GPU culling: frustum + Hi-Z, writing the visible objects into a buffer.

layout(local_size_x = 64) in;

struct Object {
    vec4 center_radius;   // xyz - centre, w - radius
    uint mesh_id;
    uint material_id;
};

layout(std430, binding = 0) readonly  buffer Objects { Object objs[]; };
layout(std430, binding = 1) writeonly buffer Visible { uint visible_ids[]; };
layout(std430, binding = 2) writeonly buffer DrawArgs { uint count; uint instance_count; uint first; uint base; };

layout(push_constant) uniform PC {
    mat4 view_proj;
    vec4 frustum[6];     // culling planes
    int  object_count;
} pc;

void main() {
    uint i = gl_GlobalInvocationID.x;
    if (i >= uint(pc.object_count)) return;

    Object o = objs[i];

    // 1. Frustum: sphere centre against the six planes
    bool in_frustum = true;
    for (int p = 0; p < 6; ++p) {
        if (dot(pc.frustum[p].xyz, o.center_radius.xyz) + pc.frustum[p].w < -o.center_radius.w) {
            in_frustum = false;
            break;
        }
    }
    if (!in_frustum) return;

    // 2. Hi-Z occlusion: sample the depth pyramid by the AABB (simplified to the centre)
    // float depth = textureLod(hiz, uv_center, 0).r;
    // if (o.center_radius.z - o.center_radius.w > depth) return;

    // 3. Atomically add to the list of visible objects
    uint slot = atomicAdd(drawArgs.instance_count, 1u);
    visible_ids[slot] = i;
}
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(n) over the scene on the GPU, O(1) on the CPU
Memory
O(n) in GPU memory
In practice
The win shows with thousands of objects; with hundreds the overhead does not pay off.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Introducing a GPU-driven pipeline into a project with small scenes: the debugging cost is not repaid.
  • Forgetting that GPU frustum culling does not remove overdraw: the pixel cost stays.
  • No fallback: on older APIs you need the normal path, or part of your audience cannot launch the game.
  • Counting draw calls the old way: they are invisible in the profiler, so you need your own telemetry.
  • Synchronising the visibility list with the CPU every frame: that brings back exactly the stalls you wanted to avoid.

Async readback: avoiding GPU stalls

Async readback: avoiding GPU stalls

The fastest way to ruin the performance of a GPU game is to read a result back to the CPU in the same frame. That is a stall: the CPU waits for the GPU and the GPU waits for the CPU. The fix is asynchronous reading with a delay of one to three frames.

fencestallreadbacktriple bufferingPBO
01 Essence

How the problem works: a `map()` or `readPixels` on a buffer the GPU has not finished with makes the driver wait for the GPU to complete. During that wait the GPU cannot start the next frame and the CPU cannot start the next frame — both sit idle. The wait can be 5–50 ms, and all of it is wasted.

The solution is to separate them in time. The GPU writes into buffer A; the CPU sets a fence (a “I am done” signal) and on the next frame (or two) checks whether the signal fired. If it did, it reads the data from A (which no longer waits for the GPU) and starts the GPU working in buffer B. You end up with a pipeline: while the CPU processes generation N−2, the GPU computes generation N.

The details: triple buffering is needed because the GPU can be two or three frames ahead; a ring of buffers beats a single one. Data the GPU writes often but the CPU reads rarely should be packed (downsampling, aggregation on the GPU) — otherwise the bandwidth kills the whole benefit. And if the CPU needs the result in the same frame (for example, a cursor collision), you need a compromise: predict on the CPU, or accept the latency.

the mathematical model
stall = max(0, t_gpu_finish − t_cpu_request), pipelined_latency ≈ k · frame_time (k = 2…3)
A good sign: the readback costs < 0.2 ms of CPU and does not block the GPU. Triple buffering: buffers A/B/C, the CPU reads A while the GPU writes C.
02 How to build it
  1. Find every place where the CPU waits for the GPU: position readbacks, occlusion queries, picking, counter reads.
  2. Make the buffers asynchronous and attach a fence to each frame.
  3. Introduce a ring of two or three buffers: the CPU reads data that is one or two frames old.
  4. Reduce the volume: read only what you need (counters, the positions of selected objects), not the whole buffer.
  5. If the CPU needs a fresh result in the same frame, compute it in parallel on the CPU or predict it.
  6. Verify with a profiler: there should be no “GPU wait” in the frame.
03 Working code
C# 
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Rendering;

// Async readback: reading GPU data without waiting.
public class AsyncReader : MonoBehaviour
{
    const int Ring = 3;                       // a ring of buffers
    readonly ComputeBuffer[] _buffers = new ComputeBuffer[Ring];
    int _head = 0;                            // where we write now

    void OnEnable()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < Ring; i++)
        {
            _buffers[i] = new ComputeBuffer(1024, sizeof(float) * 4,
                                           ComputeBufferType.Structured);
        }
    }

    // Call at the end of the frame: "capture the data once the GPU is done".
    public void Request()
    {
        _head = (_head + 1) % Ring;
        // the fence is set right after the dispatch: the signal means "the buffer is ready"
        GraphicsFence fence = Graphics.CreateGraphicsFence(
            GraphicsFenceType.AsyncQueueSynchronisation,
            SynchronisationStageFlags.ComputeProcessing);

        _pending.Add(new Pending { Buffer = _buffers[_head], Fence = fence });
    }

    struct Pending { public ComputeBuffer Buffer; public GraphicsFence Fence; }

    readonly List<Pending> _pending = new();

    void LateUpdate()
    {
        // Only take buffers whose fence has fired: waiting is not allowed
        for (int i = _pending.Count - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        {
            var p = _pending[i];
            if (!p.Fence.passed) continue;      // the GPU is not done yet - skip it
            var data = new float[1024];
            p.Buffer.GetData(data);             // the data is ready, this is not a stall
            _pending.RemoveAt(i);
        }
    }

    void OnDisable()
    {
        foreach (var b in _buffers) b?.Release();
    }
}
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per frame with the asynchronous scheme
Memory
O(k · buffer_size) for the ring
In practice
Data latency of 2–3 frames is normal, but not for picking or cursor physics.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Reading a buffer in the same frame you wrote it: that is the stall, even for “only 4 kilobytes”.
  • Accumulating pending requests without checking the fence: memory grows and the data arrives dozens of frames late.
  • Reading the whole buffer when you need ten numbers: the volume of traffic matters more than the latency.
  • Assuming a fence “solves everything”: on some drivers checking a fence also costs microseconds — measure it.
  • Demanding same-frame data where a prediction would do (cursor position, shot prediction).

Procedural geometry on the GPU: marching cubes and SDF

Procedural geometry on the GPU: marching cubes and SDF

If the world is defined by a density field (SDF, noise, metaballs), you can turn it into polygons right on the GPU. That removes the heaviest phase — mesh building — from the CPU and opens the door to millions of triangles in real time.

marching cubesSDFisosurfacevoxelizationmesh generation
01 Essence

Marching cubes extracts an isosurface from a voxel grid: each cell has eight density values, their signs pick one of 256 intersection cases, and a table builds the polygon. On the CPU this is bounded by the number of cells: 256³ = 16.7 million cells is not a per-frame task. On the GPU every cell is a thread, and only the cells where the density crosses the isolevel have to be evaluated (you can reject blocks by their min/max).

The SDF approach (signed distance field) is simpler: the surface is the zero level of a distance function, and the geometry comes out of ray marching in a shader. That is implicit geometry: there is no mesh at all, only a function and a ray. Upsides: infinite detail, easy deformation (edit the field), trivial CSG. Downsides: expensive rendering (many samples per pixel) and no data for physics — so you often combine them: SDF for rendering plus a coarse grid for physics.

Another heavy class is SDF generation (neural models such as marching cubes over the voxels of a 3D generator). Here the GPU is used for (1) building the voxels, (2) marching cubes over them and (3) mesh compression. The practical rule: compute on the GPU only what is genuinely massive and parallel, and leave the final assembly (compression, LOD, collisions) to the CPU or to GPU passes that read back asynchronously.

the mathematical model
surfaces ≈ cells_touched, mesh_size ≈ 2.4 · cells_touched (triangles per cell on average)
Optimisation: first compute the min/max density of a 4×4×4 block and discard the whole block — that saves up to 90 % of the threads.
02 How to build it
  1. Define the field source: SDF, noise, metaballs or network voxels.
  2. Split the volume into blocks; for each block compute the min/max density.
  3. Run the compute shader over the cells: cells outside [min, max] are discarded.
  4. Use the 256-case table (or the 2D cases for marching squares) to generate the triangles.
  5. Compress the vertices on the GPU if the API allows, or weld them on the CPU after a readback.
  6. Build LOD and a BVH for physics: the raw mesh is far too heavy for collisions.
03 Working code
GLSL 
#version 450
// Isosurface extraction: one thread per voxel cell.
layout(local_size_x = 4, local_size_y = 4, local_size_z = 4) in;

layout(std430, binding = 0) readonly  buffer Field { float density[]; };
layout(std430, binding = 1) writeonly buffer Triangles { float vertices[]; };
layout(std430, binding = 2) buffer Counter { uint count; };

uniform ivec3 grid_size;
uniform float iso_level;

// The 8 corners of a cell: offsets in xyz order (0..7)
const ivec3 CORNER[8] = ivec3[8](
    ivec3(0,0,0), ivec3(1,0,0), ivec3(0,1,0), ivec3(1,1,0),
    ivec3(0,0,1), ivec3(1,0,1), ivec3(0,1,1), ivec3(1,1,1)
);

float sample(ivec3 c) {
    if (any(lessThan(c, ivec3(0))) || any(greaterThanEqual(c, grid_size))) return 0.0;
    return density[c.x + c.y * grid_size.x + c.z * grid_size.x * grid_size.y];
}

void main() {
    ivec3 cell = ivec3(gl_GlobalInvocationID.xyz);
    if (any(greaterThanEqual(cell, grid_size - 1))) return;

    float v[8];
    for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) v[i] = sample(cell + CORNER[i]);

    // quick exit: the isolevel does not cross this cell
    float mn = v[0], mx = v[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < 8; ++i) { mn = min(mn, v[i]); mx = max(mx, v[i]); }
    if (iso_level < mn || iso_level > mx) return;

    // the full implementation uses the 256-case table:
    // int cubeIndex = 0;
    // for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) if (v[i] < iso_level) cubeIndex |= (1 << i);
    // int edges[12]; int edgeCount = 0;
    // ... interpolate the points on the edges, write the triangles ...
}
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(cells) on the GPU, block rejection cuts it by a factor
Memory
O(triangles) for the mesh
In practice
For a 256³ grid the order is seconds on the CPU and tens of milliseconds on the GPU.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Running over every cell without block rejection: in 90 % of cases the field is nearly empty and the threads are wasted.
  • Forgetting the grid boundaries: sampling outside produces garbage at the volume's edge.
  • Building physics from the same grid: collisions need a simplified convex or voxel mesh.
  • Expecting SDF rendering to be free: every pixel takes dozens of samples, which is pure fill-rate.
  • Generating the mesh every frame: generation has to be incremental, over the changed volume only.

Physics and broadphase on the GPU

Physics and broadphase on the GPU

When there are thousands of objects, the physics bottlenecks are broadphase (who can hit whom) and the solver (iterations that resolve the contacts). Both parallelise well and have long moved to the GPU: broadphase through grid sorting, the solver through a compute shader.

broadphaseXPBDGPU physicscontact sortingsolver
01 Essence

GPU broadphase works like this: the positions of all bodies are written into a buffer, sorted by a spatial grid (or by Morton code), and candidate contacts are generated for each pair of neighbouring cells. The sort is the same bitonic sort used for particles. The alternative is a compute-based broadphase with a hierarchical BVH that is built or refitted on the GPU (Morton sort plus a tree built through references).

The solver on the GPU: each thread solves one contact, but contacts are coupled (friction pulls on neighbouring bodies), so data has to be exchanged between iterations — usually with atomics plus two buffers, or a Jacobi scheme where every contact reads the state at the start of the iteration. XPBD (position-based) suits the GPU particularly well: positions are written atomically or through a pull scheme, and stiffness does not depend on the iteration count.

Reality is that fully GPU-resident physics is rare: game logic, triggers, collisions with the player and “important” bodies usually stay on the CPU, while the GPU handles the mass (small debris, liquid). A workable architecture is hybrid: broadphase and part of the solver on the GPU, the important bodies on the CPU, and the result read back asynchronously (topic 61) and applied with a delay of one to two frames. The delay is hidden with interpolation.

the mathematical model
contacts ≈ Σ k_density · density², solve_time ≈ iterations · contacts · cost_per_contact
The rule: sorting (O(N log²N)) is cheaper than an O(N²) broadphase. Solver: fewer iterations at a larger time step is always a win.
02 How to build it
  1. Find the real bottleneck: broadphase, narrowphase or solver — measure them separately.
  2. Move the broadphase to the GPU: sort by grid (Morton) and generate the candidates.
  3. Solve the contacts in a compute shader with the Jacobi scheme: every contact reads the state at the start of the iteration.
  4. Use XPBD: stiffness is independent of the iteration count, so fewer iterations mean less traffic.
  5. Keep the “important” bodies on the CPU and synchronise via an async readback plus interpolation.
  6. Validate against a reference: GPU physics must converge to the CPU solution within tolerance.
03 Working code
GLSL 
#version 450
// XPBD contact solver on the GPU: one thread per contact.
layout(local_size_x = 64) in;

layout(std430, binding = 0) readonly  buffer Contacts { vec4 pairs[]; };   // (i, j, rest, stiffness)
layout(std430, binding = 1) buffer Positions { vec4 pos[]; };            // xy - position, zw - inverse mass
layout(std430, binding = 2) buffer Corrections { vec4 delta[]; };

uniform float dt;
uniform int contact_count;

void main() {
    uint i = gl_GlobalInvocationID.x;
    if (i >= uint(contact_count)) return;

    vec4 c = pairs[i];
    uint a = uint(c.x), b = uint(c.y);
    vec4 pa = pos[a];
    vec4 pb = pos[b];

    vec3 d = pb.xy - pa.xy;
    float len = length(d);
    if (len < 1e-6) return;

    vec3 n = d / len;
    float pen = c.z - len;                 // penetration
    if (pen <= 0.0) return;

    float wsum = pa.z + pb.z;
    if (wsum <= 0.0) return;

    // positional correction: dx = n * pen * (w_i / sum w) * stiffness
    vec3 corr = n * (pen * c.w * (pa.z / wsum));

    // Jacobi: both corrections go into a separate buffer and are summed on the next pass
    delta[a] += vec4(corr, 0.0);
    delta[b] -= vec4(corr, 0.0);
}
04 Computational complexity
Time
Broadphase O(N log²N) instead of O(N²); solver O(contacts · iterations)
Memory
O(N + contacts)
In practice
The win shows with thousands of bodies; with hundreds the CPU is faster because it is simpler.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Moving physics to the GPU when the CPU needs the result every frame: 1–2 frames of latency ruins control feel.
  • Assuming Jacobi gives the same result as Gauss–Seidel: it converges more slowly but runs in parallel.
  • Writing positions from different contacts into one buffer without atomics: updates get lost.
  • Forgetting the broadphase: without it, O(N²) eats any gain from the GPU solver.
  • Not checking convergence: “it seems to work” on 100 bodies does not mean it is correct on 100 000.

Heavy shaders: ray marching, volumetrics and SSR

Heavy shaders: ray marching, volumetrics and SSR

When a shader is expensive, it is not the code but the number of samples per pixel. Ray marching costs dozens to hundreds of samples per pixel, so what wins is not micro-optimisation but three tricks: a lower resolution, temporal reprojection, and noise instead of an exact result.

ray marchingvolumetricsSSRtemporal reprojectiondenoise
01 Essence

Three classes of expensive effect. Volumetrics integrate the density along a ray through a volume (fog, god rays): 20–64 samples per pixel multiplied by the number of lights. SSR (screen-space reflections) traces a reflected ray through the screen buffer with a binary search: 20–50 steps. Ray marching an SDF is similar: 50–150 samples. The common trait: the cost scales with the sample count, not with the complexity of the maths.

The first remedy is to render the effect at a lower resolution (half or quarter) and upscale it. The second is temporal reprojection: reuse last frame's result projected along the camera motion, and compute the new frame only in the regions of interest (where the pixel changed a lot). The third is to trace in a sparse way (stochastic sampling + blue noise + temporal accumulation) and then denoise.

Denoising is a mandatory part: sparse ray marching produces noise that is smoothed either spatially (a bilateral blur that respects depth and normals) or temporally (accumulation over a neighbourhood). “Cheap SSR with a blur-denoise” is often indistinguishable from exact SSR with 64 steps. The main rule: every expensive technique needs a degradation path — disable it, simplify it, or lower its update rate.

the mathematical model
cost ≈ pixels · samples · shader_cost, temporal_gain ≈ f_overlap (0.5…0.95)
Half res gives a 4× fill-rate saving, quarter res 16×. Reprojection gains more the more of the screen is covered (f_overlap).
02 How to build it
  1. Measure the fill rate: how many samples per pixel your shader takes and what that costs in milliseconds.
  2. Move the effect to half resolution, add bilinear upscaling and dithering to remove banding.
  3. Enable temporal reprojection: keep the previous result and the camera motion matrix.
  4. Replace the deterministic traversal with a stochastic one (blue noise) and add denoising.
  5. Cap the effect's influence: a maximum number of samples per frame and automatic degradation under load.
  6. Provide a switch: on weak hardware the effect is disabled or simplified, not left to eat the frame.
03 Working code
GLSL 
#version 450
// Ray tracing through an SDF with an early exit and gradient stepping.
float sdf(vec3 p) {
    // a "bubble" structure: a cheap analytic function
    p = abs(p);
    return length(p) - 1.0 + 0.25 * sin(3.0 * p.x) * sin(3.0 * p.y) * sin(3.0 * p.z);
}

vec3 sdfNormal(vec3 p) {
    const vec2 e = vec2(1.0, -1.0) * 0.0015;
    return normalize(
        e.xyy * sdf(p + e.xyy) + e.yyx * sdf(p + e.yyx) +
        e.yxy * sdf(p + e.yxy) + e.xxx * sdf(p + e.xxx));
}

bool raymarch(vec3 ro, vec3 rd, out float t, int max_steps) {
    float dist = 0.0;
    t = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < max_steps; ++i) {
        vec3 p = ro + rd * dist;
        float d = sdf(p);
        if (d < 0.001) return true;          // hit the surface
        dist += d;                           // step along the SDF
        if (dist > 40.0) break;              // left the scene bounds
    }
    return false;
}

// Cost: up to max_steps samples per pixel.
// Speed-ups: half-res + temporal reprojection + stochastic jitter + denoise.
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(pixels · samples)
Memory
O(pixels) for the effect buffers
In practice
Fill rate is the most common cause of drops in 4K: quality has to scale with the resolution.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Optimising the maths instead of the sample count: 90 % of the cost is the samples.
  • Rendering the effect at full resolution “just this once”: the constant cost matters more than the one-off.
  • Without denoising, the noise from stochastic sampling looks worse than an honest but smooth result.
  • Ignoring overdraw: an expensive shader on top of an expensive shader multiplies the cost.
  • Not testing in 4K: the fill rate is four times higher and an effect that is “light” at 1080p kills the frame.

GPU profiling: timestamps, counters and occlusion queries

GPU profiling: timestamps, counters and occlusion queries

On the CPU you see how long a frame took; on the GPU you see how long a specific pass took. Tools give you that through timestamp queries, pipeline counters and occlusion queries. Without them, GPU optimisation is guessing from one overall timer.

timestamp queryGPU counterRenderDococclusion querypipeline statistics
01 Essence

A timestamp query asks the GPU for the time between two moments. Usually one per pass (scene, shadow, test, post) or one per frame; the result arrives one or two frames later, so you accumulate them and read them asynchronously (topic 61). The names differ per API (VK_EXT_calibrated_timestamps, D3D12 queries, Nsight) but the meaning is the same.

Pipeline counters give you what the time alone cannot: how many triangles, shader invocations, state switches, stalls, occlusions and full-screen quads. They are what turns “the time went into rendering” into “5000 draw calls and 12 million triangles”. Profilers (RenderDoc, PIX, Nsight Graphics, Xcode) can count them for you.

Occlusion queries are a stress test for the culling: how many pixels did the object actually write into the depth buffer? Zero means it is fully hidden and can be skipped. The query is asynchronous and the result arrives several frames later, so the decision is made with a delay (see topic 33). The occlusion depth is useful too: how many layers cover it — that decides whether an LOD is needed.

the mathematical model
pass_time = Σ timestamps, efficiency = useful_pixels / shaded_pixels
The useful metric is not “the pass took 3 ms” but “how much work it did per millisecond”: a shader that shades 10 % of the screen and costs 4 ms is expensive.
02 How to build it
  1. Enable timestamps per pass: scene, shadows, test, post, UI.
  2. Count the key metrics: draw calls, triangles, shader invocations, state changes.
  3. Compare the “worked screen” (shaded pixels) with the “useful screen”: a ratio below 50 % is an optimisation candidate.
  4. Add occlusion queries for large objects and measure how much is really visible.
  5. Look at p95/p99 across frames, not the average: one heavy pass in 30 % of frames ruins everything.
  6. Compare against a reference: “the pass took 3 ms” means nothing without “at 1080p/4K, with N particles”.
03 Working code
Python 
class GpuProfiler:
    """Accounting of the passes via timestamp queries and counters."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.passes = {}          # name -> list of durations
        self.counters = {}        # name -> value

    def begin_pass(self, name):
        self._t0 = time.perf_counter()   # a real API uses a timestamp query here

    def end_pass(self, name):
        dt = (time.perf_counter() - self._t0) * 1000.0
        self.passes.setdefault(name, []).append(dt)

    def set_counter(self, name, value):
        self.counters[name] = value

    def report(self, budget_ms=16.6):
        rows = []
        for name, vals in sorted(self.passes.items()):
            vals = sorted(vals)
            p95 = vals[min(len(vals) - 1, int(len(vals) * 0.95))]
            rows.append((name, round(sum(vals) / len(vals), 2), round(p95, 2)))
        rows.sort(key=lambda r: -r[2])
        over = [(n, p95) for n, _, p95 in rows if p95 > budget_ms]
        return {
            "passes": rows,
            "over_budget": over,
            "counters": self.counters,
            "gpu_total": round(sum(r[2] for r in rows), 2),
        }

# an expected output:
# passes: [('post', 3.1, 5.8), ('shadow', 2.0, 4.2), ('scene', 4.4, 9.1)]
# gpu_total: 19.1 ms with a budget of 16.6 -> fix post and scene first
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per query, O(samples) to collect
Memory
O(1)
In practice
Queries are not free: dozens of timestamp queries per frame cost tens of microseconds themselves.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Reading timestamp results in the same frame: the data arrives with a delay, so collect it asynchronously.
  • Assuming “the GPU is busy for 12 ms” means “the scene is heavy”: it might be the post-processing.
  • Not looking at the counters: time without a call count does not tell you what to fix.
  • Profiling with the debug overlay enabled: it adds draw calls of its own and distorts the picture.
  • Forgetting the hardware difference: the same profile on a mobile GPU can be orders of magnitude worse.

Quality scaling and graceful degradation

Quality scaling and graceful degradation

The same content has to run on a powerful PC and on a laptop with integrated graphics. So quality is not a fixed setting but a set of levers that the engine moves according to the frame budget: resolution, LOD distance, number of effects, shadow quality.

scalabilitydynamic resolutionLOD biasfallbacktier
01 Essence

The architecture of degradation is a set of independent “levers” plus a controller that picks their values from the current performance. Levers: render scale (0.5–1.0), LOD bias, the number of dynamic shadow casters, post-processing quality, the particle budget, the draw distance, texture resolution (streaming), audio quality. The controller measures the p95 frame time and changes the parameters smoothly, never in a jump.

Dynamic resolution is the most effective lever: you render at a lower resolution and upscale. There are two strategies: “render time is fixed” (drop the resolution to fit the budget) and “resolution is fixed” (drop the quality of the effects). The first preserves responsiveness, the second preserves sharpness; in practice you combine them and add hysteresis so the resolution does not “breathe”.

More important than the exact values is the absence of “steps”: if the player notices the switch, they will read it as lag. So the transitions are gradual (LOD fades, shadow cross-fades, the resolution does not jump), decisions are made on a smoothed metric rather than a single frame, and the settings do not oscillate. At startup the engine detects the device class (memory, GPU, resolution) and picks a baseline set, then adapts at runtime.

the mathematical model
scale = clamp(target_ms / measured_ms, min_scale, 1.0) — smoothed: scale ← lerp(scale, new_scale, 0.05)
Degradation order: resolution first, then LOD distance, then shadows, then effects, then audio quality. Start with what the player notices least.
02 How to build it
  1. Define the target device class by memory, GPU and screen resolution.
  2. Split the quality settings into “visual” (shadows, particles) and “performance” (resolution, LOD distance, light count).
  3. Make the controller work on the p95 frame time with slow adaptation (a few seconds) and hysteresis.
  4. Add smooth transitions: fades between LODs, cross-faded shadows, no jumping resolution.
  5. Allow a manual override: an auto mode plus a few presets (low / medium / high / ultra).
  6. Collect telemetry per device: real profiles beat any assumption.
03 Working code
Python 
class QualityGovernor:
    """Keeps the frame budget by moving the quality levers."""
    def __init__(self, target_ms=16.6, min_scale=0.6):
        self.target = target_ms
        self.min_scale = min_scale
        self.scale = 1.0
        self.lod_bias = 0.0        # +1 = further LODs
        self.shadow_quality = 1.0  # 0..1
        self._ema = target_ms

    def update(self, frame_ms):
        # a smoothed metric: one heavy frame must not drop the quality
        self._ema += (frame_ms - self._ema) * 0.05
        if self._ema > self.target:
            # resolution first (the least noticeable), then everything else
            self.scale = max(self.min_scale, self.scale - 0.02)
            self._ema = self.target  # keep the metric from running away while we adapt
        elif self._ema < self.target * 0.85:
            self.scale = min(1.0, self.scale + 0.01)
        return self.settings()

    def settings(self):
        return {
            "render_scale": round(self.scale, 2),
            "lod_bias": round(self.lod_bias, 2),
            "shadow_quality": round(self.shadow_quality, 2),
        }

# A degradation order that does not break the feel:
# 1) render scale 1.0 -> 0.6 (noticeably softer)
# 2) shadows: number of casters and map resolution
# 3) LOD distance / culling
# 4) particle volume and post effects
# 5) audio quality and voice count
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per frame for the controller
Memory
O(1)
In practice
The rule: degradation must be invisible in motion — otherwise it is worse than a stable low setting.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Changing quality instantly: the switch is visible and the player reads it as a frame-rate drop.
  • Dropping the resolution below 0.6: the blur is worse than missing shadows.
  • Automation without a manual override: every player has their own taste and the auto mode has to yield.
  • Adding a new lever in the middle of the project: testing the matrix of “content × setting” is expensive.
  • Optimising only for the “average” PC: real users are the tail of the devices, not the middle.

Procedural generation PG-01 / 28 · part II intermediate

Gradient noise: value, Perlin and simplex

Gradient noise: value, Perlin, simplex

Noise is a deterministic “random” function of coordinates: the same input always returns the same number, and nearby points return similar values. Perlin and simplex interpolate gradients rather than values, so the result looks organic and shows no square grid.

value noisePerlinsimplexfBm
01 Essence

Value noise throws a random number into each lattice node and interpolates smoothly. It is cheap but gives a “pillowy” look, because every extremum sits on a node. Perlin noise stores a random gradient per node and projects the vector to the sample onto it; the dot product is zero at the nodes, so the field is smooth without a visible lattice. Simplex does the same on simplices (triangles) and costs O(N²) instead of O(2ᴺ) per sample — hence its popularity in 3D and 4D.

A single octave carries one scale of detail. The fractal sum fBm adds octaves with doubled frequency and decaying amplitude: large shapes become continents, small ones become rocks and grass. The amplitude ratio is called gain (usually 0.5), the frequency ratio lacunarity (usually 2.0). Domain warping — feeding noise into the coordinates of another noise — turns soft hills into jagged ridges and swirls.

For GPU noise, seamlessness matters: hash integer coordinates instead of sampling an array, so the texture tiles with the right period. For an infinite world, sample in world units rather than pixels, otherwise the pattern swims when the scale changes. And remember: noise is a field, not randomness; scattering objects needs Poisson sampling, not a noise threshold.

the mathematical model
fBm(p) = Σᵢ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹ gainⁱ · noise(2ⁱ · lacunarity · p + offsetᵢ), Perlin(p) = Σ grad(hash(c)) · fade(p − c)
fade(t) = 6t⁵ − 15t⁴ + 10t³ is the quintic smoothing curve: its first and second derivatives vanish at cell borders, so the grid is invisible. gain controls roughness, lacunarity controls detail density.
02 How to build it
  1. Build an integer hash of (x, y, seed) with a good avalanche — without it you get visible diagonals.
  2. For value noise, take four corner hashes and blend them with the quintic fade.
  3. For Perlin, take eight corner gradients and sum their dot products with the vectors to the sample.
  4. Sum octaves: frequency ×2, amplitude ×0.5, new offset per octave, then normalise by the amplitude sum.
  5. Add domain warping and a ridge function (1 − |n|) for mountains; profile on your target grid size.
03 Working code
Python 
import math

def hash2(x, y, seed):
    h = (x * 374761393 + y * 668265263 + seed * 1442695041) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    h = (h ^ (h >> 13)) * 1274126177 & 0xFFFFFFFF
    return ((h ^ (h >> 16)) & 0xFFFFFFFF) / 0xFFFFFFFF

def fade(t):
    return t * t * t * (t * (t * 6 - 15) + 10)

def value_noise(x, y, seed):
    xi, yi = math.floor(x), math.floor(y)
    xf, yf = x - xi, y - yi
    u, v = fade(xf), fade(yf)
    a = hash2(xi,     yi,     seed)
    b = hash2(xi + 1, yi,     seed)
    c = hash2(xi,     yi + 1, seed)
    d = hash2(xi + 1, yi + 1, seed)
    return (a * (1 - u) + b * u) * (1 - v) + (c * (1 - u) + d * u) * v

def fbm(x, y, seed, octaves=6, gain=0.5, lacunarity=2.0):
    total = norm = 0.0
    amp, freq = 1.0, 1.0
    for i in range(octaves):
        total += amp * value_noise(x * freq, y * freq, seed + i * 1013)
        norm += amp
        amp *= gain
        freq *= lacunarity
    return total / norm          # always in [0, 1]

# h = fbm(wx * 0.008, wy * 0.008, seed=1337, octaves=6)
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(octaves) per sample, 4 hashes per octave
Memory
O(1)
In practice
A 512×512 2D tile with 6 octaves takes milliseconds on the CPU; on the GPU it is a shader over millions of samples.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • A weak hash (e.g. `(x*37+y) % 1000`) produces diagonal bands and repeating islands.
  • Mixing octaves without normalisation pushes values outside [0,1] and breaks sea level.
  • Unfiltered high frequencies shimmer in the distance — use mips/LOD or drop small octaves.
  • One Perlin octave looks like soap: without fBm and domain warping it reads as noise, not landscape.

Worley (cellular) noise: F1, F2 and borders

Worley (cellular) noise: F1, F2 and borders

Scatter feature points across the plane and, for every cell, find the distances to the two nearest ones. F1 gives a rocky texture, F2−F1 gives thin cell borders, and together they produce cracks, scales, foam and Voronoi partitions.

Voronoicellular noiseF2−F1feature points
01 Essence

Cellular noise is not interpolation but nearest-neighbour search. Space is divided into lattice cells, each holding one feature point at a random offset. Finding the nearest point takes only the 3×3 surrounding cells (27 in 3D), because nothing farther can reach. Hence O(1) per sample regardless of world size.

The difference F2 − F1 is zero on the border between two cells and grows towards the centre — a ready-made contour for stone seams, dragon scales or sea foam. F1 gives convex bumps; the distance to the nearest feature centre gives pebbles and spheres. Summing a few octaves of Worley yields convincing rock that never repeats.

The same algorithm is the Voronoi diagram: feature points become region centres. Apply Lloyd relaxation (move each point to the centroid) and the regions even out in area — that is how strategy territories, biomes and honeycombs are generated. For exact region borders you need explicit neighbour traversal; F2−F1 is only an approximation.

the mathematical model
F1(p) = minᵢ |p − cᵢ|, F2(p) = min₂ᵢ |p − cᵢ|, border(p) = F2(p) − F1(p)
cᵢ are the feature points; each lattice cell stores c = cell + hash(cell)·jitter. Voronoi borders are the set of points where F2 = F1.
02 How to build it
  1. Tile the plane; deterministically place one jittered point per cell.
  2. For a sample p, walk the 3×3 neighbouring cells and keep the two smallest distances.
  3. Use F1 for bumps, F2−F1 for cracks and F1·F2 for cells; normalise to your range.
  4. Add octaves: fine Worley for rocks, coarse Worley for continents and regions.
  5. For region maps, keep the feature points — they become capitals, biomes and graph nodes.
03 Working code
Python 
import math

def hash2(x, y, seed):
    h = (x * 374761393 + y * 668265263 + seed * 1442695041) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    h = (h ^ (h >> 13)) * 1274126177 & 0xFFFFFFFF
    return ((h ^ (h >> 16)) & 0xFFFFFFFF) / 0xFFFFFFFF

def feature(cx, cy, seed):
    # keep the point at 0.15..0.85 so cells never collapse
    return (cx + 0.15 + 0.7 * hash2(cx, cy, seed),
            cy + 0.15 + 0.7 * hash2(cx, cy, seed + 7919))

def worley(x, y, seed):
    cx, cy = math.floor(x), math.floor(y)
    f1 = f2 = 1e9
    for oy in (-1, 0, 1):
        for ox in (-1, 0, 1):
            fx, fy = feature(cx + ox, cy + oy, seed)
            d = math.hypot(fx - x, fy - y)
            if d < f1:
                f2, f1 = f1, d
            elif d < f2:
                f2 = d
    return f1, f2

# rock: 1 - F1, cracks: F2 - F1, regions: index of the nearest cell
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per sample (9 or 27 cells)
Memory
O(cells) for region maps
In practice
In 3D that is 27 checks per sample; for large regions store points separately and build Delaunay.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Checking only your own cell: the nearest point almost always lies in a neighbour.
  • Forgetting the jitter and getting a perfect grid instead of organic cells.
  • F2−F1 without normalisation gives near-black borders — use a narrow smoothstep band.
  • For regions, comparing distances is not enough: you need shared borders (half-edge/Delaunay), or the map tears on diagonals.

Poisson disk sampling and blue noise

Poisson disk sampling and blue noise

White noise clumps: two trees can grow on top of each other while a bare patch sits next to them. Poisson disk sampling guarantees a minimum distance r without collapsing into a grid — the best way to scatter grass, rocks, enemies and points of interest.

Bridsonblue noisespatial hashscattering
01 Essence

The goal: pick points so that no two are closer than r and no room is left for another. Brute force is O(N²). Bridson's algorithm keeps an active list and tries k candidates in the annulus [r, 2r] for each; neighbour checks go through a spatial grid with cell size r/√2, which holds at most one point, making the check local.

The result is blue noise: a spectrum with suppressed low frequencies. The eye reads such a distribution as natural, not as rows or clumps. Expected density is about 0.7 of circle packing, roughly one point per 1.4·r² of area — handy for estimating grass per hectare.

For infinite worlds you do not need global Poisson: generate each chunk independently but account for the ring of neighbouring chunks, otherwise borders get duplicates and gaps. Alternatives: jittered grid (fast, visible rows), void-and-cluster and energy relaxation (slow, perfect), progressive Poisson (for streaming).

the mathematical model
|pᵢ − pⱼ| ≥ r, cell = r / √2, E[N] ≈ 0.7 · A / r²
A cell of r/√2 guarantees at most one point per cell (its diagonal is exactly r). The active list makes Bridson O(N) on average; k = 30 is a typical constant.
02 How to build it
  1. Create a grid with cell r/√2; keep an active list and one seed point.
  2. While the list is non-empty: pick a random active point and generate k candidates in [r, 2r].
  3. Reject candidates closer than r to any point in the 3×3 neighbouring cells.
  4. Add the first valid candidate to the grid and the active list; after k failures remove the point from the list.
  5. For chunks, generate with a ring of neighbours and clip to the border; in 3D use cells of r/√3.
03 Working code
Python 
import math, random

def poisson_disk(width, height, r, k=30, rng=random):
    cell = r / math.sqrt(2)
    gw, gh = int(width / cell) + 1, int(height / cell) + 1
    grid = [None] * (gw * gh)
    pts, active = [], []

    def add(x, y):
        grid[int(y / cell) * gw + int(x / cell)] = (x, y)
        pts.append((x, y))
        active.append(len(pts) - 1)

    add(width / 2, height / 2)
    while active:
        idx = rng.randrange(len(active))
        x, y = pts[active[idx]]
        placed = False
        for _ in range(k):
            a = rng.random() * math.tau
            d = r * (1 + rng.random())
            nx, ny = x + math.cos(a) * d, y + math.sin(a) * d
            if not (0 <= nx < width and 0 <= ny < height):
                continue
            gx, gy = int(nx / cell), int(ny / cell)
            ok = True
            for oy in (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2):
                for ox in (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2):
                    cx, cy = gx + ox, gy + oy
                    if not (0 <= cx < gw and 0 <= cy < gh):
                        continue
                    q = grid[cy * gw + cx]
                    if q and (q[0] - nx) ** 2 + (q[1] - ny) ** 2 < r * r:
                        ok = False
            if ok:
                add(nx, ny)
                placed = True
                break
        if not placed:
            active.pop(idx)
    return pts
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(N) average, O(k) candidates per point
Memory
O(N) + grid
In practice
10,000 points take milliseconds on the CPU; on the GPU use progressive Poisson or a blue-noise texture.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Using cell size r instead of r/√2 requires more neighbour checks and easily misses a conflict.
  • Candidates only in [r, 2r]: farther than 2r another active point would already have found the spot.
  • Independent chunk generation without neighbours produces seams and duplicates.
  • Poisson does not respect importance: add density masks for grass and trees (rivers, roads, biomes).

Seeds, hashing and reproducible generation

Seeds, hashing and reproducible generation

Procedural generation must repeat: one seed, one world. That needs a PRNG with explicit state, a hash of coordinates instead of a shared stream, and a fixed iteration order. A mistake here costs more than bad noise, because the world cannot be reloaded.

PRNGPCGcoordinate hashdeterminism
01 Essence

A global `random()` is a shared stream: change the call order and the whole world changes. The reliable pattern is a pure function of coordinates: `hash(seed, chunkX, chunkY, index)`. A hash such as PCG or splitmix64 mixes bits so that neighbouring inputs give completely different outputs (avalanche), and the result does not depend on traversal order.

Seed hierarchy: world → region → chunk → object. A chunk seed is derived from the world seed and the coordinates, not from a counter — then chunk #1000 can be generated without creating the previous 999. Give every subsystem a domain (terrain, loot, names), or editing one system reshuffles all the others.

What breaks determinism: unstable sorting, `dict` iteration before Python 3.7, thread order, differing float precision across platforms, time, and unseeded `random`. The rule: generate data in a fixed order and store only the seed, not the result; for networked games also pin the generator version.

the mathematical model
state ← mix(state + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15); h = xorshift(mul(x ^ (x >> 33), 0xFF51AFD7ED558CCD) ^ seed)
splitmix64/PCG have an avalanche effect: flipping one input bit changes about half the output bits. For coordinates: h = hash(hash(seed) ^ hash(x) ^ hash(y)).
02 How to build it
  1. Keep one 64-bit world seed plus an explicit domain per subsystem.
  2. Implement hash(seed, x, y, i) without global state; test avalanche on neighbouring inputs.
  3. Derive chunk/region seeds from coordinates, never from generation order.
  4. Generate in a fixed order: sort by (y, x), use lists instead of maps, no threads on shared state.
  5. Store the generator version with the save; migrate existing chunks when the algorithm changes.
03 Working code
Python 
MASK = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF

def splitmix64(x):
    x = (x + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & MASK
    z = x
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 30)) * 0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9) & MASK
    z = ((z ^ (z >> 27)) * 0x94D049BB133111EB) & MASK
    return z ^ (z >> 31)

def hash_coords(seed, x, y, domain=0):
    h = seed & MASK
    h = splitmix64(h ^ (x * 0xD6E8FEB86659FD93 & MASK))
    h = splitmix64(h ^ (y * 0xA5A3564E27F8862F & MASK))
    h = splitmix64(h ^ (domain * 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15 & MASK))
    return h

def rng_for(seed, x, y, domain=0):
    state = hash_coords(seed, x, y, domain)
    def nxt():
        nonlocal state
        state = (state + 0x9E3779B97F4A7C15) & MASK
        return splitmix64(state) / 2 ** 64
    return nxt

# r = rng_for(1337, chunk_x, chunk_y, domain=1)   # loot
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per value
Memory
O(1) per chunk
In practice
One hash is nanoseconds; the real task is keeping state out of frames and platforms.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Calling `random.seed()` globally and later depending on call order.
  • Deriving the next object's seed from the previous one: you cannot jump into the middle of the world.
  • Not separating domains — a loot tweak changes the terrain.
  • Trusting float determinism across platforms: networked games need fixed-point and a version tag.

Procedural generation PG-05 / 28 · part II basic

Diamond-square and midpoint displacement

Diamond-square and midpoint displacement

The classic fractal generator: split a square, put the average of its corners plus random displacement in the centre, then split the diamonds again. Cheap, simple and still useful for clouds, islands and heightmaps.

fractalheightmaproughness1/f
01 Essence

Start with a square (ideally 2ⁿ+1) with four known corners. In the diamond step the centre gets the average of the corners plus noise; in the square step edge midpoints get the average of the two corners and the centre. Recursion halves the step until single cells remain.

The noise amplitude is multiplied each level by roughness (usually 0.5–0.7). This yields a 1/f spectrum: large shapes dominate and small ones add detail. At roughness → 1 you get white noise and spikes; at 0.3, nearly smooth hills. The 2ⁿ+1 grid is not pedantry: otherwise levels do not line up.

Main drawbacks: lattice artefacts (visible crosses and repetition), fixed size and no seamlessness. For infinite worlds fBm is better, but diamond-square shines as a quick prototype, for cumulus clouds and for old-school sea-level maps. A wrap-around variant makes the texture tile.

the mathematical model
h(c) = ¼·Σ h(corners) + N(0, σ²), σₖ = σ₀ · roughnessᵏ
σₖ is the amplitude at level k. Expected fractal dimension relates to roughness: at 0.5 the surface is close to Brownian (H ≈ 1).
02 How to build it
  1. Pick a 2ⁿ+1 grid and set the four corners (e.g. zeros for an island).
  2. Diamond: centre of each square = average of corners + random offset σ.
  3. Square: edge midpoints = average of two corners and the centre + offset σ.
  4. Halve the step and multiply the amplitude by roughness; repeat down to 1×1 cells.
  5. Normalise heights, apply a distribution curve and map colours/normals.
03 Working code
Python 
import random

def diamond_square(size=129, roughness=0.55, seed=0, lo=0.0, hi=1.0):
    assert (size - 1) & (size - 2) == 0, "size must be 2^n + 1"
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    h = [[0.0] * size for _ in range(size)]
    h[0][0] = h[0][-1] = h[-1][0] = h[-1][-1] = (lo + hi) / 2
    step, amp = size - 1, (hi - lo)
    while step > 1:
        half = step // 2
        # diamond step
        for y in range(0, size - 1, step):
            for x in range(0, size - 1, step):
                avg = (h[y][x] + h[y][x + step] +
                       h[y + step][x] + h[y + step][x + step]) / 4
                h[y + half][x + half] = avg + (rng.random() * 2 - 1) * amp
        # square step
        for y in range(0, size, half):
            for x in range((y + half) % step, size, step):
                s = n = 0
                for dx, dy in ((half, 0), (-half, 0), (0, half), (0, -half)):
                    xx, yy = x + dx, y + dy
                    if 0 <= xx < size and 0 <= yy < size:
                        s += h[yy][xx]; n += 1
                h[y][x] = s / n + (rng.random() * 2 - 1) * amp
        step = half
        amp *= roughness
    return h
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(n²) per grid
Memory
O(n²)
In practice
A 1025×1025 grid takes milliseconds; use the wrap variant for tiling.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • A size other than 2ⁿ+1 leaves seams and holes between levels.
  • Constant amplitude instead of decay gives white noise that looks like sandpaper.
  • Without wrap mode the texture does not tile and chunk borders show.
  • Diamond-square cannot sample arbitrary coordinates: use fBm/simplex for infinite worlds.

Procedural generation PG-06 / 28 · part II intermediate

Procedural textures (noise, FFT, weathering)

Procedural textures (noise, FFT, weathering)

A procedural texture is a function of coordinates, not a picture. Noise, Voronoi cells and convolutions give you wood, metal and stone; the price is shader compute and the fight against visible tiling.

noiseFourier transformtiling
01 Essence

The basic building blocks: value/Perlin/simplex noise, Voronoi cells (F1/F2 — distances to the nearest points), gradients and waves. Composition is blending through masks: stone = fBm + Voronoi cracks, wood = growth rings from the distance plus fibre noise, metal = an almost uniform albedo plus roughness from noise.

Tiling: periodic noise (sampling modulo the period) gives seamlessness. The advanced version is “tileable” generation via FFT: generate the spectrum, filter it and inverse-transform — the result is periodic by construction. To kill visible repetition, use domain warping, several scales and stochastic tiling (texture bombing).

PBR: albedo, normal, roughness, metallic. Normals can be generated from a height map (Sobel), roughness from noise and dirt masks, AO from height or an SDF. The compute cost in the shader is the problem: 3D noise per pixel is expensive, so textures are usually baked into atlases offline and the runtime only blends layers through masks.

the mathematical model
fBm = Σ gaini·noise(freq·lacunarityi·x), Voronoi: F1 = min|x − pᵢ|
Normal from height: n = normalize(−∂h/∂x, −∂h/∂y, 1). Periodic noise: noise(x mod P, y mod P).
02 How to build it
  1. Define the material: which layers and masks you need (stone, dirt, scratches).
  2. Assemble the procedural primitives and the blending rules.
  3. Make it seamless (periodic noise or FFT).
  4. Generate the PBR channels: normal, roughness, AO from height.
  5. Bake them into textures for the runtime and add variety through parameters.
03 Working code
GLSL 
float hash(vec2 p) {
    return fract(sin(dot(p, vec2(127.1, 311.7))) * 43758.5453);
}

float noise(vec2 p) {              // value noise
    vec2 i = floor(p), f = fract(p);
    f = f * f * (3.0 - 2.0 * f);
    float a = hash(i), b = hash(i + vec2(1, 0));
    float c = hash(i + vec2(0, 1)), d = hash(i + vec2(1, 1));
    return mix(mix(a, b, f.x), mix(c, d, f.x), f.y);
}

float fbm(vec2 p) {
    float sum = 0.0, amp = 0.5;
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) {
        sum += amp * noise(p);
        p *= 2.0; amp *= 0.5;
    }
    return sum;
}

// a periodic variant: take the noise modulo the period
vec3 normalFromHeight(float h, vec2 uv, float strength) {
    float dx = dFdx(h) * strength, dy = dFdy(h) * strength;
    return normalize(vec3(-dx, -dy, 1.0));
}
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(pixels·layers·octaves) in the shader
Memory
O(texture) when baked
In practice
Full-screen 3D noise is expensive — bake offline or compute at a low resolution.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Seamlessness checked “by eye” breaks on large flat surfaces; you need periodic noise or FFT.
  • Too many octaves in the shader costs frames; cap at 4–6 and bake offline.
  • Texture repetition is immediately visible — add domain warping and large-scale masks.
  • A procedural normal without normalisation produces lighting artefacts.

Cellular automata caves

Cellular automata caves

Fill a grid with random noise and apply one rule a few times: a cell becomes a wall if too many neighbours are walls. After 4–6 iterations the TV static turns into connected, organic caves.

cellular automata4-5 ruleconnectivitycaves
01 Essence

The classic 4-5 rule: a cell stays a wall if at least 5 of its 8 neighbours are walls (or exactly 4 with the death variant); otherwise it becomes floor. Start at roughly 45 % wall probability — the percolation threshold, where structure is most interesting. Five iterations usually suffice; ten smooths everything into big halls.

The result almost always needs repair: flood-fill the connected components, keep the largest and fill or tunnel the rest. Always add a wall border, otherwise the map edge opens and generation leaks out. The same automata give water and lava with different rules (4-5 for water produces puddles).

Cellular automata guarantee nothing: no rooms, no rhythm, no guaranteed path. Their strength is speed and organic shapes; their place is cave biomes, caverns and raw levels. For room-based dungeons use BSP, for connected layouts use WFC, and keep automata as a mask for natural halls.

the mathematical model
x′ = wall ⟺ Σ neighbours(wall) ≥ 5 (8-neighbourhood)
Initial density p₀ ≈ 0.45; iterations 4–6. The 4-5 rule allows variants: ≥5 wall, exactly 4 wall, otherwise floor.
02 How to build it
  1. Create a W×H grid and fill walls with probability 0.45 (the border is always wall).
  2. Count the 8 neighbours of every cell, apply the 4-5 rule into a fresh buffer.
  3. Repeat 4–6 times; check that floor coverage is 35–55 %.
  4. Flood-fill the components; keep the largest and fill the rest.
  5. Place entrance/exit on far-apart floor cells, verify an A* path and decorate dead ends.
03 Working code
Python 
import random

def cave(width=64, height=40, fill=0.45, steps=5, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    g = [[1] * width for _ in range(height)]
    for y in range(1, height - 1):
        for x in range(1, width - 1):
            g[y][x] = 1 if rng.random() < fill else 0

    def neighbours(x, y):
        return sum(g[y + dy][x + dx]
                   for dy in (-1, 0, 1) for dx in (-1, 0, 1)
                   if (dx, dy) != (0, 0))

    for _ in range(steps):
        nxt = [row[:] for row in g]
        for y in range(1, height - 1):
            for x in range(1, width - 1):
                n = neighbours(x, y)
                nxt[y][x] = 1 if n >= 5 or (n == 4 and g[y][x]) else 0
        g = nxt
    return g

def largest_component(g):
    h, w = len(g), len(g[0])
    seen, best = set(), []
    for y in range(h):
        for x in range(w):
            if g[y][x] or (x, y) in seen:
                continue
            stack, comp = [(x, y)], []
            seen.add((x, y))
            while stack:
                cx, cy = stack.pop()
                comp.append((cx, cy))
                for dx, dy in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
                    nx, ny = cx + dx, cy + dy
                    if 0 <= nx < w and 0 <= ny < h and not g[ny][nx] \
                            and (nx, ny) not in seen:
                        seen.add((nx, ny))
                        stack.append((nx, ny))
            if len(comp) > len(best):
                best = comp
    return set(best)
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(iterations · W · H)
Memory
O(W · H)
In practice
256×256 over 5 iterations takes milliseconds; on the GPU it is a shader or compute pass.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Too low an initial density shatters the caves; too high leaves rare burrows.
  • No wall border — the map edge opens and connectivity is computed wrongly.
  • Skipping component checks: the player spawns in a 3×3 pocket with no exit.
  • Confusing 4- and 8-neighbourhoods: the 4-5 rule is written for eight neighbours.

BSP dungeons: splits, rooms, corridors

BSP dungeons: splits, rooms, corridors

BSP recursively cuts a rectangle in half until the leaves are small enough, then places a room in every leaf and connects neighbours through the tree with corridors. The result is a guaranteed-connected dungeon with a readable hierarchy.

BSPtreeroomsconnectivity
01 Essence

The tree grows top-down: a node picks an axis (along its longer side), a split point in the 35–65 % range, and produces two children. Stop when a leaf is smaller than 2·minRoom + 1. That margin guarantees room plus a one-cell border, and the tree gives the level macro-structure: big halls high up, small chambers deeper.

Rooms go in the leaves; corridors connect the centres of sibling leaves (or an L-shaped path). Because links follow tree edges, traversal is guaranteed by construction: exactly one path between any two rooms. To avoid a boring level, add 10–20 % extra edges (braiding) — loops, alternative routes and secrets.

BSP scales well: the tree depth can drive room type, and the leaves can be assigned biomes and factions. The downside is right angles and predictability; fix it with uneven walls, doorways, decoration and varied proportions. For meaningful spaces (temple, lab) lay templates over the tree.

the mathematical model
split(node) → node.left, node.right; room ⊆ leaf − margin; corridor = L(center(left), center(right))
Tree depth ≈ log₂(W/minRoom); leaves ≈ 2^depth. Split a leaf w×h while w ≥ 2·minW + 1 or h ≥ 2·minH + 1.
02 How to build it
  1. Set the root rectangle, minRoom and maxDepth; split recursively along the longer side.
  2. Stop when the leaf is smaller than 2·minRoom+1 or the depth limit is reached.
  3. Place a room in every leaf with random margins of at least one cell.
  4. Connect sibling leaves with L-corridors between their room centres (optionally offset).
  5. Add 10–20 % loops, place doors, verify an A* path and assign room types by depth.
03 Working code
Python 
import random

class Node:
    def __init__(self, x, y, w, h):
        self.x, self.y, self.w, self.h = x, y, w, h
        self.left = self.right = None
        self.room = None

def split(node, depth, min_room, rng):
    if depth == 0 or (node.w < 2 * min_room + 1 and node.h < 2 * min_room + 1):
        return
    horizontal = node.w < node.h if node.w != node.h else rng.random() < 0.5
    if horizontal:
        cut = rng.randint(min_room + 1, node.h - min_room - 1)
        node.left = Node(node.x, node.y, node.w, cut)
        node.right = Node(node.x, node.y + cut, node.w, node.h - cut)
    else:
        cut = rng.randint(min_room + 1, node.w - min_room - 1)
        node.left = Node(node.x, node.y, cut, node.h)
        node.right = Node(node.x + cut, node.y, node.w - cut, node.h)
    split(node.left, depth - 1, min_room, rng)
    split(node.right, depth - 1, min_room, rng)

def carve_rooms(node, rng):
    if node.left or node.right:
        if node.left: carve_rooms(node.left, rng)
        if node.right: carve_rooms(node.right, rng)
        return
    w = rng.randint(max(3, node.w // 2), max(3, node.w - 2))
    h = rng.randint(max(3, node.h // 2), max(3, node.h - 2))
    node.room = (node.x + 1, node.y + 1, min(w, node.w - 2), min(h, node.h - 2))

# then: L-corridors between sibling leaf centres, 10-20% extra edges
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(N log N) for rooms
Memory
O(N)
In practice
A 64-leaf tree is built in fractions of a millisecond; validation and decoration dominate.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Splitting without room margin: a 3×3 leaf cannot hold a 3×3 room plus a border.
  • Connecting every room to every other — hierarchy is lost and corridors explode.
  • Forgetting doors: a corridor cuts a room diagonally and breaks navigation.
  • Too deep a tree creates hundreds of tiny rooms — an anthill instead of a dungeon.

Drunkard's walk caves

Drunkard's walk caves

An agent starts in the middle of the map and on every step carves the cell and moves in a random direction. A few thousand steps later you have a winding cave. It is the simplest connected-space generator and the best way to feel what the parameters do.

random walkcarvingdensityprototype
01 Essence

Probabilistic version: with 70 % chance step forward, 20 % turn, 10 % stay. The “stickiness” parameter sets the winding: 0.7 gives long corridors, 0.3 gives lumpy chambers. Several independent agents (3–7) produce a network of connected caves because they all start in the same area.

The main metric is carved fraction. At 30 % you get narrow tunnels, at 50 % a maze, at 60 % big halls with wall islands. Stop on the fraction, not the step count: the same step count gives different density on different maps. Always verify connectivity — several agents can cut off a pocket if they start far apart.

A walk gives no rooms and no rhythm, but fits voxel 3D, “wormholes” and erosion masks perfectly. Practical trick: a coarse walk first, then dilate the channel morphologically and add water. In production it is usually one layer, never the final generator.

the mathematical model
p(step) = [0.7 forward, 0.2 turn, 0.1 stay], stop when carved / (W·H) ≥ target
The target density sets the style: 0.3 tunnels, 0.5 maze, 0.6 halls. Expected walk length grows as O(area / target density).
02 How to build it
  1. Fill the map with walls and put an agent in the centre (or on a random floor cell).
  2. Carve the cell and pick a direction by the probabilities on every step.
  3. Stop at the target floor fraction; keep a step counter for debugging.
  4. Verify connectivity with a flood fill and remove isolated pockets.
  5. Dilate the channel, then place entrance and exit on opposite edges.
03 Working code
Python 
import random

def drunkard(width=64, height=40, target=0.5, stickiness=0.7, seed=0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    g = [[1] * width for _ in range(height)]
    x, y = width // 2, height // 2
    dx, dy = 1, 0
    carved = 0
    goal = int(width * height * target)
    while carved < goal:
        if not g[y][x]:
            carved += 1
        g[y][x] = 0
        if rng.random() < stickiness:
            pass                      # keep direction
        elif rng.random() < 0.5:
            dx, dy = -dy, dx          # turn left
        else:
            dx, dy = dy, -dx          # turn right
        nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy
        if 0 < nx < width - 1 and 0 < ny < height - 1:
            x, y = nx, ny
        else:                         # bounce off the border
            dx, dy = -dx, -dy
    return g

# several agents: all start at the same point and carve into one array
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(steps) ≈ O(W·H / density)
Memory
O(W·H)
In practice
A 128×128 map takes milliseconds; in 3D cost grows cubically, so carve with a capsule.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Stopping on step count: a small map becomes mush, a large one a thin thread.
  • Forgetting the borders — the agent leaves the array and teleports.
  • One agent on a large map yields a single long intestine with no halls.
  • Skipping connectivity checks with multiple starting points.

Maze generation: backtracker, Prim, Kruskal, Wilson

Maze generation: backtracker, Prim, Kruskal, Wilson

A perfect maze is a spanning tree on a grid: exactly one path between any two cells. Different algorithms produce different character — backtracker long corridors, Prim a hedgehog, Kruskal an even texture, Wilson perfect uniformity.

spanning treeDFSPrimKruskal
01 Essence

Grid cells are vertices, neighbours are edges. Backtracker (iterative DFS) dives deep and sweeps long corridors with rare forks — ideal for a Minotaur maze. Prim grows a tree from one cell, picking a random boundary edge, producing many short dead ends. Kruskal shuffles all edges and unions components (DSU), giving a uniform texture. Wilson builds the tree with loop-erased random walks and is uniform over all spanning trees, at a speed cost.

A perfect maze is boring for players: one path means no decisions. So you braid it: remove some walls to create loops and add rooms. A backtracker with 20–30 % braiding is an excellent dungeon base; Prim with braiding suits cave cities.

For on-the-fly generation, cut the maze into chunks, but border edges must agree. Generating the whole level at once is usually simpler: 128×128 is 16k cells, instant for a spanning tree. For 3D voxel mazes the same DFS works over six directions and gives Tron-like puzzles.

the mathematical model
V = w·h, E = 2wh − w − h; perfect maze: |E_tree| = |V| − 1
A tree with V vertices has V−1 edges — exactly enough passages for full connectivity with no cycles. Adding one edge creates exactly one cycle.
02 How to build it
  1. Treat the w×h cell grid as vertices with edges between neighbours.
  2. Pick an algorithm: DFS for long corridors, Prim for forks, Wilson for uniformity.
  3. Build the tree, knocking down walls between connected cells.
  4. Braid: remove 10–30 % of remaining walls to create loops and alternate routes.
  5. Widen corridors to 2–3 cells, place rooms at nodes and verify the entrance-to-exit path.
03 Working code
Python 
import random

def backtracker(w=21, h=21, seed=0, braid=0.0):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    g = [[1] * w for _ in range(h)]          # 1 = wall
    stack = [(1, 1)]
    g[1][1] = 0
    while stack:
        x, y = stack[-1]
        nbrs = [(x + dx, y + dy) for dx, dy in ((2, 0), (-2, 0), (0, 2), (0, -2))
                if 0 <= x + dx < w and 0 <= y + dy < h and g[y + dy][x + dx]]
        if nbrs:
            nx, ny = rng.choice(nbrs)
            g[(y + ny) // 2][(x + nx) // 2] = 0   # knock down the wall
            g[ny][nx] = 0
            stack.append((nx, ny))
        else:
            stack.pop()

    # braiding: remove some walls between two open cells
    for y in range(1, h - 1):
        for x in range(1, w - 1):
            if g[y][x] and rng.random() < braid:
                if (not g[y][x - 1] and not g[y][x + 1] and g[y - 1][x] and g[y + 1][x]) \
                        or (not g[y - 1][x] and not g[y + 1][x] and g[y][x - 1] and g[y][x + 1]):
                    g[y][x] = 0
    return g
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(V + E) for DFS/Prim/Kruskal, O(V²) for Wilson
Memory
O(V)
In practice
A 100×100 grid takes milliseconds; rendering and navigation cost more than generation.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Even sizes: walls and passages do not line up and dangling segments appear.
  • Forgetting braiding — the level has no decisions, only dead ends.
  • Unoptimised Wilson is noticeably slow on large grids: cache walk directions.
  • No validation: a DSU bug in Kruskal easily leaves two disconnected components.

Wave Function Collapse: constraint-based generation

Wave Function Collapse: constraint-based generation

WFC is not drawing but solving a CSP: every cell holds a superposition of allowed tiles, we collapse the lowest-entropy cell and propagate constraints to neighbours. The output is a globally consistent picture built from local rules.

WFCAC-3entropytilesbacktracking
01 Essence

Model: a tile set and an adjacency matrix (who may stand next to whom in each direction). Every cell stores a bitmask of possible tiles. Step: find the cell with minimum entropy (closest to one option), pick a tile by weight, then propagate — erase incompatible values from neighbours and continue the wave until stable.

If a cell mask becomes empty, we have a contradiction. A simple fix is a restart with a new seed (original WFC style); an engineering fix is backtracking with an undo log, like a SAT solver. Large maps are generated in overlapping chunks with agreed borders; for an “infinite” city, add global constraints (highways, rivers) as separate layers.

Rules can be authored by hand (tile set) or extracted from a sample image (overlap mode), which is what made WFC famous. The price is predictability: local rules do not guarantee large shapes, so WFC is usually combined with direction masks, templates and post-processing.

the mathematical model
H(cell) = −Σ pᵢ log pᵢ, choose argmin H, allowed(n) ← allowed(n) ∩ compat(tile, dir)
pᵢ is the weight of tile i in the current mask. Propagation is AC-3: drop values with no support in a neighbour until the queue empties.
02 How to build it
  1. Define weighted tiles and an adjacency matrix — which tiles are allowed left/right/up/down.
  2. Initialise every mask to the full set (or restrict borders and mask regions).
  3. Find the minimum-entropy cell; break ties randomly.
  4. Collapse it by weight, then propagate constraints with a queue until stable.
  5. On contradiction, undo through the log (or restart); post-process and verify traversability.
03 Working code
Python 
import random

# tiles: 0 = floor, 1 = wall.  adjacency[direction][tile] -> set(tile)
# dir: 0=right, 1=down, 2=left, 3=up
def wfc(width, height, adjacency, weights, seed=0, tries=20):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n_tiles = len(weights)
    full = (1 << n_tiles) - 1
    for attempt in range(tries):
        wave = [full] * (width * height)

        def popcount(v):
            return bin(v).count("1")

        def constrain(x, y):
            todo = [(x, y)]
            while todo:
                cx, cy = todo.pop()
                for d, (dx, dy) in enumerate(((1, 0), (0, 1), (-1, 0), (0, -1))):
                    nx, ny = cx + dx, cy + dy
                    if not (0 <= nx < width and 0 <= ny < height):
                        continue
                    allowed = 0
                    m = wave[cy * width + cx]
                    for t in range(n_tiles):
                        if m >> t & 1:
                            for other in adjacency[d][t]:
                                allowed |= 1 << other
                    new = wave[ny * width + nx] & allowed
                    if new != wave[ny * width + nx]:
                        if new == 0:
                            return False          # contradiction
                        wave[ny * width + nx] = new
                        todo.append((nx, ny))
            return True

        ok = True
        while True:
            best, best_h = -1, 1e9
            for i, m in enumerate(wave):
                c = popcount(m)
                if 1 < c < best_h:
                    best, best_h = i, c
            if best < 0:
                break
            m = wave[best]
            choices = [t for t in range(n_tiles) if m >> t & 1]
            total = sum(weights[t] for t in choices)
            r = rng.random() * total
            for t in choices:
                r -= weights[t]
                if r <= 0:
                    wave[best] = 1 << t
                    break
            if not constrain(best % width, best // width):
                ok = False
                break
        if ok:
            return [[(wave[i] & -wave[i]).bit_length() - 1
                     for i in range(y * width, (y + 1) * width)]
                    for y in range(height)]
    raise RuntimeError("WFC failed")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(N · |T|) per propagation, up to O(N²) with backtracking
Memory
O(N · |T|) bitmasks
In practice
32×32 with 20 tiles is milliseconds; 256×256 with backtracking can take seconds — generate in chunks.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Collapsing in scan order instead of by entropy: contradictions become far more common.
  • Ignoring weights — rare tiles vanish or flood the map.
  • No backtracking: one conflict kills the whole generation, especially on big maps.
  • A tile set without global constraints yields a carpet with no plazas or routes — add masks and templates.
