Browsers and mobile networks: WebSocket, WebRTC and radio

Browsers and mobile networks: WebSocket, WebRTC and radio

Browsers have no raw UDP: what remains is WebSocket (TCP), WebRTC data channels (SCTP/DTLS) and WebTransport (HTTP/3). On a phone you also get radio states, network switches and an energy budget — the network becomes probabilistic rather than stable.

WebSocketWebRTCmobilebattery
01 Essence

WebSocket is TCP: fine for lobbies, turn-based games and chat, but head-of-line blocking and growing latency under loss are real. WebRTC data channels offer unreliable, unordered delivery — the closest thing to UDP in a browser; the price is signalling, ICE and complexity. WebTransport brings QUIC and HTTP/3 to the browser, but support and infrastructure are not yet uniform.

A mobile network is not “slow Wi-Fi”. The radio moves between idle and connected states in tens to hundreds of milliseconds, and every packet can keep it awake. Short frequent sends drain the battery; batching, backoff and fewer pings help. Switching Wi-Fi ↔ LTE breaks the connection: you need fast reconnect and session resume.

In practice: keep a small input channel, cap snapshot sizes, pause on `visibilitychange`, treat `navigator.connection` as a hint rather than truth, and survive 2–3 seconds of complete packet loss without kicking the player to the menu. For cloud streaming, the control channel and the video stream are separate: a lost frame must not delay input.

the mathematical model
battery_cost ≈ E_radio · (tail_time · packet_rate), effective_latency = RTT/2 + radio_wakeup + jitter_buffer
The radio tail after a transmission can last seconds. Fewer, larger sends are often cheaper in energy than frequent tiny ones.
02 How to build it
  1. Pick the channel: WebSocket for lobby/chat, WebRTC or WebTransport for real time.
  2. Make the protocol survive 2–3 s of loss: buffering, reconnect and session tokens.
  3. Batch input and state: 20–30 sends per second is usually enough.
  4. Listen to `visibilitychange` and `online/offline`; pause the game instead of dropping the session.
  5. Test on real LTE/3G and in a subway, not only on office Wi-Fi.
03 Working code
Python 
def browser_channel(needs_unreliable, has_webrtc, has_webtransport):
    # The server decides what to offer the client.
    if needs_unreliable and has_webtransport:
        return "webtransport"        # HTTP/3, QUIC streams and datagrams
    if needs_unreliable and has_webrtc:
        return "webrtc-datachannel"  # SCTP/DTLS, maxRetransmits=0
    return "websocket"               # TCP: simple, but HOL-blocking
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per message
Memory
O(buffers) inside the tab
In practice
A tab can be frozen by the browser: never keep critical state only in JS timers.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Using WebSocket for real-time positions and blaming “lag”.
  • Pinging every 100 ms on mobile — the battery dies before the match ends.
  • Dropping the session when Wi-Fi switches to LTE and restarting the match.
  • Relying on background-tab timers: browsers throttle them.

Deterministic lockstep simulation

Deterministic lockstep simulation

An RTS does not transmit the world state, it transmits player commands: every client simulates the same thing and reaches the same result. That demands strict determinism — integer maths and a fixed update order.

fixed-pointdeterminismlockstep
01 Essence

Lockstep: every tick clients send their commands, wait for everyone's commands, and only then compute the next tick. Traffic is minimal (a few kilobytes per match) and a replay is just a command log. The price is that latency equals the slowest player, and any divergence (desync) breaks the match.

Determinism requires: a fixed step (say 20 ticks per second), integer or fixed-point arithmetic (Q16.16), a stable iteration order for containers, the same RNG implementation everywhere (xorshift with a saved state), no dependence on wall-clock time, and no reliance on hash-table ordering. Float arithmetic can produce different bits on different CPUs and compilers — the classic source of desync bugs.

Verification: each client hashes its state (CRC/FNV) every N ticks and compares. On a mismatch, save the state and the replay for analysis. To go faster, shard the simulation and parallelise with a fixed merge order; to smooth it visually, interpolate between ticks and predict your own units.

the mathematical model
xQ16.16 = round(x·216), a·b → (a·b) >> 16, hash = FNV-1a(state)
Tick: 20–30 Hz. Commands are applied at tick T + delay, identically for everyone.
02 How to build it
  1. Fix the tick rate and forbid any dependence of the simulation on real time.
  2. Move the game maths to fixed point or integers; check trigonometry and sqrt separately.
  3. Make the RNG part of the world state and include it in the hash.
  4. Sort every traversal (entities, collisions, timers) by a stable key.
  5. Compare hashes between clients and keep replays for desync debugging.
03 Working code
C# 
// Q16.16 fixed point: determinism matters more than precision
public readonly struct Fix
{
    public const int FRAC = 16;
    public readonly int Raw;
    Fix(int raw) { Raw = raw; }

    public static Fix FromInt(int v) => new(v << FRAC);
    public static Fix operator +(Fix a, Fix b) => new(a.Raw + b.Raw);
    public static Fix operator -(Fix a, Fix b) => new(a.Raw - b.Raw);
    public static Fix operator *(Fix a, Fix b) =>
        new((int)(((long)a.Raw * b.Raw) >> FRAC));   // 64-bit intermediate
    public float ToFloat() => Raw / 65536f;
}

// Deterministic RNG (xorshift32); the state belongs to the world
public struct Rng
{
    public uint State;
    public uint Next() { State ^= State << 13; State ^= State >> 17; State ^= State << 5; return State; }
}
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(#entities) per tick, O(1) per command
Memory
O(world state)
In practice
The simulation must fit into 1/20 s; rendering is interpolated separately.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Float arithmetic and different sin/cos libraries cause desync between platforms.
  • The iteration order of Dictionary/HashSet is not deterministic — sort the keys.
  • One slow player slows everyone down; you need a timeout and a handover to AI control.
  • A replay is a command log plus a simulation version; after a patch old replays no longer reproduce.

Client-side prediction and interpolation

Client-side prediction and interpolation

The network brings latency, so the client shows movement earlier than the server does: it predicts its own actions locally and interpolates everyone else's. Divergence is fixed with a soft correction, not a teleport.

Kalman filterextrapolationrollback
01 Essence

The classic scheme: input → the client applies movement immediately (prediction) → the server recomputes authoritatively → the client compares and corrects. Keep a ring buffer of inputs and states; when a server snapshot arrives, resimulate from the last confirmed tick (rollback). That is how Quake/Source and most shooters work.

Other players are rendered with interpolation and a delay of roughly 100–150 ms: show the past, but smoothly. Extrapolation (continuing the current velocity) helps when packets are lost, but produces “rubber” opponents at sharp direction changes. A Kalman filter gives an optimal estimate of position and velocity given measurement noise: x̂ₖ = x̂ₖ⁻ + K(zₖ − Hx̂ₖ⁻), where K depends on the ratio of process and measurement noise.

Smoothing the error: the position and angle offset decay exponentially (usually over 100–200 ms) rather than snapping. For shooting you need lag compensation — the server rewinds hits to the client's firing moment, otherwise at 80 ms of ping you simply cannot hit moving targets. All of this requires synchronised clocks and a stable tick.

the mathematical model
x̂ₖ = x̂ₖ⁻ + K·(zₖ − H·x̂ₖ⁻), K = P⁻Hᵀ(HP⁻Hᵀ + R)⁻¹
Model: xₖ = F·xₖ₋₁ + w, zₖ = H·xₖ + v. For position+velocity F = [[1, dt], [0, 1]], H = [1, 0].
02 How to build it
  1. Fix the server tick (say 30–60 Hz) and the snapshot protocol.
  2. The client applies its own input immediately and stores (tick, input, state) in a buffer.
  3. On a snapshot, find the confirmed tick, correct the state and resimulate the pending inputs.
  4. Render remote players with a delay and interpolation; enable extrapolation only for packet loss.
  5. Smooth the visual error and disable prediction for teleports and death.
03 Working code
C# 
struct Input { public int tick; public float dt; public Vector2 move; }
struct Snapshot { public int tick; public Vector3 pos; public Vector3 vel; }

class PredictedPlayer
{
    readonly Queue<Input> pending = new();
    Vector3 position, velocity;

    public void OnLocalInput(Input i)      // applied locally, immediately
    {
        pending.Enqueue(i);
        Simulate(ref position, ref velocity, i);
    }

    public void OnServerSnapshot(Snapshot s)
    {
        position = s.pos;                   // authoritative state
        velocity = s.vel;
        foreach (var i in pending)          // resimulate the unconfirmed inputs
            if (i.tick > s.tick) Simulate(ref position, ref velocity, i);
    }

    void Simulate(ref Vector3 p, ref Vector3 v, Input i)
    {
        v += new Vector3(i.move.x, 0, i.move.y) * accel * i.dt;
        v *= Mathf.Pow(damping, i.dt);
        p += v * i.dt;
    }
}
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per tick plus O(buffer) for the resimulation
Memory
O(input buffer)
In practice
A buffer of 1–2 seconds (60–120 ticks) is enough; longer is more expensive and unnecessary.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Teleport corrections kill the feel of control — smooth them and hide small errors.
  • Extrapolation without a time limit produces opponents that slide into walls.
  • Lag compensation without a history check lets players shoot “into the past” through walls — validate the line of fire.
  • For deterministic physics, fix the update order and avoid float instability.

Snapshot compression and delta encoding

Snapshot compression and delta encoding

The network is expensive, so you transmit changes rather than “the whole world”: deltas, quantised values and bit masks. Information theory sets the lower bound and tells you where it is safe to lose precision.

Shannon entropyquantisationdelta
01 Essence

Shannon entropy H(X) = −Σ p(x)·log₂ p(x) is the average number of bits per symbol under optimal coding. If a unit position has 1024 possible values it needs 10 bits, not 32. Quantising position to 1 cm and rotation to 1° saves three to four times the bandwidth with no visible loss.

Delta encoding: send only the fields that changed since the confirmed snapshot, plus a bit mask of the changes. The baseline is the last confirmed snapshot, not the last one you sent — otherwise a lost packet breaks the whole chain. On top of that: change of basis (positions relative to a reference), areas of interest (close objects update more often and more precisely) and packet compression (zstd/lz4).

Budgets: aim for 10–30 KB/s per player in a shooter and 2–5 KB/s in an RTS. Measure not only the average bitrate but the tail (99th percentile) — the tail is what causes lag. Evaluate every field by “bits × change frequency”; in practice 80 % of the traffic is positions and rotations.

the mathematical model
H = −Σ pᵢ·log₂ pᵢ, bits ≈ log₂(range/step)
A position in 0–1024 m with a 0.01 m step needs 17 bits instead of 32. A quaternion: three components at 10–12 bits (smallest-three).
02 How to build it
  1. Inventory the state fields and how often each changes.
  2. Quantise with a tolerance the player cannot notice (scale the scene and the speed).
  3. Build deltas against the confirmed baseline and send a change bit mask.
  4. Prioritise objects by visibility and distance (AOI) and update them at different rates.
  5. Measure the 99th percentile of snapshot size and loss, not just the average.
03 Working code
Python 
import math

def quantize(value, min_v, max_v, bits):
    levels = (1 << bits) - 1
    t = (value - min_v) / (max_v - min_v)
    q = max(0, min(levels, int(round(t * levels))))
    return q

def dequantize(q, min_v, max_v, bits):
    levels = (1 << bits) - 1
    return min_v + (q / levels) * (max_v - min_v)

def delta(baseline, current, mask_fields):
    bits = 0
    changed = []
    for name, mask in mask_fields.items():
        if baseline.get(name) != current.get(name):
            bits += mask
            changed.append(name)
    return changed, bits

def entropy(counts, total):
    return -sum((c/total) * math.log2(c/total) for c in counts if c)
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(#fields) per snapshot, O(n log n) to sort priorities
Memory
O(baseline) + buffer
In practice
Coding is cheap; assembling and sorting the state and testing visibility cost more.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • A delta against the last sent snapshot instead of the last confirmed one breaks when a packet is lost.
  • Coarse quantisation produces camera jitter and jerky interpolation.
  • Without AOI the client receives the whole map — traffic and cheats both grow.
  • Compressing already compressed textures or animations gains little; compress structured state instead.

Rollback netcode: resimulation for fighting games

Rollback netcode: resimulation for fighting games

Rollback does not wait for the opponent: the client applies a predicted input immediately and, when the real one arrives, rewinds a few frames and resimulates. It turns RTT into invisible latency, but demands a cheap simulation and full determinism.

rollbackGGPOpredictiondeterminism
01 Essence

In a fighting game a frame is 16.7 ms and one frame of delay changes combos. Rollback keeps a ring buffer of states (usually 7–8 frames) and saves a snapshot every frame. If the opponent's input is missing, the last known one is reused; when the real one arrives, the state is restored from a snapshot and every frame is resimulated with the correct input.

The cost is CPU: at 100 ms RTT and 60 fps the rollback reaches 6 frames, i.e. up to 6 resimulations per frame. The simulation must therefore be small and side-effect free: no randomness, no allocations inside the frame, no platform-dependent floating-point physics. Input is timestamped, the RNG is seeded, iteration order is deterministic.

Secrets: input delay and rollback are combined (1–2 frames of delay remove part of the rewinds); sound and VFX run outside the simulation; state must be memcpy-able; desync checks hash the state every N frames. Spectators and replays store the input log, not the state — it replays deterministically.

the mathematical model
R = clamp(ceil(RTT / frame_time) + input_delay, 0, R_max), cost ≈ R · sim_step, state_size ≤ a few KB
R is the rollback depth in frames. A higher RTT and a smaller buffer mean more resimulations; R_max is usually 7–10 frames, beyond that raise input delay.
02 How to build it
  1. Make the simulation a pure function: state + input → new state, with no platform floats.
  2. Save a state snapshot into a ring buffer on every frame.
  3. Apply predicted input and remember it; compare with the real one when it arrives.
  4. On mismatch, restore the snapshot and resimulate up to the current frame.
  5. Check desync with a state hash and keep input delay as a safety net on bad networks.
03 Working code
Python 
class Rollback:
    def __init__(self, sim, state, r_max=8):
        self.sim, self.state = sim, state
        self.history = []                 # (frame, state, inputs)
        self.r_max = r_max

    def save(self, frame, inputs):
        self.history.append((frame, self.state.copy(), inputs))
        if len(self.history) > self.r_max:
            self.history.pop(0)

    def advance(self, frame, local, remote):
        self.save(frame, (local, remote))
        self.state = self.sim.step(self.state, local, remote)

    def on_remote_input(self, frame, real_input):
        for i, (f, st, (lo, ro)) in enumerate(self.history):
            if f == frame and ro != real_input:
                self.state = st.copy()    # rollback
                for f2, st2, (lo2, _) in self.history[i:]:
                    self.state = self.sim.step(self.state, lo2, real_input)
                self.history[i] = (f, st, (lo, real_input))
                return True
        return False
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(R · sim_step) per frame
Memory
O(R · state_size)
In practice
R ≤ 8 and state ≤ 4 KB is normal; eight 0.2 ms sim steps fit into a 16 ms frame.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Storing state with pointers or allocations: snapshot and restore break.
  • Floating point and a different iteration order cause desync after a few minutes.
  • A buffer that is too small: at 120 ms RTT the rollback hits the cap and the game teleports.
  • Playing sound and particles inside the simulation: after a rollback they duplicate.

Determinism and serialisation: fixed point, quantisation, bit packing

Determinism and serialisation: fixed point, quantisation, bit packing

Determinism means the same input produces the same state on every machine. It is impossible with raw floats and requires fixed point, stable iteration order and seeded RNG. Serialisation is the other half: send state cheaply without losing meaning.

fixed-pointquantisationbitpackingchecksum
01 Essence

Floats are great for graphics and terrible for simulation: different CPUs, compilers and operation orders give different results. Fixed point Q16.16 or integer millimetres and thousandths of a degree are bit-identical. You also need a deterministic entity order, no hash-map iteration order, an explicit seeded RNG and no standard-library `rand()`.

Quantisation cuts traffic: a position in a 4 km world at 1 cm precision needs 19 bits per axis, an angle 12 bits, health 10 bits. Deltas against the previous snapshot encode only changes; a bit stream packs flags and fields without alignment. Compression (zstd/LZ4) suits large snapshots but not small packets, where overhead eats the gain.

Desync is caught with checksums: CRC32/xxHash of the state every N ticks, compared between server and client. On mismatch you need the input log and the ability to replay the match. Protocol versioning is mandatory: a field inserted in the middle breaks compatibility. And determinism has a price — sometimes sending the state is cheaper than chasing bit-exactness.

the mathematical model
x_q = round(x · 2^Q), error ≤ 2^(−Q−1), bits = ⌈log₂(range / step)⌉, desync = (hash(server) ≠ hash(client))
Q is the number of fractional bits. A 1 cm position in a 4 km world needs 19 bits; preserving meaning matters more than bit-exact graphics.
02 How to build it
  1. Move the simulation to integers/fixed point; remove platform floats and `rand()`.
  2. Fix the entity iteration order and conflict-resolution rules.
  3. Design the schema: mandatory fields, deltas, quantisation, bit flags.
  4. Hash the state and compare server/client every N ticks.
  5. Version the protocol and keep input logs to reproduce desync.
03 Working code
Python 
SCALE = 1 << 16                 # Q16.16

def to_fixed(x):
    return int(round(x * SCALE))

def mul(a, b):
    return (a * b) >> 16            # fixed point without floats

def quantize(value, lo, hi, bits):
    step = (hi - lo) / ((1 << bits) - 1)
    q = int(round((value - lo) / step))
    return max(0, min((1 << bits) - 1, q))

def pack_state(entity):
    # 19 bits per axis, 12 bits angle, 10 bits HP
    x = quantize(entity.x, -2048.0, 2048.0, 19)
    y = quantize(entity.y, -2048.0, 2048.0, 19)
    a = quantize(entity.angle % 360.0, 0.0, 360.0, 12)
    hp = quantize(entity.hp, 0, 1000, 10)
    return (x << 41) | (y << 22) | (a << 10) | hp
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per field, O(n) per snapshot
Memory
O(state) + ring buffer
In practice
Quantisation cuts 50–80 % of traffic; CRC32 over 1 KB of state costs microseconds.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Assuming floats are identical across platforms and builds.
  • Using hash maps with unpredictable iteration order inside the simulation.
  • Quantising too coarsely: the character jitters and cannot fit through doors.
  • Changing the packet format without a version — old clients break silently.

Interpolation, extrapolation and jitter buffers

Interpolation, extrapolation and jitter Buffers

Snapshots arrive unevenly: one after 30 ms, the next after 110. Rendering them directly makes the world stutter. The fix is to render 1–3 ticks in the past and interpolate between known states; extrapolation adds smoothness but lies about the future.

interpolationjitterbuffersnapshots
01 Essence

The client keeps a buffer of snapshots sorted by server time. Rendering happens at now − delay: two snapshots around that point are interpolated for positions, angles (along the shortest arc) and states. A 100–200 ms delay hides jitter but adds latency, so it is made adaptive.

Extrapolation (dead reckoning) continues motion from the last velocity when data has not arrived. It works well for bullets, vehicles and predictable trajectories, but a sharp turn produces rubber-banding and teleports. The rule: extrapolate no longer than 100–250 ms, and when the real snapshot disagrees, correct smoothly rather than snap.

A jitter buffer can be estimated as “2×jitter + 2 ticks” and adjusted from p95 inter-packet intervals. In a low-tick MMO interpolation is mandatory even on a perfect network: 10 Hz means 100 ms between states. Secret: interpolate animation phases too, or feet slide; and flag teleports and respawns so they are not smoothed across half the map.

the mathematical model
t_render = now − delay, α = (t_render − t₀) / (t₁ − t₀), p = lerp(p₀, p₁, α), delay ≈ 2 · jitter + 2 · tick
delay trades smoothness for input latency. For a 60 Hz shooter it is 2–3 ticks; for a 10 Hz MMO, 200–300 ms.
02 How to build it
  1. Receive snapshots with server timestamps and push them into a buffer.
  2. Pick the render point = now − delay and find the two neighbouring snapshots.
  3. Interpolate positions, angles and parameters; flag teleports for instant jumps.
  4. Estimate jitter from p95 and adapt the delay.
  5. Add bounded extrapolation and smooth correction on mismatch.
03 Working code
Python 
import bisect

def sample(buffer, t_render, entity):
    keys = [s.t for s in buffer]
    i = bisect.bisect_right(keys, t_render) - 1
    if i < 0:
        return buffer[0].entities[entity]
    if i >= len(buffer) - 1:
        return buffer[-1].entities[entity]          # extrapolation is separate
    a, b = buffer[i], buffer[i + 1]
    alpha = (t_render - a.t) / max(1e-6, b.t - a.t)
    pa, pb = a.entities[entity], b.entities[entity]
    return (
        pa.x + (pb.x - pa.x) * alpha,
        pa.y + (pb.y - pa.y) * alpha,
        pa.angle + shortest_arc(pb.angle - pa.angle) * alpha,
    )
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(log n) buffer lookup, O(1) per entity
Memory
O(buffer · entities)
In practice
8–16 buffered snapshots are plenty; interpolating 1000 entities costs fractions of a millisecond.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Showing the latest snapshot immediately — the world jerks on every packet.
  • A buffer that is too large: smooth, but controls lag by half a second.
  • Extrapolating forever: when the player stops, they slide through walls.
  • Interpolating angles with a plain linear formula — the character spins through 360°.

Lag compensation: rewind and hit validation

Lag compensation: rewind and hit validation

Players aim at what they see, and they see the past by RTT/2 plus interpolation. Lag compensation rewinds server hitboxes to the moment of the shot, validates the hit and restores the state. Without it “headshot” becomes “miss”.

rewindhitscanlatencyanti-cheat
01 Essence

The server keeps a position history (usually 0.5–1 s) for all entities. On a fire command it restores hitboxes to t = now − (RTT/2 + interp_delay), traces the ray and applies damage. The rewind depth is capped at 200–300 ms: more becomes shooting through walls.

The trade-off: “favor the shooter” gives fair hits to the attacker, but the victim can take damage after reaching cover. “Favor the defender” breaks the shooter's feel. Most competitive shooters choose the former and cap the rewind; projectiles need no rewind at all — the server simulates the bullet and decides where it lands.

Secrets: rewind hitboxes only, never the whole physics world; store history compactly (position + pose + flags); validate that the shot was possible (ammo, cooldown, rate of fire); log “shot behind wall” cases when tuning; and do not rewind more than a frame or two for high-precision AWP-like mechanics.

the mathematical model
t_rewind = t_now − (RTT/2 + interp_delay), clamp(t_rewind, now − 0.3 s, now), hit = ray(origin, dir) ∩ hitboxes(t_rewind)
RTT/2 is the trip to the server; interp_delay is the client's render delay. A 300 ms cap prevents shooting too far into the past.
02 How to build it
  1. Store position and pose history with server timestamps for 0.5–1 s.
  2. Accept a shot with its client timestamp and clamp the rewind window.
  3. Restore hitboxes at that time and test the ray/sphere.
  4. Validate the shot: weapon, ammo, cooldown, line of sight.
  5. Log discrepancies (a hit on a target already behind cover) and tune the window.
03 Working code
Python 
def rewind_hit(history, shooter_time, origin, direction, max_ms=300):
    t = max(shooter_time, history[-1].t - max_ms / 1000.0)
    snapshot = history.closest(t)                # nearest frame at or before t
    for box in snapshot.hitboxes:
        if ray_hits_box(origin, direction, box):
            return box.owner                    # hit registered
    return None

def validate_shot(server, player, shot):
    if shot.client_time > server.time + 0.05:
        return "future timestamp"
    if player.ammo <= 0 or server.time < player.next_shot_at:
        return "rate limit"
    if not server.visible(player, shot.origin):
        return "origin mismatch"
    return None
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(log h + k) per shot
Memory
O(history · entities)
In practice
One second of history at 60 Hz is 60 snapshots; store only what hitboxes need.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Rewinding half a second or more: victims take damage behind cover.
  • Rewinding all physics and other players — double hits and desync.
  • Not limiting fire rate: the client “fires” a whole burst in one frame.
  • Forgetting client interpolation and rewinding only RTT/2 — a systematic miss.

Interest management: AOI, grids and relevance

Interest management: AOI, grids and relevance

An MMO cannot send every player to everyone: 5,000 players × 1,000 entities is millions of updates. Interest management decides what a player actually sees and what matters, and replicates only that. AOI is the main secret of MMO scale.

AOIspatial hashrelevanceMMO
01 Essence

The simplest AOI is a radius: the client receives entities within r (say 100–200 m) plus “important” objects (quest givers, friends, vehicles). A spatial index (grid, quadtree, octree, BVH) answers “who is nearby” in O(log n + k) instead of O(n). Radii differ by type: players 150 m, NPCs 80 m, projectiles 40 m.

A radius alone is not enough: importance depends on view angle, distance, entity type, state (idle/moving), friendship and quests. Relevance score = w₁·proximity + w₂·facing + w₃·type + w₄·recent events. The per-client budget is finite (say 8 KB/s), so when it overflows the least important data is dropped, not random data.

MMO secrets: hysteresis (enter at 150 m, leave at 165 m) so entities do not flicker at the border; dormancy for far NPCs; updates grouped by zone; state handed to neighbours when crossing a zone boundary. And always: the client must never receive positions it should not see, otherwise a wallhack is trivial.

the mathematical model
N_relevant ≈ ρ · π r², traffic ≈ N_relevant · S · tick, score = w₁·(1 − d/r) + w₂·facing + w₃·type + w₄·events
ρ is entity density and S the snapshot size per entity. Doubling the radius quadruples traffic, so the radius follows the budget.
02 How to build it
  1. Build a spatial index (grid/quadtree) and update it on movement.
  2. Define radii and importance weights per entity type.
  3. Compute relevance and fit it into the client's bit budget.
  4. Add hysteresis and dormancy to remove flicker and idle ticks.
  5. Hide out-of-AOI entities at the protocol level, not only in rendering.
03 Working code
Python 
def visible_entities(grid, player, radius=120.0, budget=400):
    candidates = grid.query_circle(player.x, player.y, radius)
    scored = []
    for e in candidates:
        d = dist(player, e)
        score = (1.0 - d / radius) * 2.0
        score += 1.0 if e.kind in ("quest", "party", "vehicle") else 0.0
        score += 0.5 if player.facing(e) else 0.0
        scored.append((score, e))
    scored.sort(reverse=True)
    return [e for _, e in scored[:budget]]      # a budget, not everything
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(log n + k) per query
Memory
O(n) index + O(k) per client
In practice
10,000 entities and 2,000 players is a normal zone scale; a 32–64 m grid keeps k in the dozens.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Replicating every player in the zone and hoping compression saves you — traffic grows quadratically.
  • Hard enter/leave without hysteresis — entities flicker at the border.
  • Sending hidden entities “just in case” — a ready-made wallhack.
  • One radius for everything: projectiles, NPCs and players have different value.

Clock and tick synchronisation: offsets, ticks and timelines

Clock and tick synchronisation: offsets, ticks and timelines

The network has no shared “now”: every client has its own clock and jitter. The server defines the tick and timeline, clients estimate offset and RTT, and the simulation runs on server time — otherwise prediction, rewind and interpolation fall apart.

clocktickNTPtimeline
01 Essence

The classic estimate (as in NTP/Cristian): the client sends t0, the server replies with t1 (receive) and t2 (send), the client records t3. Then RTT = (t3 − t0) − (t2 − t1) and offset = ((t1 − t0) + (t2 − t3)) / 2. A single sample is noisy: take the minimum RTT of a series and the median offset, then slew the clock instead of jumping.

Game time is best counted in ticks: the server tick is an integer and the client knows which tick a snapshot belongs to. Separately there is frame time (rendering) and input time (when the player pressed). All three must be distinguished: binding input to a server tick is the basis of fair rewind.

Secrets: use monotonic clocks (`performance.now`), never the system clock; do not trust client timestamps without bounds; an offset can jump when the network changes — smooth it; fix a match epoch so replays and logs line up. In distributed MMOs server clocks are synchronised with NTP/PTP, otherwise events cannot be ordered causally in logs.

the mathematical model
RTT = (t₃ − t₀) − (t₂ − t₁), offset = ((t₁ − t₀) + (t₂ − t₃)) / 2, server_tick = round((client_now + offset) · tick_hz)
t0 is the client send, t1/t2 the server receive/reply, t3 the client receive. The minimum RTT gives the best offset estimate.
02 How to build it
  1. Measure time with monotonic clocks and send a ping with t0 and the server's t1/t2.
  2. Compute RTT and offset; reject outliers, use the median and the minimum RTT.
  3. Slew the offset smoothly instead of jumping.
  4. Bind player input to a server tick and keep the match timeline.
  5. Synchronise servers with NTP/PTP and log drift.
03 Working code
Python 
class ClockSync:
    def __init__(self):
        self.samples = []          # (rtt, offset)
        self.offset = 0.0

    def add(self, t0, t1, t2, t3):
        rtt = (t3 - t0) - (t2 - t1)
        offset = ((t1 - t0) + (t2 - t3)) / 2
        self.samples.append((rtt, offset))
        if len(self.samples) > 30:
            self.samples.pop(0)
        best = min(self.samples, key=lambda s: s[0])
        target = best[1]
        self.offset += (target - self.offset) * 0.05   # smooth slew
        return rtt, self.offset
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per sample
Memory
O(1) per connection + sample history
In practice
20–30 samples at match start are enough; after that, rare keepalives and adaptive correction.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Using `Date.now()`: clock changes and NTP jumps break the timeline.
  • Averaging all offsets — outliers ruin the estimate.
  • Changing the offset abruptly: the world teleports and interpolation breaks.
  • Mixing frame time, server tick and input time — rewind and prediction lie.

Bandwidth budget: prioritisation, deltas and quantisation

Bandwidth budget: prioritisation, deltas and quantisation

Every player has a budget: 5–10 KB/s in a shooter, 1–3 KB/s in an MMO — headers included. Inside that budget you must fit what matters: nearby, threatening, recently changed. Bandwidth is a resource just like frame time.

bandwidthprioritydeltaquantisation
01 Essence

Count the budget downwards: a 100 Mbit/s server for 200 players is 62 KB/s each, minus headers and service traffic; the real game budget will be 10–20 KB/s. Inside it, priorities rule: events (shot, death, loot) always go out; state goes by relevance and freshness; cosmetics (emotes, skins) go last.

Delta encoding: keep the last acknowledged snapshot per client and send only changes. Quantisation: 19 bits for a position, 12 for an angle, 10 for health. Flags become a bitmask, arrays get a length prefix. Do not compress small packets with a general compressor: overhead and latency eat the gain; LZ4/zstd make sense for big snapshots.

The algorithm: collect candidates with priorities, sort, send until the budget is exhausted, carry the rest to the next tick. Add aging: if an entity has not been updated for too long, its priority grows, otherwise a distant but important object freezes. And always measure real on-the-wire bytes, not in-memory structs.

the mathematical model
budget = rate · tick, send while Σ size_i ≤ budget, priority = relevance · freshness + aging
rate is the target bitrate per client and tick the snapshot period. Deltas and quantisation cut size_i several-fold.
02 How to build it
  1. Derive the per-client bitrate from server bandwidth and reserve room for headers.
  2. Split traffic into events (reliable) and state (budgeted).
  3. Compute priority from relevance, freshness and aging.
  4. Encode deltas against the acknowledged snapshot and quantise fields.
  5. Log real bytes per second and budget hits; tune against p95.
03 Working code
Python 
def build_snapshot(entities, last_ack, budget_bytes=400):
    items = []
    for e in entities:
        delta = e.delta_from(last_ack.get(e.id))
        prio = e.relevance * (1.5 if delta else 0.5) + e.aging
        items.append((prio, delta.size, e.id, delta))
    items.sort(reverse=True)
    out, used = [], 0
    for prio, size, eid, delta in items:
        if used + size > budget_bytes:
            continue
        out.append((eid, delta))
        used += size
    return out, used
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(n log n) sorting, O(n) packing
Memory
O(n) per client
In practice
8 KB/s at 20 Hz is 400 bytes per snapshot: enough for 10–20 entities with deltas.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Counting the budget without UDP/IP headers and service traffic — the wire shows more.
  • Sending everything “just in case” and hoping compression saves you.
  • Forgetting aging: a distant important entity stops updating and freezes.
  • Compressing every tiny packet — latency and overhead exceed the savings.

Sharding, zones and seamless worlds

Sharding, zones and seamless worlds

One process cannot hold a million players. The world is cut into zones, instances and shards, each with its own simulation process and budget; seamlessness is an illusion maintained by state transfer, neighbour caches and prefetching at the border.

shardingzoneshandoffMMO
01 Essence

Sharding comes in flavours: by region (US/EU/Asia), by zone (forest, city, dungeon), by instance (raid, PvP match), by population layer for overflow. Each shard is a process/container with a hard entity limit; gateways hold connections while the world lives in separate services. A typical zone holds 500–3,000 players, a raid instance 10–40.

Seamlessness: as a player approaches a border they are “handed over” to the neighbouring zone. Input is frozen, a snapshot is transferred, ownership changes and input resumes; meanwhile the next zone renders from cache. A slow handoff is felt as a hitch. The secret is subscribing to neighbouring entities early (prefetch) and keeping borders “thick”: AOI must cross them rather than stop.

Shared objects are a separate problem: auction house, chat, guilds, mail. They cannot be sharded per zone or you get inconsistent copies, so they become dedicated services with their own databases and caches, called with idempotent APIs. Balance zones with consistent hashing over zone_id and virtual nodes so a crashed process only loses its own zones, not the world.

the mathematical model
shards = ⌈CCU / capacity⌉, handoff_time = freeze + state_transfer + resume, load(shard) = Σ entities · tick_cost + network
capacity is how many players a process holds at the target tick. handoff_time must fit into 100–300 ms, or players feel a hitch.
02 How to build it
  1. Cut the world into zones/instances and fix a capacity per process.
  2. Separate gateways (connections) from simulation and shared services.
  3. Implement ownership transfer: freeze, snapshot, transfer, resume.
  4. Prefetch neighbouring zones and cache across the border.
  5. Balance zones with consistent hashing and monitor overload.
03 Working code
Python 
import hashlib

def shard_for(zone_id, shards):
    # consistent hashing: a failed node only moves its own share
    ring = sorted((hashlib.md5(f"{s}".encode()).hexdigest(), s) for s in shards)
    h = hashlib.md5(str(zone_id).encode()).hexdigest()
    for point, shard in ring:
        if h <= point:
            return shard
    return ring[0][1]

def handoff(player, from_zone, to_zone, snapshot):
    player.freeze()                 # input is not applied
    to_zone.adopt(player, snapshot) # ownership and state
    from_zone.release(player)
    player.resume()                 # the client receives a new tick
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per handoff, O(log n) to pick a shard
Memory
O(zone) state + caches
In practice
A zone with 2,000 players and 20,000 entities is a typical limit for one game process.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • One process for the whole world and hoping vertical scaling saves you.
  • Thin zone borders: AOI stops abruptly and players see a wall of fog.
  • Shared services (auction, chat) in every zone — desync and duplication.
  • A slow handoff: players freeze at the border and lose control.

Sessions, lobbies, matchmaking and reconnect

Sessions, lobbies, matchmaking and reconnect

A match is not just a server, it is state: who is in it, on which ticket, in which region, and what happens when someone disconnects. A session service survives game-process restarts: it issues tickets, builds lobbies, matches players and returns them to the fight after a drop.

sessionmatchmakinglobbyreconnect
01 Essence

Separate the roles: the gateway holds the WebSocket/UDP connection, the session service stores the session (player, match, token, region, rights), the matchmaker builds lobbies, the game server simulates. Clients never talk to the matchmaker directly — they get a ticket and wait for an event. This lets services restart without losing players.

Matchmaking is multi-criteria: MMR/rank, party size, region, latency, queue time, backfill after a leaver. Hard filters (region/ping) apply immediately, soft filters (rank) relax over time as the ticket ages. Otherwise top players wait for hours.

Reconnect: the player has a session token and a match slot for 60–120 s; the server keeps their entity “on leave” rather than deleting it. On return the client receives a full snapshot and continues from the current tick. Secrets: prevent ghosting (two clients on one session), make login idempotent, run regional queues and make backfill fair so a newcomer is not fed to a stacked team.

the mathematical model
wait ≈ queue_len / match_rate, quality = f(ΔMMR, Δping, party), ticket_age → relax(ΔMMR) and relax(Δping)
The matchmaker trades quality against time. Relaxing filters as tickets age is the main way to avoid endless queues.
02 How to build it
  1. Create a session service: token, region, match, rights, lifetime.
  2. Separate gateway from game server; clients talk only to the gateway.
  3. Design the matchmaking ticket: hard and soft filters, aging.
  4. Implement a reconnect slot (60–120 s) and a full snapshot on return.
  5. Log wait times, match quality and ticket cancellation reasons.
03 Working code
Python 
import time

def try_match(ticket, pool, now):
    ticket.age = now - ticket.created
    mmr_window = 50 + ticket.age * 25          # soft filter relaxes
    for other in pool:
        if other.player == ticket.player:
            continue
        if abs(other.mmr - ticket.mmr) > mmr_window:
            continue
        if abs(other.ping - ticket.ping) > 80:  # hard region/ping filter
            continue
        return (ticket, other)
    return None

def reconnect(session, slot_ttl=90):
    if session.left_at and time.time() - session.left_at > slot_ttl:
        return "slot expired"
    return {"tick": session.match.tick, "snapshot": session.match.snapshot(session.player)}
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(log n) queue search
Memory
O(players) + queue
In practice
Peak online means tens of thousands of tickets; the matchmaker must scale horizontally and stay stateless.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Keeping the match only in game-process memory: a crash loses everything.
  • Matchmaking without aging — top players wait forever.
  • Deleting the player entity immediately on disconnect — reconnect becomes impossible.
  • Allowing two clients on one session — ghosting and cheating.

MMO persistence: databases, caches, transactions and event sourcing

MMO persistence: databases, caches, transactions and event sourcing

In an MMO items and gold are money, and money cannot be lost when a process crashes. Persistence is transactions, idempotency and ordering: who owns the record, what is the source of truth, and how to survive a restart without dupes or vanished bags.

databaseredistransactionsevent sourcing
01 Essence

The classic setup: a relational database (PostgreSQL/MySQL) for inventory, characters and the auction house; Redis for hot data and locks; the game process keeps dirty objects in memory and flushes in batches. The danger is the flush moment: if the process dies between debiting gold and granting a sword, one player loses. The fix is a database transaction, not two independent UPDATEs.

For distributed operations use a saga/outbox: write the event into an outbox in the same transaction, apply it asynchronously, and make retries safe with an idempotency key. Event sourcing stores an event log and derives state as a fold, which enables rollback, auditing and recovery. The cost is volume and schema evolution.

Secrets: shard by player_id, not by guild; cache with TTL and version; locks need timeouts and fencing tokens; never trust “I had that item” from a client; the auction house and mail are separate services with their own transactions; backups and restore drills are part of gameplay, not just DevOps. And remember: item duplication is almost always born from retries without idempotency.

the mathematical model
state = fold(events), write_conflict = version mismatch, retries → idempotency_key → exactly-once effect
Record versions (optimistic locking) prevent lost updates; an idempotency key turns a retry into a no-op.
02 How to build it
  1. Separate hot state (memory/Redis) from cold state (DB) and define ownership.
  2. Make operations transactional: debit and grant in one transaction.
  3. For cross-service operations use outbox/saga and idempotency keys.
  4. Shard by player_id and add versioning and locks with fencing tokens.
  5. Regularly test restore from backup and event replay.
03 Working code
Python 
def transfer_item(conn, from_id, to_id, item_id, idem_key):
    with conn.transaction():
        seen = conn.execute(
            "SELECT 1 FROM idempotency WHERE key = %s", (idem_key,)).fetchone()
        if seen:
            return "already applied"          # retry is safe
        cur = conn.execute(
            "UPDATE items SET owner = %s WHERE id = %s AND owner = %s",
            (to_id, item_id, from_id))
        if cur.rowcount != 1:
            raise ValueError("item not owned by sender")
        conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO idempotency(key, applied_at) VALUES (%s, now())", (idem_key,))
    return "ok"
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per operation, O(log n) per index
Memory
O(players) per shard + cache
In practice
Thousands of writes per second per shard is normal; p99 commit time matters more than average TPS.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Two independent UPDATEs without a transaction: gold debited, item never granted.
  • Retries without an idempotency key — duplicated items and currency.
  • The cache as the source of truth without invalidation — desync and phantom bags.
  • Locks without timeout/fencing tokens — permanent deadlocks after a crash.

Anti-cheat: statistical anomaly detection

Anti-cheat: statistical anomaly detection

Anti-cheat is a layered system: an authoritative server, statistical anomaly detection, client-side checks and a ban economy. Z-score catches outliers, but you must be careful with false positives.

z-scoreanomaliestrust
01 Essence

Basic hygiene first: the server never trusts the client for position, damage or resources. The client sends input, the server sends the result. For particularly sensitive data, run the fog of war on the server: the client never receives enemy positions it cannot see. That removes a whole class of wallhacks without any statistics at all.

Statistics: for every player, track metrics such as headshot ratio, reaction time, accuracy at long range, and the distribution of aim angles. The z-score z = (x − μ)/σ shows how far a metric has drifted from the population. But among millions of players you will find dozens of honest outliers, so use robust estimators (median/MAD), combinations of metrics and Bayesian priors rather than a single threshold.

Detection without a reaction is worthless: review replays of suspicious matches, shadow ban suspects into a separate pool, ban in waves, and provide appeals. Client-side anti-cheats (signatures, memory integrity) raise the price of cheating but give no guarantees; kernel-level solutions are a privacy question of their own. The success metric is not “we caught everyone” but “playing honestly is comfortable”.

the mathematical model
z = (x − μ)/σ, robust: z′ = 0.6745·(x − median)/MAD
MAD = median(|x − median(x)|). |z′| > 3.5 is the classic outlier criterion for normal data.
02 How to build it
  1. Close the basic holes: server authority, input validation, server-side fog of war.
  2. Collect telemetry: hits, latencies, angles, movement, economy — tagged per match.
  3. Build robust distributions per skill bucket rather than over the whole base.
  4. Fuse signals and send only the top percentiles to manual or ML review.
  5. Act in waves, keep evidence, offer appeals, and never reveal the thresholds.
03 Working code
Python 
import statistics as st

def robust_z(x, population):
    med = st.median(population)
    mad = st.median([abs(v - med) for v in population]) or 1e-9
    return 0.6745 * (x - med) / mad

def suspicious(player, population):
    signals = {
        "headshot_rate": robust_z(player["hs"], population["hs"]),
        "snap_angle":    robust_z(player["snap"], population["snap"]),
        "reaction_ms":  -robust_z(player["react"], population["react"]),
    }
    # require agreement between several signals, not a single outlier
    votes = sum(1 for v in signals.values() if v > 3.5)
    return votes >= 2, signals
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per metric, O(n) to recompute statistics
Memory
O(#players·#metrics)
In practice
Threshold checks run in real time; distribution recomputation is offline, roughly daily.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • One z-score threshold over the whole population produces a wave of false bans among strong players.
  • Cheats adapt: the detector has to be updated and the thresholds kept secret.
  • Kernel anti-cheats clash with privacy and with Linux/Steam Deck — take platforms into account.
  • Public bans without evidence destroy trust; shadow bans and waves are better.

Security: DDoS, rate limits, auth and encryption

Security: DDoS, rate limits, auth and encryption

A network service lives on the internet, so it will be attacked, flooded and reverse-engineered. Defence is layered: anycast and scrubbing for volumetric attacks, limits and queues for L7, tokens and TLS against spoofing, and server-side validation against cheating input.

DDoSrate limitauthencryption
01 Essence

DDoS comes in three flavours: volumetric (L3/L4, gigabits), protocol (SYN/QUIC floods) and application (L7, expensive requests). Infrastructure: anycast, CDN/scrubbing centres, per-IP/account limits, proof-of-work under suspicion, login queues. Game servers must not expose their real IPs: clients connect to an edge proxy that holds the session.

Authentication: short-lived tokens bound to an account/device, TLS/DTLS for transport, nonce/sequence against replay. Never trust the client: validate speed, cooldowns, distance, line of sight and item ownership. Encryption does not stop cheats, but it protects against MITM and simplifies trust.

Rate limiting: token buckets per account/IP/connection, separate limits for expensive operations (chat, auction, crafting), backoff and ban waves. Secrets: log rejection metrics but store no unnecessary personal data; keep secrets in a KMS, not the repository; validate match tickets on the server (a client cannot “join” someone else's match); and during an attack degrade features rather than lose every player.

the mathematical model
allowed(t) = min(cap, tokens + rate·t), request_cost ≤ tokens, valid = signature ∧ freshness ∧ ownership ∧ cooldown
A token bucket caps the average rate while allowing bursts; server-side validation is the last line of defence against cheating input.
02 How to build it
  1. Hide game servers behind an edge proxy; enable anycast/scrubbing.
  2. Issue short-lived session tokens bound to the account.
  3. Rate-limit per IP/account/operation and protect expensive endpoints.
  4. Validate everything on the server: movement, damage, economy, ownership.
  5. Monitor anomalies and rehearse a degradation plan for launch peaks.
03 Working code
Python 
import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate=20, cap=60):
        self.rate, self.cap = rate, cap
        self.tokens, self.last = cap, time.monotonic()

    def allow(self, cost=1):
        now = time.monotonic()
        self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens < cost:
            return False
        self.tokens -= cost
        return True

def validate_intent(player, intent, now):
    if intent.ts > now + 0.05 or intent.ts < now - 0.5:
        return "stale timestamp"
    if not player.owns(intent.item):
        return "not owned"
    if player.cooldown(intent.skill) > now:
        return "cooldown"
    return None
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per token check
Memory
O(1) per connection + counters
In practice
Signature and limit checks take microseconds; the bottleneck is attack bandwidth and scrubbing cost.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Exposing game-server IPs — an attack finds the target directly.
  • Trusting client-side speed/damage checks — the first cheat breaks the economy.
  • One global rate limit: a legitimate spike blocks everyone.
  • Logging tokens and personal data in plain text.

Operations: metrics, SLOs, traces and live ops

Operations: metrics, SLOs, traces and live ops

Networks break in the tails, not the averages: p99 RTT, 2 % loss on one route, a login queue at peak. Operations means a dashboard, SLOs and controlled degradation instead of “fix it after release”.

observabilitySLOmetricslive-ops
01 Essence

Metrics: RTT p50/p95/p99 per region, loss, reorder, jitter, server tick time, snapshot size, queue depth, CCU, auth errors, matchmaking time. Metrics without region/version/platform breakdowns are useless: a 40 ms average RTT can hide a region at 200 ms.

An SLO defines the error budget: for example 99 % of matches with p95 RTT < 80 ms and 99.9 % successful logins. Alerts fire on burn rate, not on a single spike. Traces link a match, a session and database queries by one id; logs are structured and sampled so you do not drown.

Live ops: feature flags, canary releases, content and balance rollbacks without a patch, regional switches, degradation (disable cosmetics/voice, lower the tick), status communication. Load bots must play like humans: move, shoot, join matches; synthetic metrics without behaviour miss the bottlenecks. After an incident, run a blameless postmortem with concrete actions.

the mathematical model
error_budget = 1 − SLO, burn_rate = observed_error / allowed_error, p99 ≠ 3·p50 (heavy tail)
An SLO is a contract with players. Burn-rate alerts catch sustained degradation instead of a random spike.
02 How to build it
  1. Define 5–7 key SLIs: latency, loss, login success, tick time, matchmaking.
  2. Break metrics down by region, platform, version and network type.
  3. Alert on burn rate and build dashboards for the on-call engineer.
  4. Add feature flags, canary releases and a degradation plan.
  5. Run load bots and postmortems regularly.
03 Working code
Python 
import statistics

def slo_report(samples, slo=0.99, target_ms=80):
    lat = sorted(samples)
    p95 = lat[int(len(lat) * 0.95)]
    good = sum(1 for x in lat if x <= target_ms) / len(lat)
    budget = 1.0 - slo
    burn = (1.0 - good) / budget if budget else 0.0
    return {"p95_ms": p95, "good": good, "burn_rate": burn,
            "alert": burn > 2.0}          # 2× is sustained degradation
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per metric write
Memory
O(series × retention)
In practice
Metric cardinality is the main enemy: never put player_id into labels.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Looking only at averages: the p99 tail is the player experience.
  • Metrics without region/platform breakdowns hide entire outages.
  • Alerting on everything: on-call stops reacting.
  • Load bots that stand still: they never find the bottlenecks.

Network testing: netem, chaos and load bots

Network testing: netem, chaos and load bots

Netcode cannot be tested on localhost. You need controlled delay, jitter, loss, reorder and duplicates — as on real networks; deterministic replays to reproduce bugs; bots that behave like humans; and chaos tests that break services on purpose.

netemchaosload testreplay
01 Essence

Linux `tc netem` supports delay, jitter, loss, duplicate, reorder, corrupt and rate; Windows/macOS have equivalents (clumsy, Network Link Conditioner). Inside the engine it helps to have your own deterministic network simulator: delay packets by N ticks, drop by probability, reorder — reproducibly, so a bug repeats in CI. Profiles: 3G (200 ms RTT, 2 % loss), bad Wi-Fi (50 ms jitter), intercontinental (150 ms RTT).

Replays: recorded inputs + seed + version = a reproducible match. That is how you debug desync, rollback and lag compensation without live players. Chaos tests: kill the game process, drop Redis, add 500 ms to the database, cut the connection at a zone border — and verify the player returns and the economy stays intact.

Load bots must imitate behaviour: movement, shooting, purchases, chat, reconnects; otherwise TPS looks great while p99 dies on live players. Secrets: test in production at night with a small percentage, use shadow traffic, compare metrics before/after a release, keep test regions with real RTT, and always test mobile networks — a browser emulator will not show you radio behaviour.

the mathematical model
coverage = delay × jitter × loss × reorder × duplicates, replay = (inputs, seed, version), bot_fidelity = actions / second × state coverage
The condition matrix matters more than one “bad” profile. Without a replay a network bug cannot be reproduced; without bots it cannot be found.
02 How to build it
  1. Add a deterministic network simulator to the engine (delay/jitter/loss/reorder).
  2. Define real-network profiles: 3G, bad Wi-Fi, intercontinental, mobile.
  3. Record input replays and run them in CI on every build.
  4. Deploy load bots with behaviour and reconnects.
  5. Run chaos tests and a postmortem for every failure found.
03 Working code
Python 
import random, heapq

class NetSim:
    def __init__(self, delay=0.1, jitter=0.02, loss=0.02, seed=1):
        self.delay, self.jitter, self.loss = delay, jitter, loss
        self.rng, self.q, self.now = random.Random(seed), [], 0.0

    def send(self, payload):
        if self.rng.random() < self.loss:
            return                      # dropped
        d = max(0.0, self.delay + self.rng.uniform(-1, 1) * self.jitter)
        heapq.heappush(self.q, (self.now + d, payload))

    def tick(self, dt):
        self.now += dt
        out = []
        while self.q and self.q[0][0] <= self.now:
            out.append(heapq.heappop(self.q)[1])
        return out                      # reorder possible with different d
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per packet in the simulator
Memory
O(simulator buffer + replays)
In practice
An in-engine simulator is cheaper and more reproducible than external netem; netem is for testing the real stack.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Testing only on localhost and perfect Wi-Fi.
  • Manual network checks without profiles and without reproducible replays.
  • Bots that do not move or shoot: the load does not resemble live traffic.
  • Chaos tests without guardrails: they take production down for everyone.

Balance and progression BAL-01 / 24 · part IV basic

Armour and the damage mitigation curve

Armour and the damage mitigation curve

Mitigation is a function, not a flat subtraction. Linear, multiplicative and logarithmic forms feel completely different in the early and late game, and the curve — not the armour number — decides where the game breaks.

armourmitigationtime-to-killcurve
01 Essence

Three classic shapes. Linear (damage − armour) nullifies every weapon below a threshold and collapses the late game: once damage overtakes armour, defence disappears. Multiplicative (damage · 100/(100 + armour) — the Warcraft III and Dota scheme) approaches zero asymptotically and never grants immunity: read 100/(100+armour) as the share of damage that gets through, not as a subtraction. Logarithmic (damage · (1 − k·ln(1 + armour))) plateaus quickly and always needs a hand-written cap.

The main metric is not the mitigation percentage but effective health: EHP = HP / (1 − mitigation). With the multiplicative scheme EHP grows linearly with armour: +100 armour always adds +100 % of base HP, which makes balancing easy because every point of armour keeps a constant value. With the logarithmic scheme each further point gives less, and players feel cheated when the numbers in the UI grow but survivability does not.

In practice, keep mitigation in the 0–75 % band and add a flat armour layer only for weak hits (minions, damage over time). Always show the player the resulting percentage, not the raw armour number: the interface is part of the balance. And balance at the edges of the range — the weakest and the strongest build — not on the average one.

the mathematical model
D = A · 100 / (100 + R) ⇒ EHP = HP · (100 + R) / 100
A — incoming damage, R — armour, D — damage that lands. With this form every 100 armour adds exactly +100 % of base health, so the price in EHP is linear. Logarithmic variant: D = A · (1 − k·ln(1 + R/R₀)).
02 How to build it
  1. Set a base TTK for an unarmoured character: that is the reference point.
  2. Pick the mitigation form and compute EHP at 5–6 control points of armour.
  3. Plot “armour → EHP” and “armour → mitigation %”: the second curve is what players see, the first is what you feel.
  4. Cap the maximum mitigation (usually 60–80 %) and add a separate armour-penetration layer.
  5. Recompute every weapon's damage through the target archetype's EHP rather than in absolute numbers.
03 Working code
Python 
def mitigation(armour, model="multiplicative", k=0.06, cap=0.8):
    if model == "linear":                 # flat subtraction: breaks late game
        return min(armour, 1.0)
    if model == "multiplicative":         # WC3 / Dota style: never reaches 100%
        return armour / (100.0 + armour)
    if model == "logarithmic":            # fast plateau, needs a cap
        return min(cap, k * __import__("math").log(1 + armour / 10.0))
    raise ValueError(model)

def damage_after(attack, armour, hp, **kw):
    m = mitigation(armour, **kw)
    dealt = attack * (1 - m)
    return dealt, hp * (1 + armour / 100.0)      # (damage, effective HP)

# breakpoints every designer should print once:
for a in (0, 25, 50, 100, 200, 400):
    d, ehp = damage_after(100, a, 1000)
    print(f"armour {a:>3}: {d:6.1f} dmg, EHP {ehp:7.0f}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per hit
Memory
O(1)
In practice
The numbers matter, not the code: any of the three forms is one line, and all the work is in the balance sheet.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Linear armour subtraction: one weapon becomes useless and another becomes omnipotent.
  • Adding mitigation percentages together: two 40 % sources give 64 %, not 80 % — only the share that gets through multiplies.
  • Showing raw armour without the resulting percentage — the most common “the numbers don't work” complaint.
  • Forgetting damage over time and weak hits: under a percentage scheme they become pointless and need their own layer.

The damage formula: additive and multiplicative layers

The damage formula: additive and multiplicative layers

Damage is assembled from layers: base, flat additions, percentage multipliers and final effects. The order and grouping of those layers decide whether one synergy explodes the build or everything stays predictable.

damage formulamodifiersbucketsstacking
01 Essence

The standard production scheme is D = (base + flat) · Π(1 + bucketᵢ) · Π(1 + crit) · (1 − mitigation). The keyword is bucket: modifiers add up inside a group and multiply between groups. So “+10 % damage” from three sources gives +30 % in one bucket and +33.1 % in three different ones. That distinction is exactly what creates “unexpected” builds.

If everything is additive, the late game degenerates into one best stat; if everything multiplies, explosions appear (ten sources of +20 % give ×6.2). A workable compromise: flat additions and the main stat are additive, rare “exclusive” bonuses are multiplicative, and the number of multiplicative sources is hard-capped.

Order matters: crit lands after armour and after flat additions; elemental amplification applies before mitigation; “damage dealt” and “damage taken by the target” are different multipliers. Write the order down once and implement it in a single function. As soon as the formula is smeared over ten places, balance stops being reproducible.

the mathematical model
D = (B + Σflat) · Π(1 + sᵢ) · Π(1 + mⱼ) · (1 − r) · crit
B — base weapon or skill damage, flat — flat additions, sᵢ — additive percentages within a bucket, mⱼ — exclusive multipliers (cap their count), r — target mitigation.
02 How to build it
  1. List every damage source in one table: base, flat, bucket percentages, exclusive multipliers, crit.
  2. Write a single calculation function and forbid any other place where damage is modified.
  3. Build a spreadsheet “build calculator” with three reference builds per level: weak, average, broken.
  4. Cap the number of exclusive multipliers (usually 2–3) and check the upper bound at +50 % level.
  5. Log each layer's contribution during combat — those numbers are what patches are made from.
03 Working code
Python 
def damage(base, flat=(), additive=(), exclusive=(), crit=1.0, mitigation=0.0):
    """One place for the whole formula: base → flat → buckets → exclusive → crit → armour."""
    value = base + sum(flat)
    bucket = 1.0 + sum(additive)          # +10% and +15% in one bucket = +25%
    for s in exclusive:                   # rare, capped in count
        bucket *= (1.0 + s)
    value *= bucket
    value *= crit                          # after armour in most games
    return value * (1.0 - mitigation)

print(damage(100, flat=[12], additive=[0.10, 0.15], exclusive=[0.2], crit=2.0, mitigation=0.25))
# 112 · (1.25 · 1.2) · 2.0 · 0.75 = 252.0
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(k) in the number of modifiers
Memory
O(k)
In practice
Keep modifiers in an array and multiply in one pass: it simplifies both debugging and logging.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Adding percentages from different systems together: “+20 % damage” and “+20 % attack” are not the same thing.
  • Crit applied before flat additions gives a different curve — fix the order and never change it between patches.
  • No upper bound on damage: the “everything into one multiplier” build breaks bosses and PvP.
  • A formula smeared across the codebase turns a rebalance into weeks of work instead of an hour.

03
Balance and progression BAL-03 / 24 · part IV basic

Effective HP, TTK and shots-to-kill

Effective HP, TTK and shots-to-kill

Players do not feel percentages — they feel shots and seconds. STK (shots-to-kill) and TTK translate abstract stats into the feel of combat tempo, and they should be the unit of balance.

EHPTTKSTKbreakpoints
01 Essence

TTK (time to kill) is the time from the first hit to death; STK is how many hits it takes. STK is discrete and therefore more important: the difference between 3 and 4 shots is huge, between 3.1 and 3.4 invisible. Balance by thresholds: a weapon must kill a specific target in a specific number of hits, and only then do you round the damage.

The link to defence: TTK = EHP / DPS. If damage and health both grow linearly, TTK stays healthy while the growing numbers deliver the feeling of power. If health outgrows damage, the late game turns into sponges; if it lags behind, into one-shots. A useful trick: fix the TTK at levels 1, 10, 30 and 60, then bend the curves to hit those four points.

In PvP, TTK is also a reaction budget: 0.15–0.3 s is a duel on reflexes (shooters), 1–3 s is tactics and positioning (MMOs, MOBAs), 5–15 s is a fight over resources (bosses, tanks). Changing TTK changes the genre more than any new mechanic.

the mathematical model
TTK = EHP / DPS, STK = ceil(EHP / (D · hit_rate))
EHP = HP / (1 − mitigation); DPS = damage · rate · hit share. Compute TTK at 3–4 campaign levels and at the edges of the build range, never on the average.
02 How to build it
  1. Set the target TTK for your genre and for the weak / average / strong player rotation.
  2. Fold health and defence into a single EHP number per class and level.
  3. Compute STK for every weapon against every class — that is a matrix, not a list.
  4. Check the thresholds: “one extra shot” must never be a random side effect of fractions.
  5. Recompute after every damage change: the TTK table should refresh automatically.
03 Working code
Python 
import math

def ehp(hp, mitigation=0.0, shield=0.0):
    return (hp + shield) / (1.0 - mitigation)

def ttk(target_hp, mitigation, dps, hit_rate=1.0):
    return ehp(target_hp, mitigation) / (dps * hit_rate)

def stk(target_hp, mitigation, damage, hit_rate=1.0):
    return math.ceil(ehp(target_hp, mitigation) / (damage * hit_rate))

for hp, mit in ((100, 0.0), (100, 0.3), (250, 0.45)):      # three archetypes
    print(f"hp {hp} mit {mit:.0%}: ttk {ttk(hp, mit, 80):.2f}s, "
          f"stk {stk(hp, mit, 34)}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(#weapons × #targets)
Memory
O(1)
In practice
An STK matrix for 8 weapons and 5 classes takes a minute in a spreadsheet and catches 90 % of balance errors.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Balancing percentages without checking STK — then “+5 % damage” silently changes the shot count.
  • The same TTK everywhere: PvP and raid content must differ by a factor, not by a few percent.
  • Ignoring hit rate: for a weapon with spread, hit rate matters more than raw damage.
  • Health growing faster than damage in the late game — the classic “sponge”.

Balance and progression BAL-04 / 24 · part IV intermediate

Damage variance, hit chance and dispersion

Damage variance, hit chance and dispersion

Randomness makes combat alive, and the same randomness makes balance unfair. Damage spread, hit chance and miss streaks are about managing variance, not about “a bit of random”.

varianceRNGhit chanceexpected value
01 Essence

A damage spread (say 80–120 %) preserves the mean and adds drama, but it multiplies the number of “unfair” outcomes. Count not the mean but the probability of killing in N hits: with a wide spread and low HP it can differ several-fold for the same build. A narrow spread (±5 %) gives predictability, a wide one (±30 %) gives excitement; competitive modes usually remove it.

Hit chance is a separate axis. The classic “roll to hit, then roll damage” scheme (D&D, XCOM) creates misses the player remembers for a long time, which is why modern games replace a miss with dispersion (spray, cone) — the player sees the cause. If a chance stays, show it and keep it in the 60–95 % band: 50 % feels like a coin flip and destroys tactics.

Streak variance: even an honest 30 % chance produces runs of 8 misses with noticeable frequency. For comfort, use pity / PRD, a free first hit, guaranteed crits after a run of misses, or deterministic damage. The rule: randomness belongs in outcomes, not in the ability to play.

the mathematical model
E[D] = p · d̄, Var[D] = p·(1−p)·d̄² + p·σ²d, P(streak of k misses) = (1−p)ᵏ
p — hit chance, d̄ — average damage, σ²d — damage variance. At p = 0.7 nine misses in a row happen in 0.002 % of attacks — which still happens daily across 10 000 players.
02 How to build it
  1. Decide what exactly is random: hit, damage, crit or AI behaviour — and do not mix everything at once.
  2. Set target means and acceptable spread; compute P(kill in N) at the edges of the build range.
  3. Remove randomness from threshold mechanics: if 4 hits must kill, they must kill.
  4. Add streak protection (PRD, guarantee after k misses) if fairness complaints appear.
  5. Log outcome distributions in playtests, not just averages.
03 Working code
Python 
import random

def roll_damage(rng, base=100, spread=0.2, crit_p=0.25, crit_mult=2.0):
    d = base * rng.uniform(1 - spread, 1 + spread)
    return d * (crit_mult if rng.random() < crit_p else 1.0)

def p_kill_within(rng, hits, hp, **kw):
    return sum(1 for _ in range(100_000)
               if sum(roll_damage(rng, **kw) for _ in range(hits)) >= hp) / 100_000

rng = random.Random(7)
print("P(kill in 3) =", p_kill_within(rng, 3, 300))   # the tail matters, not the mean
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per roll
Memory
O(1)
In practice
A Monte Carlo run of 10⁵ fights takes a second and reveals tails invisible in the mean.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Checking only average damage: the tails of the distribution are the feeling of unfairness.
  • Randomness punishing skill (a miss on perfect play) — the main source of frustration.
  • Damage variance applied before armour and crit gives unexpectedly wide tails.
  • No pity in rare-trigger mechanics: streaks read as a bug.

Balance and progression BAL-05 / 24 · part IV intermediate

Damage over time: stacks, refresh and ticks

Damage over time: stacks, refresh and ticks

Damage over time is not “damage stretched across seconds” but a separate economy: how many effects are active at once, how they refresh and what happens when the same effect is applied twice.

DoTstackingtick rateuptime
01 Essence

Four stacking policies: refresh (resets the duration, damage does not add), stack (independent instances), extend (adds time to the remaining duration) and replace (overwrites with the strongest). The choice affects both DPS and server load: 40 independent stacks on 20 targets is 800 timers per tick.

Ticks are discrete, so real DPS depends on phase: a 10 s effect ticking every 2 s gives 5 ticks, but one applied mid-window gives 5 one time and 4 the next. Round durations to a multiple of the tick or accrue continuously. For interruptible DoTs, account for uptime — the fraction of time the effect is actually active, not its theoretical DPS.

For the player a DoT is a promise of future damage, so it must be visible and predictable: a timer, ticking numbers, a sound. Otherwise it feels like “damage out of nowhere” and in PvP reads as cheating. Decide separately whether DoTs from different sources stack and whether the effect ends when its caster dies.

the mathematical model
DPS_DoT = Σᵢ (dᵢ · ticksᵢ / durationᵢ) · uptime, ticks = floor(duration / tick)
dᵢ — damage of one tick of effect i. With n identical stacks DPS grows linearly, but the simulation load does too: cap the maximum stacks and the length of the effect list.
02 How to build it
  1. Choose a stacking policy per effect type and write it into the design document.
  2. Tie ticks to the shared game tick instead of a timer per effect.
  3. Compute real tick counts for typical durations: 6 s at a 1 s tick — 5 or 6 ticks?
  4. Cap the maximum stacks and total DoT per target, or an “all DoT” rotation breaks bosses.
  5. Show the timer and the DoT contribution in the combat log: the player must see where the damage comes from.
03 Working code
Python 
class Dot:
    def __init__(self, dmg, duration, tick=1.0, policy="refresh", max_stacks=3):
        self.dmg, self.duration, self.tick = dmg, duration, tick
        self.policy, self.max_stacks = policy, max_stacks
        self.stacks, self.left, self.acc = 0, 0.0, 0.0

    def apply(self):
        if self.policy == "stack":
            self.stacks = min(self.max_stacks, self.stacks + 1)
        elif self.policy == "refresh":
            self.stacks = 1
        elif self.policy == "extend":
            self.left += self.duration
        self.left = max(self.left, self.duration) if self.policy != "extend" else self.left
        self.stacks = max(self.stacks, 1)

    def advance(self, dt):
        if self.left <= 0:
            return 0.0
        self.left -= dt
        self.acc += dt
        dealt = 0.0
        while self.acc >= self.tick:
            self.acc -= self.tick
            dealt += self.dmg * self.stacks        # one tick per stack
        return dealt
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(#effects) per tick
Memory
O(#effects per target)
In practice
Thousands of targets with a dozen effects need a flat array and a single pass, not a list of objects with callbacks.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • A timer per effect instead of a shared tick: the server drowns on mass AoE.
  • Rounding durations up without accounting for the tick: one extra tick is 20 % more DPS.
  • Invisible DoT in PvP — the player dies “by themselves” and calls it a bug.
  • Unlimited stacking: one rotation out-damages the entire arsenal.

Balance and progression BAL-06 / 24 · part IV intermediate

Shields, absorption and regeneration

Shields, absorption and regeneration

A shield is a buffer that changes not only survivability but tempo: it lets you wait out damage, devalues small hits and breaks the balance when its regeneration is free.

shieldabsorbregeneffective HP
01 Essence

A shield as a separate pool (Halo, Destiny) regenerates after a pause and turns combat into a rhythm of “hide, recover”. A shield as instant absorption (WoW, LoL) is an active resource with a cooldown, valued for timing. A shield as percentage reduction is already armour, and mixing the three is a bad idea: the player cannot tell what actually saved them.

Regeneration is the main source of endless fights. If a shield recovers faster than the opponent deals damage, the fight never ends. Make regeneration slower than the opponent's DPS in an average fight and add reset conditions: damage interrupts regen, out of combat it speeds up.

Also design the order: shield before or after armour? Usually a shield absorbs already-mitigated damage, otherwise it becomes super-valuable on tanks. And mind the UI: two bars are harder to read than one, so sometimes showing the total is better.

the mathematical model
EHP = (HP + Σshield) / (1 − mitigation), growth = d(shield)/dt − incoming DPS
While regen < incoming DPS the shield is a one-off buffer; once regen exceeds DPS the fight becomes unwinnable-by-either-side. That single line is all the check you need.
02 How to build it
  1. Decide whether the shield is a pool, a cooldown absorption or a percentage: do not mix.
  2. Set the delay and regeneration rate and compare them with typical enemy DPS.
  3. Fix the order: mitigation → shield or shield → mitigation.
  4. Add a counter-mechanic: shield damage, penetration, a “break” effect when overloaded.
  5. Test the mirror match: two identical builds must not end in a draw.
03 Working code
Python 
class Health:
    def __init__(self, hp, shield=0.0, regen=0.0, delay=4.0, mitigation=0.0):
        self.hp, self.max_hp = hp, hp
        self.shield, self.max_shield = shield, shield
        self.regen, self.delay, self.idle = regen, delay, 0.0
        self.mitigation = mitigation

    def take(self, dmg):
        dmg *= (1.0 - self.mitigation)
        absorbed = min(self.shield, dmg)
        self.shield -= absorbed
        self.hp -= (dmg - absorbed)
        self.idle = 0.0                       # damage interrupts regeneration
        return absorbed, dmg - absorbed

    def tick(self, dt):
        self.idle += dt
        if self.idle >= self.delay:           # regen faster than incoming DPS = stalemate
            self.shield = min(self.max_shield, self.shield + self.regen * dt)
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per hit
Memory
O(1) per unit
In practice
Networked shields must replicate separately from HP: the player has to see the shield actually absorb.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Shield regeneration without a delay: the player simply waits and wins.
  • A shield computed before armour — a hidden survivability multiplier for tanks.
  • Two bars in the UI with no explanation: players confuse shield and health.
  • A shield that no counter-mechanic can break devalues all other damage.
