Balance and progression BAL-07 / 24 · part IV intermediate

Crowd control and diminishing returns

Crowd control and diminishing returns

Stun, slow and fear are the strongest effects in a game because they take away not health but the ability to play. So they are balanced by duration, categories and diminishing returns rather than by damage.

CCdiminishing returnsimmunityPvP
01 Essence

The basic PvP rule: a second CC of the same type is shorter, a third shorter still, a fourth is immunity. Multipliers like 1 / 0.5 / 0.25 / 0 give a predictable curve and prevent perma-stunning. Group effects by category (hard control, fear, slow, silence), because the player perceives “stun + root” as one long stun.

CC duration is a budget, not a number: 8 seconds of stun is death in a MOBA and an ordinary mechanic in an MMO. Measure the share of time the target cannot act (CC uptime): above 30–40 % the fight stops being a game. Compute the worst case separately — a chain of three players with control.

PvE usually needs the opposite: bosses must resist control or the mechanic becomes “hold and hit”. The answer is immunity to hard control, vulnerability to positional effects (slow, knockback), and phases where control is allowed.

the mathematical model
T_eff = T_base · DR(n), DR = [1, 0.5, 0.25, 0, ...], CC_uptime = ΣT_eff / T_fight
n — index of a CC of the same type on that target within a window (usually 15–20 s). Keep PvP CC uptime below 35 % even in the worst case.
02 How to build it
  1. Sort every effect into categories and decide which count as “the same”.
  2. Set the DR reset window (usually 15–20 s) and the multiplier table.
  3. Cap hard-control duration in PvP and add a “trinket” / reduction.
  4. For PvE make bosses immune to hard control but vulnerable to positional effects.
  5. Test the “three players in a row” chain — that is the worst case, not the average.
03 Working code
Python 
DR_TABLE = (1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.0)      # 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th CC of the same kind

class CcTracker:
    def __init__(self, window=18.0):
        self.window = window
        self.last = {}                  # category -> (time, count)

    def duration(self, category, base, now):
        t, n = self.last.get(category, (-1e9, 0))
        if now - t > self.window:
            n = 0
        n = min(n + 1, len(DR_TABLE))
        self.last[category] = (now, n)
        return base * DR_TABLE[n - 1]

cc = CcTracker()
for i in range(4):
    print("stun", i + 1, "->", cc.duration("stun", 4.0, now=i * 5.0), "s")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per effect
Memory
O(#categories) per target
In practice
Keep DR counters on the server: client-side computation is the first thing people exploit.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Different categories counted separately while the player experiences them as one long stun.
  • No DR reset over time: the target stays controlled for the whole fight.
  • DR computed on the client: desync and an exploit in one bottle.
  • Hard control in PvE without immunities: the boss becomes a training dummy.

Balance and progression BAL-08 / 24 · part IV advanced

Survivability budget: stacking mitigation and caps

Survivability budget: stacking mitigation and caps

Defensive bonuses from different sources combine in different ways, and that is exactly what decides whether a tank becomes immortal. A survivability budget is the engineering way to keep total damage reduction in a corridor.

stackingdiminishing returnscapsbudget
01 Essence

If two 40 % reductions multiply as shares of damage that gets through, the total is 64 %; if they add, 70–80 %. The first is safer, but it also breaks with a dozen sources: 10 × 10 % = 65 %, 20 × 5 % = 64 %. The rule: always multiply the shares that get through and show the player the total, not the individual bonuses.

A hard cap (for example “no more than 70 % total reduction”) is crude but honest. A soft cap (beyond 50 % every further percent costs twice as much) preserves progress but needs explaining. A third route is diminishing returns on the stat: R_eff = R · k/(k + R), where each point of armour is still useful but never infinitely so.

Do not forget indirect survivability: dodge, parry, block, healing, absorption are all multipliers too. Fold them into a single figure — “average incoming damage over 10 seconds of combat” — and balance that, not the individual stats.

the mathematical model
D = A · Π(1 − mᵢ), R_eff = R · k / (k + R), survivability = EHP · Σ(1/(1 − mᵢ))
mᵢ — independent reduction sources. Multiplying the shares that get through is the only scheme that never yields negative damage or immortality.
02 How to build it
  1. List every defensive source and convert it to “share of damage that gets through”.
  2. Multiply those shares for the worst-case build and check the total stays above 0.25.
  3. Introduce a hard or soft cap and make sure the player can see it in the UI.
  4. Add a counter layer: penetration, elemental damage, “true” damage.
  5. Recompute the budget after every new item or talent — that is where it breaks most often.
03 Working code
Python 
from functools import reduce

def incoming(attack, mitigations):
    through = reduce(lambda acc, m: acc * (1.0 - m), mitigations, 1.0)
    return attack * through, through

def soft_cap(value, k=50.0):
    """Diminishing returns that never reach a hard ceiling."""
    return value * k / (k + value)

builds = {
    "glass cannon": [0.00],
    "bruiser":      [0.20, 0.15],
    "tank":         [0.40, 0.25, 0.10],
    "stacked tank": [0.40, 0.25, 0.10, 0.10, 0.10, 0.05],
}
for name, m in builds.items():
    dmg, through = incoming(1000, m)
    print(f"{name:13s} through {through:5.0%}  ->  {dmg:6.0f} dmg")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(#sources)
Memory
O(#sources)
In practice
The worst build matters more than the average one: it is what players find on day one.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Adding reduction percentages until damage goes negative or immunity appears.
  • A cap the player cannot see: they buy an item that does nothing.
  • Forgetting dodge and healing — they belong to the same budget.
  • Balancing the average build when only the maximum one breaks.

Balance and progression BAL-09 / 24 · part IV basic

The XP curve and the cost of a level

The XP curve and the cost of a level

Experience is the currency of time. The curve sets how many minutes a player pays for the next level, and it alone decides whether progression feels like growth or like a wall.

XPcurvelevel capexponent
01 Essence

Three base shapes. Linear (XP = k·n) gives an even tempo but levels stop feeling meaningful. Quadratic (XP = k·n²) is the RPG classic: total XP to level N grows as N³, so every next level costs longer, but not explosively. Exponential (XP = k·rⁿ, r ≈ 1.1–1.5) suits games with endless growth and a soft cap: every level multiplies the time, and sooner or later the player hits a natural ceiling.

Count not experience but time: XP curve · XP earn rate = minutes per level. If the earn rate grows together with the curve, the player never notices the ramp; if it does not, a wall appears around level 20. A good rule: time per level grows by 3–8 % per level up to the cap and no more.

Design the soft cap separately: after the maximum level XP turns into mastery points or currency. That keeps play meaningful without devaluing content. And mind perception: the bar must move even when the level is far away, otherwise the player feels stuck.

the mathematical model
XP(n) = a · n^b, Total(N) = Σ XP(n) ≈ a·N^(b+1)/(b+1), T(n) = XP(n) / rate(n)
b = 1 is linear, b = 2 quadratic (the classic), b > 2 a hard wall. Compare T(n) at levels 1, 10, 30 and 60: the ratio should not differ by more than 3–5×.
02 How to build it
  1. Set the target time to the maximum level (say 40–60 hours for an RPG).
  2. Pick the exponent b and fit a so the total matches the target time.
  3. Compute time per level including the growth of XP income; plot T(n).
  4. Add a soft cap: after the maximum — mastery points, not emptiness.
  5. Check the curve on a “slow” player: they must not stall in the middle.
03 Working code
Python 
def xp_to_next(level, a=100, b=2.0):
    return int(a * (level ** b))

def total_xp(level, a=100, b=2.0):
    return sum(xp_to_next(n, a, b) for n in range(1, level))

def time_per_level(level, xp_per_min, a=100, b=2.0):
    return xp_to_next(level, a, b) / xp_per_min

# b = 1.8 keeps the curve steep but not a wall; b = 2.5 is a classic wall
for level in (1, 10, 30, 60):
    print(f"L{level:02d}: {xp_to_next(level):>9,} xp  "
          f"({time_per_level(level, 900):5.1f} min at 900 xp/min)")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per level
Memory
O(1)
In practice
Recomputing the whole table is one loop; keep it in data, not in code.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • An exponential without a cap: at level 50 the player sees a level once a week.
  • The curve ignores the growth of XP income, so the real tempo drifts.
  • A maximum level with no “after”: the player loses the goal and leaves.
  • Fixed quest XP with rising level costs makes old quests worthless.

Balance and progression BAL-10 / 24 · part IV intermediate

Stat growth: linear, geometric and soft caps

Stat growth: linear, geometric and soft caps

How strength, health and damage grow with level is a question about shape, not numbers. The shape decides whether +10 levels feels like +10 levels and whether high-level content breaks.

stat growthpower curvescalingcaps
01 Essence

Linear growth (strength = 10 + 2·level) is predictable and convenient for PvP: the gap between levels is constant. Geometric growth (strength = 10 · 1.08^level) delivers a feeling of power but requires content to grow the same way — otherwise old enemies become dust and new ones a wall. The hybrid: linear growth for the main stat, weaker geometric growth for secondary ones.

Soft caps on a stat (diminishing returns) let the player keep investing with decreasing returns. R_eff = R·k/(k+R) is nice because it never produces “extra” points yet never nullifies investment either. Hard caps are easier to explain but create dead points in a build.

The key check is content scaling: should a player ten levels above an enemy win automatically? In PvE often yes (feeling of growth), in PvP no (that is not a contest). Choose the mode consciously and encode it in one coefficient, not in ten places.

the mathematical model
S(n) = S₀ + g·n | S(n) = S₀ · rⁿ | S_eff = S · k/(k + S)
r = 1.05–1.10 is gentle geometric growth; r > 1.2 demands the same growth in content and almost always leads to number inflation.
02 How to build it
  1. Decide what grows with level: main stat, health, damage, or all of them.
  2. Pick a shape for each axis and check the “player / enemy” ratio at 5 levels.
  3. Add soft caps on the most explosive stats (crit, speed, damage reduction).
  4. Build a “build power” table at levels 1/10/30/60 — it must grow smoothly.
  5. Check whether growth invalidates old content; sometimes a downscale is the answer.
03 Working code
Python 
def linear(level, base=10, per_level=2.0):
    return base + per_level * level

def geometric(level, base=10, rate=1.08):
    return base * (rate ** level)

def soft_cap(stat, k=100.0):
    return stat * k / (k + stat)

for level in (1, 10, 30, 60):
    raw = geometric(level)
    print(f"L{level:02d}  linear {linear(level):7.1f}  "
          f"geometric {raw:8.1f}  capped {soft_cap(raw):7.1f}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per level
Memory
O(1)
In practice
The growth table is data. Once it is hard-coded, every patch becomes a refactor.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Geometric stat growth with linear enemy growth: by level 30 the content no longer exists.
  • A cap the player does not know about: points “disappear” and read as a bug.
  • All stats growing at once gives a quadratic power spike — a frequent cause of a broken late game.
  • No downscale in PvP: level decides the outcome instead of skill.
06 Where you can see it in games

Balance and progression BAL-11 / 24 · part IV intermediate

Soft caps and diminishing returns

Soft caps and diminishing returns

A soft cap is a way to let the player keep investing without breaking the balance. It turns “useless” points after the cap into slow but still noticeable growth.

soft capdiminishing returnscurvestats
01 Essence

R_eff = R·k/(k+R) gives a smooth curve: at R = k the effectiveness is half, at R = 3k it is three quarters. The alternative is a piecewise-linear cap: 1:1 up to the threshold, then 0.5:1, then 0.25:1. It is simpler for the UI and clearer for the player: “beyond 40 % speed every further percent costs twice as much”.

The cap must be visible. Designers often forget that the feeling of cheating comes not from diminishing returns but from hiding them. Show “+0.4 % (soft cap)” in the tooltip and let the player decide whether to keep investing.

Soft caps are also a tool for balance between builds: they prevent one stat from becoming the dominant strategy. But do not use them as a patch: if one stat is always best, the problem is its price, not the absence of a cap.

the mathematical model
S_eff = S · k / (k + S) | S_eff = S (S ≤ C) S_eff = C + (S − C) · 0.5 (C < S ≤ 2C) | …
k — the half-effectiveness point, C — the cap threshold. The smooth version reads better in formulas, the piecewise one in the UI.
02 How to build it
  1. Find the stats that explode under linear investment (crit, speed, damage reduction).
  2. Choose a smooth or piecewise cap and set the half-effectiveness point.
  3. Show the cap in the UI: the value, the threshold and “x % after the cap”.
  4. Verify that an “all into one stat” build does not beat any balanced build.
  5. Recompute the curve after any change to the damage or armour cap.
03 Working code
Python 
def soft_cap(value, k=100.0):
    return value * k / (k + value)

def piecewise(value, c=50.0, rates=(1.0, 0.5, 0.25)):
    total, prev = 0.0, 0.0
    for rate in rates:
        span = min(value, c) - prev
        if span <= 0:
            break
        total += span * rate
        prev = min(value, c)
        c *= 2
    return total

for v in (25, 50, 100, 200, 400):
    print(f"{v:4} -> smooth {soft_cap(v):6.1f}  piecewise {piecewise(v):6.1f}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per value
Memory
O(1)
In practice
Piecewise caps are cheaper to explain and easier in the UI; smooth ones are better for simulations.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • A cap with no display: the player thinks the item does not work.
  • Capping everything: builds stop differing and the game loses depth.
  • Too hard a cap creates a dead zone, too soft a cap solves nothing.
  • A soft cap used as a patch instead of repricing the stat.

Balance and progression BAL-12 / 24 · part IV advanced

Point budgets: skill trees and the price of choice

Point budgets: skill trees and the price of choice

A skill tree is a budget, not a list of upgrades. The value of a choice comes from what the player gives up, so you balance the cost of the path rather than the power of the nodes.

skill treebudgetopportunity costbuild
01 Essence

Every level grants points; every node costs points and requires prerequisites. Full build power is the sum of nodes, while the budget is the points available across the campaign. If the sum of all nodes is 3× the budget, the player must choose; at 1.2× there is barely a choice. The target ratio is usually 2:1–4:1.

Path cost is a hidden currency. A “+10 % damage” node for 3 points that requires 2 useless nodes really costs 5. Compute efficiency per point (EPP) and plot it: abnormally high-EPP nodes always become mandatory, low-EPP ones are never taken.

The tree and the items must compete: if the tree grants the same percentages as gear, one of the two is redundant. A good practice is for the tree to provide qualitative changes (new options, mechanics) and for gear to provide quantitative ones.

the mathematical model
Budget = points per campaign, Σnodes ≈ 2…4 × Budget, EPP = node effect / (cost + path cost)
EPP is efficiency per point. If one node's EPP is 3× the median, it is mandatory and must be reworked or moved in the tree.
02 How to build it
  1. Set the point budget for all content (levels plus bonuses) and the target number of full builds.
  2. Describe nodes with effect and cost, compute EPP and plot it.
  3. Add prerequisites and cap the number of “mandatory” nodes (usually 1–2 per tree).
  4. Test three canonical builds: narrow, wide and hybrid — all must be playable.
  5. Leave a respec path: one mistake must not cost the player 20 hours.
03 Working code
Python 
BUDGET = 60          # points earned across the campaign
NODES = {
    "power.1": dict(cost=1, requires=[], effect=0.05),
    "power.2": dict(cost=2, requires=["power.1"], effect=0.08),
    "power.3": dict(cost=3, requires=["power.2"], effect=0.15),
    "utility.1": dict(cost=1, requires=[], effect=0.03),
}

def path_cost(node, nodes):
    cost, seen = 0, set()
    stack = [node]
    while stack:                          # prerequisites are paid for too
        n = stack.pop()
        if n in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(n)
        cost += nodes[n]["cost"]
        stack.extend(nodes[n]["requires"])
    return cost

for name, node in NODES.items():
    epp = node["effect"] / path_cost(name, NODES)
    print(f"{name:10s} cost {path_cost(name, NODES)}  EPP {epp:.3f}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(#nodes) per build
Memory
O(#nodes)
In practice
The tree is a graph. Validate it automatically: unreachable nodes and cycles are caught in seconds.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • The sum of nodes equals the budget: there is no choice, only one build.
  • Hidden path cost ignored — part of the tree ends up dead.
  • “Tax” nodes (+1 %) taken only to unlock the next one: they annoy instead of delighting.
  • No respec: one mistake at hour 15 kills the motivation.

Progression pacing: gates, time-to-level and the power curve

Progression pacing: gates, time-to-level and the power curve

Progression is a schedule. When the player gets a new ability, how many hours until the next one and how long they get to try it — all of that is planned like a timeline, not as a side effect of numbers.

pacinggatesretentionpower curve
01 Essence

Measure time between “candies”: a new mechanic, a new item tier, a new region. The first hour should deliver 2–3 noticeable upgrades, then the interval grows. If more than 45–60 minutes pass between upgrades, the player gets bored; under 5 minutes and they never get to use them.

Gates (level, resource, boss) are not only restrictions but promises. A gate the player can see in advance (“requires level 15”) motivates; a hidden gate feels arbitrary. Show the condition and the progress towards it.

The power curve needs “plateaus”: a sharp jump at a new tier, then a flat stretch where the player learns the new game. Constant linear growth without plateaus is exhausting, and too frequent jumps devalue the previous rewards.

the mathematical model
interval(n) = T₀ · gⁿ, T₀ ≈ 8–12 min, g ≈ 1.15–1.35 up to the cap; gate = max(level, resource, boss)
The interval curve sets the rhythm: by hour 10 an upgrade should arrive every 30–45 minutes, not every 5 minutes and not every 3 hours.
02 How to build it
  1. Build a timeline of the first 10 hours: what the player receives and when.
  2. Mark the gates and check that each is visible in advance.
  3. Plot the power curve (DPS/EHP/utility) by hour and look for dips and spikes.
  4. Add plateaus after large upgrades — time to master the new toy.
  5. Compare the timeline with a real playtest: players almost always go faster than planned.
03 Working code
Python 
T0, G = 8.0, 1.25          # minutes to first upgrade and growth per upgrade

def upgrade_times(hours=10, t0=T0, g=G):
    t, out = t0, []
    while t <= hours * 60:
        out.append(t)
        t *= g
    return out

times = upgrade_times()
for i, m in enumerate(times, 1):
    gap = m - (times[i - 2] if i > 1 else 0.0)
    print(f"upgrade {i:2d} at {m / 60:5.2f} h  (gap {gap:5.0f} min)")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per point
Memory
O(1)
In practice
The timeline is a table. Without it, balance is argued from feelings instead of numbers.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • No noticeable upgrades in the first 60 minutes — the most common cause of churn.
  • Hidden gates (“needs 5000 gold”) with no progress indicator.
  • Linear growth without plateaus: the player never feels the new power.
  • Upgrades every 2 minutes: the player cannot use them and stops valuing them.

Balance and progression BAL-14 / 24 · part IV basic

Reward per action: XP, drops and scaling

Reward per action: XP, drops and scaling

A reward is not a number but a ratio: how much XP an action gives against how much XP is needed. As soon as that ratio shifts, old content becomes either mandatory or pointless.

rewardscalingeconomy of timequests
01 Essence

The simplest healthy scheme scales the reward from the player's level, not the mob's level. Then all content stays relevant. The reverse scheme creates grey zones: the player outgrows a location and it is no longer needed — fine for a linear campaign, fatal for an open world.

Compute reward per minute for every activity: combat, quests, dungeons, PvP, crafting. If one type pays three times more, the rest become decoration. A useful practice is to convert all activities into one currency (say “XP per minute”) and compare them in a table.

Separate the reward for risk from the reward for time. A hard boss must pay for the attempt, not only for the kill; otherwise players pick the safest and dullest activity. Conversely, passive activity must never out-earn active play.

the mathematical model
reward = base · (1 + k·(level_target − level_player)) · multiplier(content) rate = reward / minutes
k is small (0.05–0.15): a mild bonus for content above your level and a penalty for content far below. Keep the rate ratio between activities within 1.2–1.5×.
02 How to build it
  1. Build a table of activities with typical time and reward.
  2. Compute the rate (reward/minute) for each and even out the discrepancies.
  3. Tie scaling to the player's level or to the level difference.
  4. Add a reward for the attempt where content is hard and requires many tries.
  5. Recompute the table whenever progression tempo changes.
03 Working code
Python 
ACTIVITIES = {
    #                minutes  base_xp  risk
    "mob grind":     (0.5,      90,     1.0),
    "quest":         (4.0,      650,    1.1),
    "dungeon run":   (20.0,    3400,    1.4),
    "boss attempt":  (6.0,      420,    1.8),   # reward for trying, not only winning
    "pvp match":     (12.0,    2100,    1.6),
}

for name, (minutes, xp, risk) in ACTIVITIES.items():
    print(f"{name:14s} {xp / minutes:7.0f} xp/min  (risk x{risk})")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per reward
Memory
O(1)
In practice
The “activity → reward/minute” table is the cheapest balance tool in existence.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Scaling rewards from the mob's level: old locations turn into garbage.
  • One activity pays several times more — the rest become decoration.
  • A reward only for winning hard content, so players choose safe farming.
  • A reward that never scales: by mid-game it has been devalued.

Balance and progression BAL-15 / 24 · part IV intermediate

Rarity bands and loot tables

Rarity bands and loot tables

Loot is a distribution, not a list. Rarity bands shape the distribution, weights set probabilities, and item level scales the numbers inside a band.

loot tablerarityweightsitem level
01 Essence

The classic structure is a rarity tier (common, uncommon, rare, epic, legendary) with weights like 1000 / 300 / 80 / 18 / 2. Probability = weight / total weight. The important part is not the absolute percentages but the ratios: how many times rarer a legendary is than an epic. Ratios are what players feel.

Item level (ilvl) sets the stat budget: the sum of stats on an item is f(ilvl). Inside a rarity band the budget is multiplied by a coefficient (say rare ×1.35). Then item power is predictable and rarity is a multiplier rather than a lottery of random numbers.

For the feeling of luck, guarantees and pity-weighted rolls matter: dry streaks of 50 kills at a 2 % chance happen regularly. Add a failure counter that raises the weight, and a ceiling (“guaranteed drop within N”). And always show where the item came from: the sense of the source is part of the reward.

the mathematical model
P(tier) = wᵗ / Σw, budget = B(ilvl) · rarity_mult, Σstats = budget
Weights set ratios, ilvl sets scale. Keep rarity_mult in the 1.0–1.6 band: a wider gap makes the lower tiers garbage.
02 How to build it
  1. Define rarity tiers and weights; check the ratios, not just the percentages.
  2. Define the stat budget as a function of ilvl and a multiplier per tier.
  3. Build drop tables per source (mob, chest, boss) with independent weights.
  4. Add a failure counter and a guarantee for the top tiers.
  5. Validate the distribution by simulation: 10 000 drops and a histogram by tier.
03 Working code
Python 
import bisect, random

TIERS = [("common", 1000, 1.00), ("uncommon", 300, 1.10),
         ("rare", 80, 1.25), ("epic", 18, 1.45), ("legendary", 2, 1.70)]
WEIGHTS = [w for _, w, _ in TIERS]
CUMSUM = []
acc = 0
for w in WEIGHTS:
    acc += w
    CUMSUM.append(acc)

def roll_tier(rng):
    return TIERS[bisect.bisect_left(CUMSUM, rng.random() * acc)][0]

def stat_budget(ilvl, mult):
    return round((10 + 2.5 * ilvl) * mult, 1)

rng = random.Random(3)
counts = {}
for _ in range(10_000):
    t = roll_tier(rng)
    counts[t] = counts.get(t, 0) + 1
print({k: round(v / 100, 2) for k, v in counts.items()}, "%")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(#tiers) per drop
Memory
O(1)
In practice
One roll over cumulative weights is cheaper than a roll per tier.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Watching absolute percentages and missing the ratios between tiers.
  • A random stat budget inside a tier: the player cannot tell whether the item is “good”.
  • No guarantee: dry streaks read as broken drops.
  • Drops without a source: the player cannot connect the reward to the action.

Balance and progression BAL-16 / 24 · part IV advanced

Gacha: rates, soft pity and expected pulls

Gacha: rates, soft pity and expected pulls

A gacha mechanic is a distribution of pulls until the reward. You must count the median and p90 pulls, not the chance per pull: they decide how much a player spends or how soon they leave.

gachapityexpected valuemonetisation
01 Essence

With a fixed chance p, the number of pulls until success is geometric: E = 1/p, median ≈ ln2/p, p90 ≈ ln10/p. At p = 0.6 % the expectation is 167 pulls, but 10 % of players will not get the reward within 383. It is the tail, not the mean, that reads as “the gacha is greedy”.

Soft pity raises the chance after a threshold (for example +6 % per step after pull 74), hard pity guarantees it at N. Soft pity compresses the tail while barely moving the mean; hard pity makes the upper bound known and turns spending into a plan. Together they give both predictability and revenue.

Transparency is mandatory: published rates, a counter to the guarantee, and history. A hidden pity system is a legal and reputational risk, not a “secret trick”. And compute the full cost of the reward in currency: 1/p · pull price is the real price of the character.

the mathematical model
P(k) = (1−p)^(k−1)·p, E = 1/p, median ≈ ln2/p, p90 ≈ ln10/p
With soft pity the chance at step k is p_k = p + c·max(0, k − s). Hard pity H makes P(k > H) = 0 and the expectation ≈ 0.7–0.9·H.
02 How to build it
  1. Choose the base chance and the target median and p90 pulls.
  2. Add soft pity: threshold s and step c tuned so that the median hits the target.
  3. Add hard pity and check the expectation by simulation rather than by formula.
  4. Publish the rates and make the guarantee counter visible.
  5. Compute the full cost in currency and compare it with direct purchases.
03 Working code
Python 
import random

def pulls_until_hit(rng, p=0.006, soft_start=74, soft_step=0.06, hard=90):
    for k in range(1, hard + 1):
        chance = p + (soft_step * (k - soft_start) if k >= soft_start else 0.0)
        if rng.random() < min(1.0, chance) or k == hard:
            return k

def simulate(n=200_000, **kw):
    rng = random.Random(42)
    data = sorted(pulls_until_hit(rng, **kw) for _ in range(n))
    return (sum(data) / n, data[n // 2], data[int(n * 0.9)], data[-1])

mean, med, p90, worst = simulate()
print(f"mean {mean:.1f}  median {med}  p90 {p90}  worst {worst}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per pull
Memory
O(1)
In practice
Simulating 10⁶ players takes seconds on a laptop and immediately reveals p99 — the number behind most complaints.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Counting only the mean and ignoring p90 — p90 is what generates complaints.
  • Hidden pity: legal risk and loss of trust once discovered.
  • Hard pity without a visible counter: the player cannot tell how much is left.
  • A soft-pity step that is too steep breaks the reward economy after the threshold.

Balance and progression BAL-17 / 24 · part IV intermediate

Currencies: faucets, sinks and the accumulation rate

Currencies: faucets, sinks and the accumulation rate

An economy is a bathtub: faucets pour currency in, sinks drain it out. If the faucets are wider than the sinks, the currency devalues; if narrower, the player cannot afford anything and leaves.

currencyfaucetsinkeconomy
01 Essence

Every currency has a faucet (source: rewards, selling loot, quests) and a sink (spend: repairs, crafting, auction fees, consumables, cosmetics). The health of the economy is the inflow-to-outflow ratio per hour: 0.9–1.1 on average, with seasonal swings. Compute it separately for each currency.

The sink should be voluntary but attractive: a tax you cannot avoid feels like punishment, while an optional spend with tangible benefit feels like a decision. Good sinks: repair after death, crafting accelerators, cosmetics, auction listings, stat re-forging.

On having many currencies: each new one is a new faucet and sink, and the player must understand where it comes from. If a currency exists for a single purchase, make it a resource instead. The rule: no more than 3–4 “real” currencies, everything else is an item.

the mathematical model
ΔM = (Σfaucets − Σsinks) · dt, inflation ≈ ΔM / M, price ≈ k · M / supply
M — the server's money supply. If inflow consistently exceeds outflow by 5–10 % per hour, prices multiply overnight — that is MMO inflation.
02 How to build it
  1. List every faucet and sink per currency with numbers per hour of play.
  2. Compute the ΔM balance and the target prices of key goods.
  3. Make the sink mandatory in meaning but optional in action.
  4. Add automatic statistics: currency mass on the server, median prices.
  5. Install a “fuse”: if prices rise above X, trigger an additional sink.
03 Working code
Python 
FAUCETS = {"quests": 1200, "mob drops": 900, "vendor junk": 400}   # gold / hour
SINKS = {"repairs": 600, "crafting": 800, "auction fee": 500}

inflow, outflow = sum(FAUCETS.values()), sum(SINKS.values())
delta = inflow - outflow
print(f"in {inflow}/h  out {outflow}/h  delta {delta:+}/h  ratio {inflow / outflow:.2f}")

# what one hour of play does to the money supply
supply = 1_000_000
for hour in range(1, 6):
    supply += delta
    print(f"hour {hour}: supply {supply:,}  (+{delta * hour / 1_000_000:.1%} of the start)")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(#faucets + #sinks)
Memory
O(1)
In practice
Measure not “how much gold exists” but “how much gold per hour per player” — that is the controllable quantity.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Faucets wider than sinks — hyperinflation within the first week.
  • Unavoidable sinks (a tax on air) feel like punishment.
  • Too many currencies: the player loses track of where things come from.
  • No metrics on currency mass: inflation is discovered when it is too late.
06 Where you can see it in games

Balance and progression BAL-18 / 24 · part IV advanced

Inflation and sinks in a live economy

Inflation and sinks in a live economy

MMO inflation is inevitable: players farm faster than they spend. The question is not how to avoid it but how to keep it in a corridor before content loses its value.

inflationsinkmoney supplylive ops
01 Essence

Inflation in a game is the growth of money supply relative to goods. While new players outnumber leavers, gold inflow rises and prices rise with it. Symptoms: basic resources get expensive while new items cost the same, and veterans buy everything. Metrics: the median price of a basic resource and the gold mass per active player.

Tools: an auction tax (proportional, not fixed), repairs, consumables, burning materials in high-tier crafting, lotteries and bets, seasonal resets, transfer fees. Crucially, the sink must grow with the money mass — progressive, not fixed.

A separate problem is concentration: even with a healthy total, 1 % of players may hold 80 % of the gold and control the market. That is cured not only by sinks but by institutions: purchase limits, regional markets, bound items, anti-flipping fees.

the mathematical model
π ≈ (inflow − sink) / M · dt, progressive sink = α · M^β (β > 1)
A progressive sink (β > 1) brakes inflation harder the richer the server is, without hurting newcomers.
02 How to build it
  1. Instrument: gold mass, median prices of the top-10 goods, wealth share of the top 1 %.
  2. Make sinks progressive: the more money in the economy, the higher the effective fee.
  3. Add a mandatory but fair sink (repairs, consumables) and optional prestigious ones.
  4. Plan seasonal resets or new tiers so money does not sit idle.
  5. React to metrics: if a price rises 30 % in a week, trigger an additional sink.
03 Working code
Python 
def era_tick(money, faucet_rate, sink_rate, beta=1.15, alpha=0.0004, dt_hours=1.0):
    """Progressive sink: the richer the economy, the stronger the drain."""
    sink = sink_rate + alpha * (money ** beta)
    money += (faucet_rate - sink) * dt_hours
    return max(money, 0.0), sink

money = 1_000_000.0
for hour in range(0, 72, 12):
    for _ in range(12):
        money, sink = era_tick(money, 250_000, 30_000)
    print(f"hour {hour:3d}: money {money:12,.0f}  sink/h {sink:9,.0f}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per transaction
Memory
O(#goods)
In practice
This must be measured server-side and regularly: an economy is an observed system, not a static table.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • A fixed sink against a growing money mass: inflation is guaranteed.
  • Sinks that hit newcomers (expensive repairs at the start) but not the rich.
  • Ignoring wealth concentration: a handful of players capture the market.
  • A seasonal reset without compensation: veterans leave, the economy and trust reset together.

World of WarcraftEVE OnlineRuneScapeAlbion Online

Balance and progression BAL-19 / 24 · part IV intermediate

Grind, energy and session loops

Grind, energy and session loops

Grind is a repeatable action with a reward. It is not bad in itself; it is bad when the repetition offers no new skill and no new decision, only time.

grindsessionenergyretention
01 Essence

Three kinds of repetition: skilful (the same task, but the player improves), variable (conditions and decisions change) and empty (time in exchange for a number). The first two are normal; the third is what people mean by grind. The sign of an empty loop: the player can do it without looking at the screen.

Session limits (energy, daily rewards, raid cooldowns) control tempo but conflict with the pleasure of a long session. The rule: a limit should protect the player from overplaying, not punish enthusiasm. Daily bonuses work better as “catch-up” (accumulating over missed days) than as burning rewards.

Measure time to the first interesting reward in the loop and the number of decisions per minute. If a five-minute loop spends four minutes on a familiar route, shorten it or add variance (modifiers, random events, escalation).

the mathematical model
loop efficiency = reward / (action time + travel time)
Measure per loop, not per hour: the loop is what the player repeats a hundred times. If travel time exceeds action time, the loop feels like work.
02 How to build it
  1. Break the loop into steps and time each one in a real playtest.
  2. Remove dead time: running, waiting, loading, repeated dialogue.
  3. Add variance: modifiers, random events, different objectives.
  4. Make limits catch-up rather than burn-off.
  5. Compare the reward per loop with other loops — they must be comparable.
03 Working code
Python 
CYCLE = [("travel", 95), ("fight", 70), ("loot", 15), ("travel back", 95)]

def cycle_efficiency(steps, reward=900):
    action = sum(s for n, s in steps if n in ("fight", "loot"))
    total = sum(s for _, s in steps)
    return total, action / total, reward / (total / 60)

total, share, per_min = cycle_efficiency(CYCLE)
print(f"cycle {total}s  action share {share:.0%}  reward {per_min:.0f}/min")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per loop
Memory
O(1)
In practice
A stopwatch on a playtest yields more than any spreadsheet.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Running and waiting take more time than the action itself.
  • Burning daily rewards: missing a day punishes more than it motivates.
  • Energy that stops the player exactly when they are engaged.
  • An empty loop without variance: the player can play without looking at the screen.

Meta-balance

5 topics

Power creep, the difficulty curve, boss tuning, PvP and balance simulation: how to keep a game alive for years.

Balance and progression BAL-20 / 24 · part IV advanced

Power creep and horizontal progression

Power creep and horizontal progression

Every new item tier devalues the previous one. The life of a game is a race between power inflation and content inflation, and it can only be won by planning both.

power creepprogressioncontentlive ops
01 Essence

Vertical growth (“every expansion +50 ilvl”) is simple and understandable, but requires enemies, rewards and old raids to grow the same way. After three years the numbers triple and old content becomes decoration. Horizontal growth (new variants, not bigger numbers) preserves content but demands choice design.

A workable hybrid: a small vertical step (5–10 % per season) plus horizontal mechanics (sets, talents, specialisations). Verticality delivers the feeling of growth, horizontality gives a reason to try something new. Keep a “reference build” for checking: a new season must not make it unplayable.

Plan number squashing in advance: once damage exceeds 10⁹ the UI breaks and the player loses the sense of scale. A squish is not a sign of failure but a planned operation, and it must be done without losing the feel.

the mathematical model
power(n) = power(0) · (1 + v)ⁿ, content(n) = content(0) · (1 + v')ⁿ, balance ⇔ v ≈ v'
v — seasonal vertical growth, v' — content growth. If v > v' for two seasons in a row, old content becomes irrelevant; if v < v', the player feels stagnation.
02 How to build it
  1. Set the seasonal vertical step (usually 5–10 %) and keep it for a year.
  2. Add horizontal mechanics so a season changes the game, not only the numbers.
  3. Define a reference build and test it every season.
  4. Plan a stat squish ahead: once every 2–3 years or when the limit is exceeded.
  5. Watch difficulty inflation: old raids must stay playable (or be deliberately retired).
03 Working code
Python 
def season_power(base=1000, rate=0.08, seasons=8):
    return [base * (1 + rate) ** n for n in range(seasons)]

def old_content_share(new_power, old_content_hp, ratio=3.0):
    """How much of the old content stays meaningful."""
    return old_content_hp * ratio / new_power

powers = season_power()
for n, p in enumerate(powers):
    print(f"season {n}: power {p:8.0f}  old content relevance {old_content_share(p, 1000):.2f}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per season
Memory
O(#content)
In practice
Recomputing content after a squish is the expensive part; do it in one go, not piecemeal.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Vertical growth without content growth: old raids and items lose all value.
  • Horizontal growth without vertical: the player does not feel stronger.
  • A stat squish without retuning the feel: players see smaller numbers and assume a nerf.
  • A new progression currency every season: the player loses track of the system.

Difficulty curves, DDA and accessibility

Difficulty curves, DDA and accessibility

Difficulty is not a number but the ratio of demand to the player's capability. The curve must grow a little slower than skill so the player lives in the “hard but doable” zone.

difficultyDDAaccessibilityonboarding
01 Essence

Demand rises with levels, capability rises with experience and gear. If demand outpaces it, the player hits a wall; if it lags, the game becomes boring. A good curve is a sawtooth: a difficulty spike, then a plateau where the player learns the new tools, then the next spike.

Dynamic difficulty (DDA) adapts to the player. It is attractive but visible: if enemies “adjust”, rewards lose value and death stops meaning anything. Safe forms: adapt tempo (enemy count) rather than damage; offer hidden help after a run of deaths; offer to lower the difficulty instead of doing it silently.

Accessibility is part of balance, not a separate feature. Damage, speed, timing, reticle-size settings and assist options widen the audience without breaking the curve for everyone else. The rule: give tools, do not silently change the rules.

the mathematical model
difficulty(t) ≈ k · skill(t)^0.85, flow zone: 0.7 ≤ demand/capability ≤ 1.1
An exponent below 1 means the game “yields” as skill grows — that is the feeling of mastery. Above 1 is a wall.
02 How to build it
  1. Define the demand axis (damage, timings, enemy count, resources) and the capability axis.
  2. Plot the curve by chapter as a sawtooth: spike → plateau → spike.
  3. Find points where demand exceeds capability by more than 20 %.
  4. Add DDA only to tempo and only as hidden help, never to damage.
  5. Ship accessibility settings without changing the base curve for others.
03 Working code
Python 
def requirement(chapter, base=10, rate=1.18):
    return base * (rate ** chapter)

def capability(chapter, skill=0.16, gear=0.10):
    return 10 * ((1 + skill) * (1 + gear)) ** chapter

for ch in range(0, 12):
    req, cap = requirement(ch), capability(ch)
    flag = "  <-- wall" if req / cap > 1.2 else ""
    print(f"chapter {ch:2d}  req {req:7.1f}  cap {cap:7.1f}  ratio {req / cap:4.2f}{flag}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per level
Memory
O(1)
In practice
Collect death telemetry: a map of “where players die” is the best difficulty-balance tool there is.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • DDA on damage: the player notices and stops believing in their own success.
  • Difficulty grows faster than capability — a wall mid-game.
  • Accessibility settings buried and never mentioned in the difficulty menu.
  • No telemetry: “where it is hard” is decided from tester feelings.

Boss tuning: phases, DPS checks and enrage

Boss tuning: phases, DPS checks and enrage timers

A boss fight is a contract: how much damage is required, how many mistakes are allowed and how long an attempt lasts. All three numbers are set in advance, not tuned after release.

bossphasesDPS checkenrage
01 Essence

The fight budget has three quantities: required DPS (health / duration), tolerable incoming damage (tank health / duration) and allowed mistakes (how many mechanics can be failed before a wipe). The first two are numbers, the third is design. If the allowed mistakes are zero, the fight becomes choreography.

A DPS check is useful when it tests the build and execution, and harmful when it depends only on gear. A 20 % damage gap between “geared” and “ungeared” is a fair check; a 3× gap is a progression gate. An enrage timer is a crude form of the same thing; escalating mechanics are better than a hard stop.

Plan phases as a change of task rather than a change of number: from damage to positioning, from solo to coordination. And keep the attempt duration comfortable: 3–6 minutes for action, 8–12 for raids; longer and a wipe at the last seconds feels like wasted time.

the mathematical model
DPS_required = HP_boss / T_attempt, mistakes = (T · HPS_available − unavoidable damage) / damage_per_mistake
Compute for the average player of your audience, not the top 1 %. The top should win easily — that is the reward for mastery.
02 How to build it
  1. Set the target fight duration and compute the required DPS for the reference build.
  2. Compute the incoming-damage budget for the tank and the tolerable number of mechanic failures.
  3. Split the fight into phases by task type (damage → position → coordination).
  4. Make enrage an escalation of mechanics, not instant death.
  5. Test the fight on both an under-geared and an over-geared player.
03 Working code
Python 
def boss_budget(hp=2_000_000, target_time=300, tank_hp=180_000,
                unavoidable_dps=450, error_damage=25_000):
    dps = hp / target_time                          # the DPS check
    slack = tank_hp - unavoidable_dps * target_time  # health left for mistakes
    return dps, int(max(0, slack) // error_damage)

for gear in (0.85, 1.0, 1.2):                 # under-, reference, over-geared
    dps, errors = boss_budget(hp=2_000_000 * gear)
    print(f"gear x{gear:.2f}: required dps {dps:7.0f}, tolerable mistakes {errors}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(1) per check
Memory
O(1)
In practice
Keep an attempt log: time, DPS, deaths per mechanic — that is the boss's balance.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • A DPS check that depends only on gear: the player “cannot pass” rather than “cannot play”.
  • Enrage as instant death: a wipe at 99 % feels like a cheat.
  • Fights longer than 10 minutes without intermediate checkpoints.
  • Balancing around top players: the average player never sees the content.

PvP balance: normalisation, rating and gear

PvP balance: normalisation, rating and gear

In PvP, balance is not just character numbers but the distribution of player skill. Weapons and armour should define style, not the outcome by default.

PvPnormalisationratinggear
01 Essence

Three models: full normalisation (all stats equal, skill wins — as in template arenas), scaling (gear compressed into a narrow corridor, a 5–10 % difference), full accounting (gear decides). The first is fairer but loses RPG progression; the third is more interesting for an MMO but scares newcomers away in competitive modes.

Balance by rank, not overall: a weapon with a 48 % win rate at low rank and 58 % at high rank is a design issue (a high skill ceiling), not an “imbalance”. Also look at pick rate: if an item appears in 90 % of builds, the problem is the lack of alternatives, not the win rate.

And perceived unfairness: losing to “better gear” demotivates more than losing to skill. So even with full gear accounting it is worth limiting the power gap between players in the same match.

the mathematical model
winrate(item) = wins / matches by rank, pick_rate = appearances / builds
Target a 48–52 % win rate across all ranks. The anomaly is not 55 % but a difference of more than 5 pp between ranks.
02 How to build it
  1. Choose the model: normalisation, scaling or full gear accounting.
  2. Collect statistics by rank: win rate, pick rate, match duration.
  3. Introduce seasonal limits (bans, item caps, stat templates).
  4. Limit the power gap between players in the same match.
  5. Look at the high ranks separately: skill ceilings show up there more than “imbalances”.
03 Working code
Python 
STATS = {   # item: {rank: (wins, matches)}
    "sword":  {"low": (520, 1000), "mid": (505, 1000), "high": (585, 1000)},
    "dagger": {"low": (480, 1000), "mid": (500, 1000), "high": (415, 1000)},
}

for item, ranks in STATS.items():
    rates = {r: w / m for r, (w, m) in ranks.items()}
    spread = max(rates.values()) - min(rates.values())
    print(f"{item:7s} " + "  ".join(f"{r} {v:.0%}" for r, v in rates.items())
          + f"   spread {spread:.0%}" + ("  <-- skill ceiling" if spread > 0.05 else ""))
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(#items × #ranks)
Memory
O(#matches)
In practice
Measure by rank and by build: an aggregate win rate hides both problems.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Balancing on the overall win rate and hiding rank differences.
  • Ignoring pick rate: “not overpowered” can still be “mandatory”.
  • A gear gap of more than 20 % within one match reads as unfair.
  • Normalisation that kills build identity makes the game flat.

Balance simulation, Monte Carlo and A/B tests

Balance simulation, Monte Carlo and A/B tests

Balance cannot be proven by a formula — it can be measured. Simulation gives numbers before release, telemetry after, and an A/B test answers “did it get better” without relying on intuition.

Monte CarlosimulationA/B testtelemetry
01 Essence

Monte Carlo answers questions like “what percentage of fights ends in three hits” and “how often is a miss streak longer than six”. The model is simple: agents, actions, distributions. The main thing is to look at tails and confidence intervals rather than means — 10 000 runs give about 1 pp of precision, enough for design decisions.

Telemetry after release answers different questions: where people die, what items they take, where they quit. Look at cohorts (newcomers, veterans, ranks) and distributions, not aggregate averages. A single “average” 50 % win rate can hide two broken modes.

An A/B test is the only way to verify that a change actually improved a metric. It needs random assignment, a sufficient sample, a pre-declared metric and a fixed duration. Common mistakes: checking results daily and stopping when it looks good, changing several variables at once, measuring retention with a single button.

the mathematical model
SE = √(p(1−p)/n), 95 % CI ≈ p ± 1.96·SE, n ≈ 16·p(1−p)/Δ²
For a 2 pp difference at p ≈ 0.5 you need roughly 10 000 observations per arm. Stopping earlier means measuring noise.
02 How to build it
  1. State the balance question as a measurable quantity (TTK, win share, time to level).
  2. Build a Monte Carlo model with distributions rather than fixed numbers.
  3. Compute tails and confidence intervals; run a sensitivity check on the parameters.
  4. After release collect cohort telemetry and compare it with the model.
  5. Validate the change with an A/B test using a pre-declared metric and duration.
03 Working code
Python 
import random, statistics

def duel(rng, a=(100, 12, 0.75), b=(110, 10, 0.70), limit=60):
    """Simple stochastic duel: (hp, damage, hit chance)."""
    hp_a, dmg_a, hit_a = a
    hp_b, dmg_b, hit_b = b
    for turn in range(limit):
        if rng.random() < hit_a:
            hp_b -= dmg_a * rng.uniform(0.85, 1.15)
        if hp_b <= 0:
            return "a", turn
        if rng.random() < hit_b:
            hp_a -= dmg_b * rng.uniform(0.85, 1.15)
        if hp_a <= 0:
            return "b", turn
    return "draw", limit

rng = random.Random(11)
outcomes = [duel(rng) for _ in range(20_000)]
wins_a = sum(1 for w, _ in outcomes if w == "a") / len(outcomes)
turns = [t for w, t in outcomes if w == "a"]
se = (wins_a * (1 - wins_a) / len(outcomes)) ** 0.5
print(f"win A {wins_a:.1%} ± {1.96 * se:.1%}   median turns {statistics.median(turns):.0f}")
04 Computational complexity
Time
O(n) per run
Memory
O(1)
In practice
10⁵ runs take seconds. 10⁵ runs of a full combat simulation take minutes; cache results and look at deltas.
05 Where people usually get it wrong
  • Counting means and ignoring tails — the tails cause the complaints.
  • Stopping an A/B test at the first good-looking result.
  • Changing several variables at once makes the effect unassignable.
  • Telemetry without cohorts: averages hide a broken segment.

Thirty-six ways to play

Every genre is described with the same structure: loop, session, tempo, key numbers, typical breakages and references. Genres are grouped into six families, from action to social games.

A genre is a contract with the player: it promises a tempo, a type of decision and a price for mistakes. Genres can be mixed, but the promise must stay single — otherwise the player cannot tell what they are playing.

a quick genre chooser

Genre atlas GEN-01 / 36 · part V intermediate

First-person shooter

First-person shooter

A genre where information, aim and reaction time form a closed loop. Maps, weapons and modes all exist to serve that loop.

aimTTKmap controlgun feel
01 What this genre is

Loop: see → take position → shoot → reload/relocate. A session lasts 5–20 minutes, a fight 2–15 seconds. The value of the genre lies in readability: the player must instantly understand where the enemy is, where to run and how much time there is. Any mechanic that slows scene reading (excess effects, a cluttered HUD) hurts more than a new gun helps.

Design rests on three numbers: TTK (0.3–1.2 s in arcade shooters, 0.15–0.4 in tactical ones), movement speed relative to map size, and spread. Together they define gun feel: a heavy weapon turns slowly, kicks hard and reloads long; a light one aims fast but deals less per hit. Balance weapons by STK at reference distances, not by DPS.

The genre breaks on maps: a single dominant sightline turns the game into a sniper duel, too much cover into corner camping. Design a map as three layers (long, medium, close range), check rotation times between key points (8–12 s) and the number of simultaneously exposed angles (no more than 3).

Loop
Session: spawn → rotate → duel → death/win → spawn · TTK 0.15–1.2 s
TTK = EHP / DPS; STK = ceil(EHP / damage). The target TTK defines the subgenre: arcade — longer, tactical — shorter and deadlier.
Session5–20 min
TempoTTK 0.15–1.2 s
Key metrichit share and time to first contact
02 How to build it
  1. Set TTK and STK for 3–4 weapon archetypes and build a matrix by distance.
  2. Design the map as three range layers and check rotation times.
  3. Define each weapon's role: distance, tempo, cost of a mistake.
  4. Tune gun feel — recoil, muzzle flash, sound, hitmarker — before cosmetics.
  5. Check readability: silhouettes, enemy contrast, HUD information priority.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • A TTK that is too low turns fights into “whoever sees first wins” and kills counter-play.
  • A cluttered HUD and heavy effects stop the player from reading the scene.
  • A map with a single dominant sightline.
  • Spread used instead of honest recoil: the player cannot tell why they missed.

Genre atlas GEN-02 / 36 · part V advanced

Battle royale

Battle royale

A battle royale is a risk economy: one life, growing pressure, and a reward for aggression traded against a reward for patience. The map, loot and timers only manage that balance.

shrinkinglootriskone life
01 What this genre is

Loop: drop → loot → rotate → skirmish → shrinking zone. A session lasts 15–25 minutes, and everything rests on one life: the cost of a mistake is maximal, so the player constantly trades risk for information. That makes the genre closer to poker than to a shooter: the decision “take the fight or disengage” matters more than accuracy.

Balance rests on zone tempo and loot density. Shrinking too fast leaves no time to build a kit; too slow turns the match into a walk. Target density: 3–5 hot drops for 60 players, 60–120 s to first contact, 12–16 minutes to the final circle. Loot must create different kits, not just a power gradient.

The main failure is the snowball: the winner of a fight gains loot, position and confidence. Cure it through economy: a kill should pay partially (ammo, consumables) rather than duplicating the full kit, plus catch-up mechanics (squad respawn, faster healing).

Loop
Match: 100 → 1 in T ≈ 15–25 min, P(survive) ≈ (1/2)^(fights)
Each even fight roughly halves the chance of making it to the end. That is why early aggression is about information and loot, not just kills.
Session15–25 min
Tempozone 12–16 min
Key metricsurvival by time and fights per match
02 How to build it
  1. Set map size and zone tempo for the target match length.
  2. Design 3–5 hot drops with different risk and reward.
  3. Decide what a fight win grants: a partial reward, not the full kit.
  4. Add catch-up mechanics for players who are behind (respawn, faster healing).
  5. Audit the time distribution: how much of the match is idle versus in contact.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • A snowball: the fight winner takes everything and never loses afterwards.
  • Slow shrinking turns the match into a walk without decisions.
  • Loot as a power gradient instead of a style choice.
  • No reason to fight: the game rewards waiting only.
04 Where you can see it in games
PUBGFortniteApex LegendsWarzone

Genre atlas GEN-03 / 36 · part V advanced

Fighting game

Fighting game

Fighting games are the most mathematically strict action genre: combat is broken down into frames, and a duel is decided by system knowledge and reading the opponent.

frame dataneutralmixupdeterminism
01 What this genre is

Loop: neutral → confirm → combo → okizeme/mixup → repeat. A match lasts 2–5 minutes, but learning takes months. The value of the genre is predictability: the same input always yields the same result, so skill is measured exactly. Hence the requirements: a fixed tick (usually 60 Hz), determinism and rollback netcode online.

Design rests on frame data: startup, active, recovery frames, plus/minus on block. Balance is not “character power” but the set of options in neutral and the cost of a mistake. A character with a long weapon wins at range but loses up close; everyone must have answers, not equally convenient ones.

The genre breaks on option inflation: if a character answers everything, neutral disappears and the game becomes combo execution. The second risk is the entry barrier: without a training mode, frame explanation and a sensible rank ladder, a newcomer leaves after ten losses in a row.

Loop
input → frame N: startup, active, recovery; advantage = (hit/block stun) − recovery
Every move is a window in frames at 60 Hz: 1 frame ≈ 16.7 ms. Plus on block means the attacker acts before the defender.
Sessionmatch 2–5 min
Tempowindow 1–20 frames
Key metricwin rate by rank and combo length
02 How to build it
  1. Fix the tick and determinism: online fighting is impossible without them.
  2. Build a move table: startup/active/recovery, damage, plus on block.
  3. Design neutral: each archetype gets its own ranges and answers.
  4. Ship a training mode showing frames and hitboxes.
  5. Balance by win rate across ranks rather than overall.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • A character that answers every situation makes neutral disappear.
  • No training mode: the entry barrier kills the online population.
  • An unstable tick or floats in the simulation: desync and eaten inputs.
  • Combos longer than 8–10 seconds: both player and spectator lose the thread.

Genre atlas GEN-04 / 36 · part V basic

Platformer

Platformer

A platformer is jump physics and trust in them. The player learns to read a trajectory in a second, and all difficulty is built on honouring that contract.

jump arccoyote timelevel designfeel
01 What this genre is

Loop: run → jump → land → next challenge. Sessions are short (10–40 s per room) and teaching happens through the level, not through text. The key numbers are jump height, jump length, acceleration, max speed and time to double jump. They define the vocabulary of movement every room is built from.

Mandatory conveniences that make control feel good: coyote time (0.08–0.15 s to jump after leaving a ledge), jump buffer (a press 0.1 s before landing), variable jump height and edge magnetism. Without them the player feels the game “does not listen”, even if it is technically fair.

A level is designed as proposal and answer: show a mechanic in a safe zone, complicate it, combine it with another, test it under pressure. The genre breaks on unfair jumps (precision you cannot see) and blind screens — the player must see the landing spot in advance.

Loop
h = v₀²/(2g), t_air = 2v₀/g, range = v₀ₓ · t_air
h is jump height, v₀ initial speed, g gravity. These three numbers define the geometry of every level: draw levels on the same grid as the physics.
Sessionroom 10–40 s
Tempoprecision ±2 frames
Key metricshare of deaths on a room's first attempt
02 How to build it
  1. Set jump physics and build the reference level grid from it.
  2. Add coyote time, jump buffer and variable jump height.
  3. Design a teaching room for every new mechanic.
  4. Escalate through combinations, not frame-perfect precision.
  5. Verify that the landing spot is visible before the jump.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • No coyote time: the player falls off flat ground.
  • Jumps that demand precision the screen does not show.
  • The camera does not reveal the landing spot.
  • Difficulty from input precision instead of understanding the mechanic.

Genre atlas GEN-05 / 36 · part V intermediate

Shoot 'em up and bullet hell

Shoot 'em up and bullet hell

Bullet hell is about reading a dense visual field and micro-positioning. Difficulty here is created by patterns, not by enemy speed.

patternhitboxscorereading
01 What this genre is

Loop: clear a wave → collect pickups → boss → new pattern. An arcade session lasts 3–8 minutes, a full run 25–40 minutes. The key contract is a tiny player hitbox (2–4 pixels) against a large sprite: the player must feel they “slipped through”, and that is what builds trust in the difficulty.

Patterns are built from formulas: spiral, fan, delayed ring, wall with a gap. Alternate density and emptiness: a screen full of bullets with no gap is not difficulty but noise. The rule: a path must always exist, and it must be visible 0.5–1 s before it becomes mandatory.

Score is the second axis: chains, multipliers and grazing (passing millimetres from a bullet) turn survival into optimisation. Without it the genre stays short and flat. It breaks on unfair patterns (a bullet spawning on the player), unclear hitboxes and visual noise that hides danger.

Loop
patterns: ρ(θ) = a + b·sin(kθ + φt), bullet speed v = const
Pattern density is set by the sine and its rotation speed. Test passability with a corridor: the minimum gap must be 3–4× the hitbox.
Session3–8 min
Temporeaction 0.2–0.4 s
Key metricsurvival by wave and score per minute
02 How to build it
  1. Set the player hitbox size and make it visually obvious.
  2. Build a pattern library: fan, spiral, ring, wall with a gap.
  3. Verify every pattern is at least 3–4× wider than the hitbox.
  4. Add a scoring system: chains, multipliers, grazing.
  5. Alternate density and pauses so the eye can reset.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • A bullet spawning on top of the player is an unfair death.
  • A pattern with no gap turns difficulty into noise.
  • A hitbox bigger than the sprite: the player stops trusting their eyes.
  • No scoring system: the genre loses depth after one clear.

Hack & slash and character action

Hack & slash and character action

A slasher is a dance with a crowd: the player manages not only damage but space, target order and their own style.

comboenemy designrankcamera
01 What this genre is

Loop: approach a group → control the crowd → combo → finish → rank. A session lasts 1–3 minutes per arena. The key is enemies as instruments: a heavy enemy demands a dodge, a shield-bearer requires an angle, an archer forces a close-in. If all enemies are the same, combos collapse into one memorised sequence.

The combat system rests on cancels and priority: a light attack cancels into a dodge, a heavy one does not; an air attack extends a chain; a block has a window. It is the restrictions that create depth: the player learns to pick safe continuations instead of mashing maximum output.

Ranking (style meter, combo counter) is not decoration but a teaching device: it tells the player what “good” means and makes them take risks. The genre breaks on the camera (a crowd behind the back), invulnerable phases and enemies that cannot be read: attack telegraphs must be visible 0.3–0.6 s ahead.

Loop
style DPS = Σ damage · combo multiplier / time, telegraph 0.3–0.6 s
The multiplier grows with move variety and drops on repetition. Rank is a function of variety, not only of kill speed.
Sessionarena 1–3 min
Tempotelegraph 0.3–0.6 s
Key metricaverage rank and damage taken without dodging
02 How to build it
  1. Design 5–7 enemy types with different answers and telegraphs.
  2. Define cancel rules: what can be interrupted and what cannot.
  3. Add a style rank and show the player what earned it.
  4. Test the camera and crowd readability: an enemy behind the back must be audible.
  5. Tune hitstop, knockback and hit sound — that is half the feel.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • All enemies identical — combos degenerate into one sequence.
  • Attacks without telegraphs: death reads as unfair.
  • The camera loses enemies behind the player.
  • A rank with no explanation: the player cannot tell how to score higher.

Strategy

6 topics

RTS, turn-based 4X, MOBA, tower defense, auto battlers and wargames: genres of decisions, economy and information.

07
Genre atlas GEN-07 / 36 · part V advanced

Real-time strategy

Real-time strategy

An RTS is three games at once: economy, scouting and combat. The winner is whoever allocates attention better, not whoever clicks faster.

economymap controlcountersAPM
01 What this genre is

Loop: workers → economy → army → pressure → expansion. A match lasts 15–40 minutes and the peak load comes in the first five, when tempo is decided. The genre is built on economic compounding: one extra worker now is one extra unit two minutes later, so economy balance matters more than unit balance.

Combat is rock-paper-scissors with a cost of error: every unit has a counter, but switching to it takes time and resources. Map design sets the number of expansions, chokepoints and watchtowers. The key parameter is time to first contact (usually 2.5–5 minutes): less and the game becomes a rush, more and it becomes a base simulator.

The genre breaks on information overload: if the player cannot track three fronts, clicks win instead of strategy. Helpers: control groups, automation (queues, rally points), audio alerts and a readable minimap. And determinism is mandatory — otherwise lockstep multiplayer falls apart.

Loop
income = Σ workers · gather rate · (1 − losses), army(t) = ∫(income − spending)dt
Economy is an integrator: a 10 % income lead gives an army lead that grows over time. That is why nerfing economy usually hits harder than nerfing a unit.
Sessionmatch 15–40 min
Tempofirst contact 2.5–5 min
Key metricattention distribution and economy tempo
02 How to build it
  1. Balance the economy: timing of the second and third base, gather rates.
  2. Define the counter matrix and the cost of switching to a counter.
  3. Design the map: expansions, chokepoints, watchtowers.
  4. Add attention tools: control groups, alerts, minimap readability.
  5. Verify simulation determinism for lockstep multiplayer.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Economy stronger than army: the player builds instead of fighting.
  • Information overload: click speed decides the match.
  • One dominant unit: the counter matrix stops working.
  • A non-deterministic simulation desyncs in multiplayer.

Genre atlas GEN-08 / 36 · part V intermediate

Turn-based strategy and 4X

Turn-based strategy and 4X

4X is a game about curves: every empire grows, and whoever tuned their growth curve better wins — not whoever rolled better dice.

exploreexpandexploitexterminate
01 What this genre is

Loop: explore → expand → exploit → exterminate. One turn is 20 seconds of decision, one campaign 10–30 hours. The genre rests on compounding decisions: science yields technology, technology yields production, production yields army and expansion. A mistake in the first 30 turns costs more than a lost battle.

The core design problem is the late game: with dozens of cities and units, every turn becomes management. Cures: automation (governors, queues, templates), fewer decisions and a rising cost per turn. A good test: how many minutes a mid-game turn takes — more than 60 seconds is almost always bad.

The second risk is the snowball: the leader grows fastest and the game is decided by 30 % of its length. Cures: rising expansion cost, size penalties, AI coalitions, and alternative victory conditions (culture, science, diplomacy) that do not require domination.

Loop
growth = (science · production · territory)^(1/3) · era bonus, expansion cost ∝ n^1.5
Expansion cost must grow faster than its benefit (exponent 1.3–1.7), otherwise expansion is always optimal and the game is decided in the first hour.
Sessioncampaign 10–30 h
Tempoturn 20–60 s
Key metrictime per turn in mid-game
02 How to build it
  1. Tune science, production and growth curves so none dominates.
  2. Make expansion and empire upkeep progressively more expensive.
  3. Add late-game automation and cut decisions per turn.
  4. Check alternative victories: they must not be the default path.
  5. Test the AI for snowballing: the leader must not run away.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • A snowball decides the leader by a quarter of the campaign.
  • The late game becomes management instead of decisions.
  • One strategy is always optimal (usually expansion).
  • Randomness in critical checks: losing to a die roll.
04 Where you can see it in games
Civilization VIEndless LegendStellarisHeroes of Might and Magic III
09
Genre atlas GEN-09 / 36 · part V advanced

MOBA

MOBA

A MOBA is a team game about distributing resources and power across a map. The winner is whoever converts advantage into structures, not whoever gets more kills.

lanessnowballteamroles
01 What this genre is

Loop: lane → farm → fight → objective → teamfight. A match lasts 20–45 minutes, and there are three economies: personal gold (farm), team resources (objectives) and time (power windows). The map — three lanes plus a jungle — defines roles and rotation rhythm.

Balance is about power windows: an early-game hero must dominate until minute 15 and lose later. If the windows do not overlap, the match is predictable; if they overlap too often, roles blur. A kill must be worth less than an objective, otherwise fights become the goal and the map stops mattering.

The main disease is the snowball plus toxicity: one player who falls behind spoils the game for five. Cures include catch-up mechanics (objective XP, kill-streak bounties) and systemic design, not just reports. The second risk is opacity: the player must understand why they lost.

Loop
gold(t) = farm + bounty − deaths, power window = item tier × level
A kill grants ~300 gold and XP, but killing a streaking player grants more — a brake on the leader. Target match length 20–35 minutes for the standard mode.
Sessionmatch 20–45 min
Tempopower window 10–20 min
Key metricwin rate by role and gold distribution
02 How to build it
  1. Design the map: lanes, jungle, objectives and their spawn timers.
  2. Define roles and the power window of each archetype.
  3. Tune rewards: kill < objective, streaks pay more.
  4. Add catch-up mechanics and anti-snowball penalties.
  5. Ship transparent post-match stats: where the advantage was lost.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • A snowball decides the match by minute 15.
  • Fights matter more than the map: lanes and objectives lose value.
  • Power windows do not overlap — the match is decided at the draft.
  • An opaque loss: the player cannot tell what they did wrong.
04 Where you can see it in games

Genre atlas GEN-10 / 36 · part V basic

Tower defense

Tower defense

Tower defense is an optimisation problem: a finite budget against a growing threat. All the depth is in where the tower goes, not in how much damage it does.

pathingeconomywavesscaling
01 What this genre is

Loop: wave → income → build/upgrade → wave. A level takes 15–30 minutes. The economy is simple: a wave pays, a tower costs — so every tower competes with future towers. Map design sets the geometry of the path: a long winding path grants more time under fire, a short one less.

Balance is the wave curve against the income curve. If enemy health grows faster than income, the game becomes survival; if slower, a stroll. A good practice is to compute “effective time under fire” for each position and verify that an upgrade always beats a new tower in a specific situation — otherwise one strategy dominates.

The genre breaks on the optimal solution: if a perfect layout exists, the player finds it online and the game ends. Cures: random waves, different enemy types (armour, flying, shields), map choices and modifiers. And time acceleration is mandatory — waiting for a wave must not exceed 10–15 % of the session.

Loop
position DPS = Σ towers / time in zone, income(w) = base · (1 + k)^w, HP(w) = hp₀ · (1 + k')^w
k' should slightly exceed k: the threat outgrows income, otherwise the game is over by wave 20. A 3–8 % per-wave gap is the workable corridor.
Sessionlevel 15–30 min
Tempowave 20–60 s
Key metricleaks and income by wave 20
02 How to build it
  1. Design the map and compute time under fire for every position.
  2. Set income and wave-health curves with a slight threat lead.
  3. Add enemy types that demand different towers.
  4. Verify upgrades and new towers compete instead of one dominating.
  5. Add time acceleration and random wave modifiers.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • One optimal layout: the game ends after a guide.
  • Enemy health grows slower than income: no threat by wave 20.
  • Waiting for waves takes more than 15 % of the session.
  • Enemy types do not require different towers.

Auto battler

Auto battler

An auto battler is about assembling a build under a limited market and a shared pool. Combat is a deterministic check of that decision, not a place for skill.

drafteconomysynergyRNG
01 What this genre is

Loop: buy → place → fight → income. A round lasts 20–40 seconds, a match 20–30 minutes with eight players. The key is the shared pool: if three players chase one composition, it becomes unavailable. That creates lobby reading and rewards flexibility.

Economy is the second axis: interest on savings versus power now. The player chooses between spending everything for strength and saving for interest. That choice is the heart of the genre, and it breaks if interest is always right (everyone plays greedy) or never right (everyone rolls to zero).

Synergies must be clear but not obvious: 2–3 tiers per type, 4–6 units per build, and counters that exist. The genre breaks on uncompensated RNG: if a player loses because the needed unit never appeared on round 4, they do not feel they lost fairly. Cures: guaranteed units, choices of several, rerolling.

Loop
income = base_per_round + floor(gold/10) · 1 (max 5), power = Σ units · synergies
The classic scheme gives 1 interest per 10 gold, capped at +5 per round. Then “greedy” is a strategy with a price rather than a free advantage.
Sessionround 20–40 s
Tempomatch 20–30 min
Key metricshare of rounds decided by composition
02 How to build it
  1. Set the pool size and unit appearance odds by tier.
  2. Tune economy: income, interest, reroll cost.
  3. Design 4–6 synergies with counter-compositions.
  4. Limit RNG: guarantees, multi-choice, reroll.
  5. Validate combat by simulation: the result must follow from the lineup.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Interest always optimal: everyone plays greedy.
  • RNG without compensation: losing to a missing unit.
  • Synergies without counters: one composition dominates.
  • Combat so random that the lineup does not matter.

Genre atlas GEN-12 / 36 · part V advanced

Tactical games and wargames

Tactical games and wargames

A tactical game is chess with incomplete information and a cost of loss: every move is visible, and every death is irreversible.

initiativecoverfog of warpermadeath
01 What this genre is

Loop: scout → plan → move → react. A mission takes 20–60 minutes. Unlike an RTS, decisions here are discrete and only reversible backwards, so information matters more than speed. Fog of war, noise, smoke and recon become the central mechanics.

The combat maths is initiative and action economy: who moves first, how many actions a unit has, whether an enemy turn can be interrupted (overwatch). The cost of error is set by permanent death and injuries: if a unit heals back in a turn, all caution disappears. The genre's favourite trick is partial success: a hit is possible but not guaranteed, and the cost of a miss is visible in advance.

The genre breaks on unfair randomness (a point-blank miss on the decisive turn) and on “solved” missions with one correct order of operations. Cures: showing odds, undoing an action before information is revealed, saving mid-mission, and difficulty levels that change information rather than damage.

Loop
hit = clamp(0.05, base + acc − cover − range, 0.95), actions = 1–2 per unit
Keep hit chance in the 5–95 % band: 100 % kills tension, 0 % kills trust. Cover grants −20…−40 %, range up to −30 %.
Sessionmission 20–60 min
Tempoodds 5–95 %
Key metricshare of missions finished without losses
02 How to build it
  1. Define the action economy: actions per unit, interruptible turns.
  2. Tune odds and cover; show probabilities before the shot.
  3. Introduce fog of war and recon tools.
  4. Make the cost of error real: injuries, permadeath, resources.
  5. Verify each mission has 2–3 viable plans, not one.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • A point-blank miss on the decisive turn makes the game feel broken.
  • One correct sequence of actions: the mission is pre-solved.
  • Death without consequences removes all caution.
  • Difficulty through damage instead of information.
04 Where you can see it in games
XCOM 2Into the BreachBattle BrothersJagged Alliance 3
