Role-playing

6 topics

JRPG, CRPG, action RPG, MMO, souls-like and roguelite: character growth, builds and the cost of a mistake.

13
Genre atlas GEN-13 / 36 · part V intermediate

JRPG

JRPG

A JRPG is an ensemble of characters and a turn-based battle where the strength of the group matters more than individual tactics. Story and progression go hand in hand.

partyturn orderstorygrowth
01 What this genre is

Loop: story → dungeon → battle → growth → story again. A session lasts 30–90 minutes, the campaign 30–60 hours. The key is the party: each hero has a role, and combat tests whether the player can use them together. Balance is therefore built on a “hero × enemy” matrix rather than on a single character.

The battle system is turn order plus resources: MP or action points, delays, elements, statuses. The more layers there are, the more transparency matters: the player must see the turn queue, weaknesses and the consequences of a choice. Randomness is acceptable in damage, not in key decisions.

The genre breaks on mandatory grinding: if a boss cannot be beaten without five hours of farming, the story tears. Cures include the XP curve, enemy scaling and alternative paths (gear, tactics, elements). The second risk is unused heroes: if four of eight are always benched, party balance is not working.

Loop
damage = (ATK² / (ATK + DEF)) · element · (1 + buff) · rand(0.9, 1.1)
The quadratic ATK²/(ATK+DEF) form gives a gentle level advantage without nullifying defence — a genre classic.
Session30–90 min
Tempocampaign 30–60 h
Key metricshare of battles won without losses
02 How to build it
  1. Define party roles and the weakness matrix.
  2. Design the battle resource: MP, action points or turn delay.
  3. Make the turn queue and elemental hints transparent.
  4. Verify every hero is “necessary”: each needs a niche.
  5. Remove mandatory grind: offer paths through tactics and gear.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Mandatory grinding before a boss tears the story apart.
  • Half the party is never used.
  • An opaque turn queue and hidden weaknesses.
  • Randomness in key decisions (fear, instant death).

CRPG

CRPG

A CRPG is a rule system with a story built into it. The player does not just pick a line — they build a character whose skills open or close paths.

dialoguebuildschoicesystems
01 What this genre is

Loop: explore → dialogue/skill check → combat → reward. A campaign lasts 40–80 hours. The foundation is tabletop rules: attributes, skills, rolls, classes. The value of the genre is that choosing persuasion over lockpicking changes the content available, not merely the numbers.

Design rests on checks: d20 + modifier against difficulty. Transparency of the roll (showing the DC, the bonuses, the consequences) is the main tool of trust. The second layer is combat: turn-based or with pause; in both cases position and resources matter (spells, consumables, rest).

The genre breaks on fake choice (different lines with the same outcome) and on a “mandatory” build. Cures: several routes to a goal, warnings about consequences, the ability to retreat and return later, no dead ends. And separately: UI readability — complex systems require good tooltips, otherwise the player plays blind.

Loop
success ⇔ d20 + mod ≥ DC, P = (21 − (DC − mod)) / 20
At +5 against DC 15 success is 55 %. Show the DC and the modifier: the player must understand the risk before clicking.
Sessioncampaign 40–80 h
Tempocheck d20
Key metricshare of decisions that change content
02 How to build it
  1. Define attributes, skills and classes with clear niches.
  2. Make checks transparent: DC, bonus, consequences.
  3. Design 2–3 routes to every key goal.
  4. Tune resources: rest, spells, consumables.
  5. Verify no build is mandatory.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Fake choice: different lines lead to one outcome.
  • One mandatory build (say, max persuasion).
  • Opaque checks: the player cannot tell why they failed.
  • Dead ends: the player is stuck with no way back.

Baldur's Gate 3Disco ElysiumPathfinder: WotRPillars of Eternity

Action RPG and looter shooter

Action RPG and looter shooter

An action RPG is the loop “kill → something dropped → you got stronger”. Design here is drop density and the speed at which the player rebuilds.

lootbuildsdensityendgame
01 What this genre is

Loop: clear → loot → compare → upgrade. A session lasts 20–60 minutes and the endgame is endless. The genre lives on decision frequency: an item should appear every 30–90 seconds and a meaningful upgrade every 20–40 minutes. Less often and the player gets bored; more often and they cannot evaluate it.

Item comparison is the main interface of the game. A good practice is to show the difference in key numbers (damage, survivability, speed) rather than two lists of stats. The second layer is the build: synergies, sets, legendary effects. Legendaries should change the rules, not add +10 % — otherwise loot becomes a scale.

The genre breaks on number inflation (every season +ilvl) and on an endgame that reduces to farming one dungeon. Cures: seasonal mechanics, several activities with comparable rewards, “flat” alternatives to verticality (horizontal effects) and fast resets (respec, tinkering).

Loop
build DPS = damage · speed · crit · (1 + synergies), upgrade = max(0, ilvl_new − ilvl_old)
Upgrade frequency matters more than magnitude: one significant item every 20 minutes feels better than ten small ones per hour.
Session20–60 min
Tempoloot every 30–90 s
Key metricupgrades per hour and time to a new build
02 How to build it
  1. Set drop tempo: an item every 30–90 s, an upgrade every 20–40 min.
  2. Make item comparison readable: key numbers, not lists.
  3. Invent legendary effects that change the rules.
  4. Balance the endgame: several activities with comparable rewards.
  5. Limit number inflation and plan horizontal effects.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Legendaries as “+10 %”: loot becomes a scale.
  • Comparing items by two lists of stats: the player cannot tell which is better.
  • An endgame that is one dungeon on repeat.
  • Number inflation between seasons devalues builds.
04 Where you can see it in games

MMORPG

MMORPG

An MMO is not a game but a society with a schedule. Balance here includes not only numbers but groups, roles, time and social obligations.

socialpersistencerolesendgame
01 What this genre is

Loop: level → group content → raid/PvP → season. A session lasts 1–4 hours, a character's life — years. The defining feature is the persistent world: everything players do stays, so economy, reputation and raid schedules become part of the design.

Group content rests on roles: tank, healer, damage. That creates queue times and demands balance not only of power but of necessity: if a tank is not needed, the institution of roles collapses. The second layer is the schedule: raids, seasonal events, cooldowns. The player must know “what to do today”.

The main diseases are devaluing old content, inflation, toxicity and “mandatory” activities (dailies you cannot skip). Cures: horizontal progression, honest seasons, catch-up mechanics and respect for time: if the game demands three hours a day, the audience narrows to students.

Loop
progress = content(season) / (time · mandatory activities), group = tank + healer + 3 dps
The classic dungeon group is five: 1 tank, 1 healer, 3 damage. Queue time depends on role scarcity, not on damage balance.
Session1–4 h
Temposeason 8–12 weeks
Key metricretention and queue time by role
02 How to build it
  1. Define roles and their necessity in a group.
  2. Plan the season and the activity schedule.
  3. Add catch-up mechanics for new and returning players.
  4. Limit mandatory dailies: the game must not demand attendance.
  5. Tune the economy and inflation metrics (see Part IV).
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Mandatory dailies turn the game into a job.
  • Tank or healer scarcity: queues and toxicity.
  • Old content loses value every season.
  • Economy inflation and market capture by veterans.

Souls-like

Souls-like

A souls-like is combat where defence costs a resource and the world does not explain itself. Difficulty here is the language the game speaks.

staminatelegraphriskworld
01 What this genre is

Loop: explore → encounter → die → learn → win. A session lasts 30–120 minutes, a boss 10–40 attempts. The foundation is the stamina economy: attacking, dodging and blocking share one resource, so the player cannot do everything at once and must choose. That is the source of tension.

Attack telegraphs must be readable and honest: wind-up, sound, movement — at least 0.3–0.6 s. Death must explain itself, otherwise the player learns by trial and error instead of by mechanics. The second layer is the world: withholding explanation creates exploration, but requires consistent rules — the same sign must mean the same thing.

The genre breaks on “cheap” attacks without warning, on progress losses that do not teach (a long run back to the boss), and on ambiguity: if the player cannot understand why they died, difficulty becomes punishment. Cures: short run-backs, saved progress, honest hitboxes and explicit rules.

Loop
stamina(t) = max(0, stamina₀ − Σcost + regen·t), block damage = damage · (1 − block) − stamina_cost
Stamina regen is usually 30–50 per second against a pool of 100–140: two or three actions then a pause. That sets the rhythm of combat.
Session30–120 min
Tempotelegraph 0.3–0.6 s
Key metricattempts per boss and deaths to unknown attacks
02 How to build it
  1. Tune the stamina economy: cost of attack, dodge, block.
  2. Make telegraphs readable and consistent for the same threats.
  3. Shorten the run back to bosses and save exploration progress.
  4. Verify every death explains its cause.
  5. Make the world consistent: one sign, one meaning.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Attacks without telegraphs: death does not teach.
  • A long run back to the boss is punishment without learning.
  • Inconsistent world rules turn exploration into guessing.
  • Difficulty for its own sake: the player leaves without understanding the system.

Dark SoulsElden RingSekiroLies of P

Roguelike and roguelite

Roguelike and roguelite

A roguelike is a game where losing grants knowledge and the next run is different. Value lies in situational variety, not campaign length.

proceduralpermadeathsynergyruns
01 What this genre is

Loop: run → random items → synergies → death → new run. A run lasts 20–60 minutes and meta-progression happens between them. The key is variance: the player must meet different combinations, not replay one map with different numbers.

Design rests on decision density: a choice every 30–60 seconds (item, room, risk). Synergies must be clear and explosive but priced: a strong combination should demand conditions. Meta-progression is a fine line: it motivates, but if it grants power rather than variety, the game becomes a grind.

The genre breaks on unfair runs (no option that gives a chance) and on sameness. Cures: guaranteed “safety net” items, a choice of several rewards, difficulty modifiers, and a clear rule: the player should lose because of decisions, not because options were absent.

Loop
P(winning run) ≈ f(synergies, skill), run length 20–60 min
Target win rate: 5–15 % for a newcomer, 40–60 % for a veteran. Above 80 % and variance has vanished; below 2 % and runs feel hopeless.
Sessionrun 20–60 min
Tempodecision every 30–60 s
Key metricwin rate and build variety encountered
02 How to build it
  1. Build an item pool with synergies and prices.
  2. Tune decision frequency: a meaningful choice every 30–60 s.
  3. Make meta-progression about variety, not raw power.
  4. Add safety nets: guaranteed items, multi-choice rewards.
  5. Check the win rate for a newcomer and a veteran.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Unfair runs with no chance of a working build.
  • Meta-progression in raw power turns the game into a grind.
  • Unpriced synergies: one combination always wins.
  • Too little variety: runs look alike.
04 Where you can see it in games

Management sim and tycoon

Management sim and tycoon

A tycoon game is about feedback: the player builds a system, the system answers in numbers, the player improves it. The pleasure comes from understanding, not from action.

economyoptimisationfeedbackspreadsheets
01 What this genre is

Loop: build → see the numbers → find the bottleneck → improve. A session lasts 1–3 hours, a campaign 10–40 hours (or endless). The key is readable causality: the player must see why profit grew and what limits it. If numbers change without explanation, the game becomes guesswork.

Main curves: demand, supply, wear, wages, prices. A good tycoon presents one bottleneck at a time: the player solves it and the next appears. Ten simultaneous problems is not depth but anxiety. Second rule: the numbers must look good — growth of 8–12 % per cycle feels like progress, 1 % feels like stagnation.

The genre breaks on the optimal solution (one strategy always wins) and on the spreadsheet trap: the player spends time in tables, not in the game. Cures: random events, local markets, several goals (profit, reputation, resilience) and automation of repetitive actions.

Loop
profit = Σ (price − cost) · volume − fixed, growth = k · (1 − load)
A load limit is a natural brake: the closer the system is to capacity, the more the next step costs. That creates the “easy at first, hard at the end” curve.
Session1–3 h
Tempocycle 1–5 min
Key metricprofit growth per cycle and time to the first bottleneck
02 How to build it
  1. Define 3–4 linked curves (demand, cost, wear, reputation).
  2. Make the bottleneck visible in the UI.
  3. Limit simultaneous problems: one at a time.
  4. Add events that break the optimal strategy.
  5. Automate routine: the player should think, not click.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • One optimal strategy: the game is solved after the first playthrough.
  • Numbers change without a cause: the player learns nothing.
  • Too many simultaneous problems: anxiety instead of depth.
  • Routine without automation turns the game into a spreadsheet.

City builder

City builder

A city builder balances growth against maintenance: every new district needs water, roads, schools and patience. A game about how growth always creates the next problem.

zoningtrafficservicesgrowth
01 What this genre is

Loop: zone → roads → services → growth → new problem. A session lasts 2–5 hours and a city lives for dozens. The key is spatial causality: the player sees how a decision on the map changes the flow of people and trucks. Here the map is the interface, not the backdrop.

Curves: population, taxes, traffic, pollution, happiness. A good city builder gives feedback through the map (jams, smoke, empty houses) rather than through a table. That makes difficulty visible. Crucially, growth must be limited by infrastructure, otherwise the city expands forever and the game ends.

The genre breaks on traffic (the main technical and design problem) and on the dead middle, when the city already works and there are no new decisions. Cures: specialised districts, events (disasters, crises), goals and scenarios, and an honest traffic simulation — without it the map loses meaning.

Loop
population' = inflow − outflow, inflow ∝ happiness · housing · jobs · access
Growth almost always runs into traffic and services. Design the map so main arteries keep a 30–40 % capacity reserve.
Session2–5 h
Tempotick 1–5 s
Key metricaverage commute time and capacity reserve
02 How to build it
  1. Design the map as a grid with natural chokepoints.
  2. Tie happiness to service access, not to an abstract number.
  3. Limit growth by infrastructure: water, power, roads.
  4. Add district specialisation and events.
  5. Verify the traffic simulation: it decides whether the map is readable.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Traffic breaks the city and the player cannot see why.
  • Unlimited growth: the city sprawls and the game ends.
  • A dead middle: everything is built, no decisions left.
  • Happiness as an abstract number with no map connection.

Genre atlas GEN-21 / 36 · part V intermediate

Factory and automation

Factory and automation

A factory game is a puzzle about throughput: every machine has a rhythm and the whole plant must keep time. The pleasure is a perfect ratio.

throughputratiosblueprintsscaling
01 What this genre is

Loop: extraction → processing → assembly → logistics → the next product. A session lasts 2–6 hours, a project dozens. The genre rests on exact ratios: if one machine produces 0.5 items per second and the next consumes 0.75, the plant starves. The player finds those numbers themselves, and that is the main reward.

Scaling is the second axis: what works with ten machines breaks with a hundred. Logistics (belts, trains, drones) becomes the bottleneck rather than production. Good design offers clean multiples (1:2, 1:3) and planning tools: blueprints, copy-paste, load calculators.

The genre breaks on “spaghetti” — endless manual laying — and on unreadable recipes. Cures: blueprints, ghost placement, quick upgrades, and honest progression: a new tier must require new thinking, not just more machines.

Loop
throughput = min(production, consumption, logistics), ratio = t_produce / t_consume
A plant is always limited by its weakest link. Design recipes with multiple times (0.5 / 1 / 2 s) so the ratios are obvious.
Session2–6 h
Tempotick 1/60 s
Key metricmachine load and the plant bottleneck
02 How to build it
  1. Set recipes with multiple production and consumption times.
  2. Make logistics a separate problem with its own constraints.
  3. Add blueprints and copy-paste so scaling is not drudgery.
  4. Limit production bottlenecks, not the player's attention.
  5. Verify progression: every tier changes the thinking, not just the numbers.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Manual laying as the core mechanic turns the game into labour.
  • Recipes without clean multiples cannot be computed in your head.
  • Logistics does not scale: a hundred machines break everything.
  • Progression only in numbers: the new tier is the same machines, but more.

Life sim and social simulation

Life sim and social simulation

A life sim is a schedule of needs and relationships. It is not about winning but about managing time and emotional ties.

needsrelationshipsroutineemergence
01 What this genre is

Loop: need → action → time → consequence. A session lasts 1–3 hours and the game can run for months of real time (or be accelerated). The foundation is the hierarchy of needs: sleep, food, socialising, creativity. Every action costs time, so the player constantly bargains with the schedule.

The second layer is relationships: meetings, conversations, conflicts. What matters is not a “friendship bar” but memory: events that change behaviour. A good life sim produces emergent stories — combinations of simple rules that read like a plot. That is the genre's value.

The genre breaks on routine (the same actions every hour) and on an “optimal schedule” the player finds and then stops thinking about. Cures: events, randomness, social obligations, a limited day and characters with their own goals that interfere with the player's plans.

Loop
energy(t) = Σ needs, action = f(time, cost, mood)
The key balance is the day: 24 hours should fit 60–70 % of what the player wants. If they can do everything, choice disappears; if under half, the game becomes a fight with a timer.
Session1–3 h
Tempoday 24 in-game hours
Key metricwhether the player achieves their plans
02 How to build it
  1. Define needs and how fast they decay.
  2. Make time the main resource: actions compete for the day.
  3. Add memory and relationships that affect behaviour.
  4. Design events that break the schedule.
  5. Verify the player can accomplish 60–70 % of their plans.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Routine without events turns the game into a timetable.
  • An optimal schedule: the player stops thinking afterwards.
  • Needs decay too fast and the game becomes a timer.
  • Relationships as one bar with no memory.

Survival

Survival

Survival is the needs curve against the threat curve. The game starts with “where is water” and ends with “how do I defend the base”, and both are the same question.

resourcesthreatcraftingbases
01 What this genre is

Loop: gather → build → survive the night → expand. A session lasts 1–4 hours, a world 20–100. The key is scarcity pressure: first there is no water, then no food, then no safety. Every decision (push further or fortify) has a time cost.

Design rests on the day-night cycle and the threat: enemies come at night, food runs out in winter, weather ruins plans. A good curve: the first 30 minutes are survival, the first 3 hours are the base, then exploration and technology. If the threat does not grow, the game becomes a sandbox; if it grows faster, a punishment.

The genre breaks on resource grinding (three hours of chopping wood) and on progress loss that does not teach (dying and losing your inventory with no explanation). Cures: partial loss on death, faster gathering, resource automation and honest threat telegraphs — the player must see that the night will be rough.

Loop
survival ⇔ stock(t) > consumption(t), threat(t) ≈ k · progress(t)
The threat must grow with progress: the stronger the base, the more dangerous the night. Otherwise the late game becomes a farm without risk.
Session1–4 h
Tempoday cycle 10–20 min
Key metricdeaths by hour and resource shortage
02 How to build it
  1. Design the first 30 minutes: three shortages in a row, each solved by a new tool.
  2. Tie threat growth to player progress, not to a timer.
  3. Cut routine gathering: tools, automation, acceleration.
  4. Make death instructive: partial loss and an explained cause.
  5. Check the curve: when does the player stop fearing the night?
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Grinding wood and stone takes longer than everything else.
  • No threat growth: the late game is a farm without risk.
  • Death wipes hours of progress without teaching.
  • No night telegraph: the player cannot tell why they died.

Sandbox and creative games

Sandbox and creative games

A sandbox sells a tool, not a challenge. Its value is how far the player can go beyond what the developers made.

creationtoolssharingno goals
01 What this genre is

Loop: imagine → build → show → improve. A session runs from 20 minutes to forever. There is no difficulty curve — there is an expressiveness curve: first the player builds a cube, then a house, then a machine, then a world. The design task is to reduce friction at every step.

Tools matter more than content: brushes, copy-paste, undo, layers, physics, scripting. A good sandbox offers a simple start and a deep ceiling: a cube is one button away, logic circuits require study. And it must be shareable: export, gallery, codes.

The genre breaks on emptiness (nothing and no reason to build) and on a complex interface. Cures: optional goal hints, templates, learning through small tasks, a gallery of other players' work and the ability to play in others' creations. The community is part of the design, not the marketing.

Loop
expressiveness = tool power / interface friction
The entry barrier is inversely proportional to friction: every extra button filters out some players. First one “place block” button, then everything else.
Session20 min – ∞
Tempono fixed goal
Key metricshare of players publishing their work
02 How to build it
  1. Make the basic action (place/remove) a single button.
  2. Add layers of depth: physics, logic, scripting — optionally.
  3. Design sharing: export, gallery, codes.
  4. Add optional goals and templates for newcomers.
  5. Verify the player can show something within 10 minutes.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Emptiness: nothing to build and no reason to.
  • An interface harder than the game: newcomers leave at the first step.
  • No way to share: creation stays unseen.
  • Tools without examples or onboarding.
04 Where you can see it in games

Metroidvania

Metroidvania

A metroidvania is a map locked by abilities. A new ability opens old doors, and the world is read anew.

gatingbacktrackingmapabilities
01 What this genre is

Loop: explore → find an ability → return → open a new path. A session lasts 1–3 hours, the game 10–25. The key is map knowledge: the player memorises inaccessible places and returns to them. The map is therefore the main interface, and abilities are keys rather than damage upgrades.

World design: an ability must open several paths at once (otherwise returning becomes a linear quest), and backtracking must be short. Good practice: teleports, elevators, shortcuts, and map markers so the player does not forget where they saw a door.

The genre breaks on blind backtracking (the player cannot remember where to go) and on abilities useful exactly once. Cures: a map with markers, hints, several uses of each ability in combat and exploration, and a tangible upgrade before a hard boss.

Loop
world = graph of rooms, edge open ⇔ ability ∈ inventory
An ability should open 2–4 graph edges, otherwise it is one-use. Validate the graph for dead ends and for “doors with nothing behind them”.
Session1–3 h
Tempogame 10–25 h
Key metricbacktracking time and forgotten doors
02 How to build it
  1. Draw the room graph and mark which ability opens which edge.
  2. Verify every ability opens several paths.
  3. Shorten backtracking: teleports, elevators, map markers.
  4. Make abilities useful in combat, not only as keys.
  5. Validate the graph for dead ends and empty rewards.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Blind backtracking: the player cannot remember the map and quits.
  • Key abilities needed only once.
  • Doors with nothing behind them break expectations.
  • Long transitions between zones.

Puzzle games

Puzzle games

A puzzle is teaching through levels. The player must discover the rule themselves, not read it in a hint.

rulesinsightlevelsteaching
01 What this genre is

Loop: understand the rule → apply it → complicate it. A session lasts 15–45 minutes, the game 3–15 hours. The key is rule purity: one rule, many consequences. If there are five rules interacting randomly, the puzzle becomes guesswork.

Teaching is a sequence: show the rule in safe conditions, then test it at the edge, then combine it with another. A good practice: it is impossible to lose in teaching levels, and undo is free. Difficulty grows through the number of consequences, not through size.

The genre breaks on unfair puzzles (the solution requires knowledge the player never got) and on hints that give the answer outright. Better to have a hierarchy: nudge → direction → almost the answer. And clear visual feedback: the player must see that their action worked.

Loop
difficulty ≈ available moves + depth of consequences
Difficulty comes from depth, not from field size. Verify there is exactly one “beautiful” solution and several dead ends.
Session15–45 min
Tempolevel 1–10 min
Key metricshare solved without hints
02 How to build it
  1. Define one rule and its consequences.
  2. Build a level chain: show → test → combine.
  3. Make undo free and obvious.
  4. Add a hint hierarchy instead of the answer.
  5. Verify feedback: the player must see the result of an action.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Five rules interacting randomly.
  • A puzzle requires knowledge the player never received.
  • A hint that gives away the answer.
  • Difficulty through size instead of depth.

Immersive sim

Immersive sim

An immersive sim is a set of systems that interact. The player invents a solution, and the game must accept it — not just the entries in a menu.

systemicemergentstealthchoice
01 What this genre is

Loop: observe → plan → execute → unexpected consequence. A level takes 1–2 hours. The foundation is systemic rules: fire burns, water conducts, sound carries, bodies can be carried, glass breaks. The more consistent the rules, the more solutions exist.

Level design is “one task, many entrances”: vents, roof, hacking, persuasion, noise. The key is consistency: if a rule works in one place it must work everywhere. Otherwise the player stops trusting the world and stops experimenting.

The genre breaks on “two paths” (quiet and loud) that are actually the same, and on systems that only work in set pieces. Cures: explicit teaching through the environment, logs and hints, and — crucially — handling absurd solutions (what happens if the player carries a barrel into the lift?).

Loop
solutions = combinations(rules, tools, environment)
The number of solutions grows combinatorially. Test 3–5 “crazy” solutions in every room — they are the genre.
Session1–2 h
Tempolevel 20–60 min
Key metricpaths to the goal and unplanned solutions
02 How to build it
  1. Define 8–12 consistent systemic rules.
  2. Design levels with 4–5 entrances to each goal.
  3. Verify the rules behave identically in all zones.
  4. Test “stupid” solutions and make sure the game handles them.
  5. Teach through the environment, not through text.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Rules that only work in set pieces stop all experimentation.
  • Two paths that are the same in substance.
  • The game does not handle absurd solutions.
  • Teaching by text instead of by environment.

Stealth

Stealth

Stealth is a game about information: the player sees the guard, the guard does not see the player. Everything else is managing sound, light and time.

visibilitysoundpatrolfailure
01 What this genre is

Loop: observe → route → pass → new zone. A level takes 30–90 minutes. The key is readable detection rules: what the guard sees, what they hear, how long it takes to notice. Without that, stealth becomes guessing at a radius.

Tools: cover, light and shadow, noise (footsteps, thrown objects), distraction, bodies. Good design offers several routes of different difficulty and honest failure: being spotted is a new task, not a reload. If detection always means death, the player stops experimenting.

The genre breaks on unpredictable patrols and on a “vision system” that cannot be learned. Cures: a detection indicator, audio cues, predictable patrols and soft failure — the guard raises the alarm but the player still has a chance to slip away.

Loop
detection ⇔ visibility · light · distance / cover + noise > threshold
The threshold should be visible in the UI (an indicator) and patrols predictable: the player learns a system, not randomness.
Session30–90 min
Tempodetection 0.5–3 s
Key metricshare of levels cleared without an alarm
02 How to build it
  1. Define the detection formula and show it to the player.
  2. Design patrols as a schedule, not as randomness.
  3. Give 2–3 routes per level and distraction tools.
  4. Make failure soft: an alarm, not instant death.
  5. Verify that light and sound read visually.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Random patrols: the player cannot learn the system.
  • Detection equals death, so experimentation stops.
  • A hidden vision formula: the player cannot tell why they were spotted.
  • No visual feedback for light and noise.

Horror

Horror

Horror is managing tension, not monsters. It works while the player feels a lack of control and does not know what comes next.

tensionpowerlessnesssoundpacing
01 What this genre is

Loop: exploration → threat signal → decision (run/hide/fight) → release. A session lasts 45–120 minutes. The key is power asymmetry: the player is weaker, slower, sees worse. Give them a full arsenal and horror becomes action.

Tools: sound (more important than graphics), limited vision, resources (batteries, ammo), predictable and unpredictable threats. The rhythm is a wave: tension → peak → release → pause. Without pauses the player adapts and stops being afraid. Good horror alternates threat and safety.

The genre breaks on cheap jump scares without setup, on endless chases (fatigue) and on unfair rules (a monster seeing through walls). Cures: honest rules, the ability to prepare, teaching through safe encounters and clear signals — the player must know when they are in danger.

Loop
tension(t) = lack_of_control · uncertainty / habituation
Habituation grows with every repetition: the same chase is scary the first time and annoying the fifth. Change the shape of the threat, not only its strength.
Session45–120 min
Tempopeak 10–60 s
Key metricresource spend and safe minutes
02 How to build it
  1. Design power asymmetry: speed, visibility, resources.
  2. Build the rhythm “tension → peak → pause”.
  3. Limit resources so decisions matter.
  4. Make the rules honest: the threat obeys the same laws.
  5. Change the shape of the threat, not just its strength.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • A full arsenal turns the genre into action.
  • Endless chases exhaust the player and breed habituation.
  • Unfair rules: a monster that sees through walls.
  • Jump scares without setup: scary once, irritating afterwards.

Narrative adventure

Narrative adventure

A narrative game sells consequences, not mechanics. It works when a choice changes not just a line but how the player sees the story.

storychoicedialoguepacing
01 What this genre is

Loop: scene → choice → consequence → new scene. A session lasts 40–120 minutes, the game 5–20 hours. The key is agency: the player must feel the decision belongs to them. Even if the outcome is fixed, the form of participation matters: whom they believed, what they said, whom they saved.

Tools: timed dialogue, examining objects, moral dilemmas, relationships. A good practice is local consequences: you do not need to rewrite the whole plot — it is enough for the scene, the tone or access to information to change. Global branching is expensive and often not worth it.

The genre breaks on fake choice (all lines lead to the same place) and on exposition instead of action. Cures: show rather than tell, scenes where the player does something rather than listens, and honesty: if a choice is illusory, do not present it as important.

Loop
agency ≈ (choice impact) · (visible consequences)
An illusory choice with a dramatic presentation feels worse than no choice at all. Better fewer branches with real consequences.
Session40–120 min
Tempogame 5–20 h
Key metricshare of scenes affected by the player
02 How to build it
  1. Decide which decisions really change the scene.
  2. Make consequences visible: characters remember, the world changes.
  3. Show rather than tell: action instead of exposition.
  4. Limit global branching: local changes are cheaper and stronger.
  5. Verify the player understands what they chose.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Fake choice with a dramatic presentation.
  • Exposition instead of scenes.
  • Global branching that does not pay off.
  • The player cannot tell what they chose.

Racing games

Racing games

Racing is physics and tracks. The sense of speed matters more than realism, and a track must forgive a beginner's mistakes while punishing an expert's.

physicstrackssense of speedprogression
01 What this genre is

Loop: choose a car → qualify → race → upgrade. A race lasts 5–20 minutes, a career 20–60 hours. The key is the grip model: arcade (stable, forgiving) or simulation (demanding precision). Mixing them in one product only works through settings, not through “average” physics.

A track is designed as a rhythm: straights, fast corners, hairpins, blind crests. A good track offers several lines and overtaking spots. The sense of speed comes from the camera, FOV, motion blur, sound and vibration — not only from the speedometer.

The genre breaks on rubber banding, which devalues skill, and on physics too hard to learn. Cures: assists (ABS, stability) that can be switched off, a ghost of the best lap, and fair penalties for cutting corners.

Loop
v_max ≈ P / (ρ·C_d·A)^(1/3), grip = μ·N, braking distance ≈ v²/(2μg)
Top speed grows as the cube root of power, so upgrades give less and less. Braking distance grows quadratically: brake early.
Sessionrace 5–20 min
Tempolap 1–3 min
Key metriclap-time gap between novice and expert
02 How to build it
  1. Choose the model: arcade, simulation, or arcade with assists.
  2. Design the track as a rhythm with several lines.
  3. Tune the sense of speed: camera, FOV, sound, effects.
  4. Add assists that can be disabled.
  5. Check penalties and rubber banding: skill must decide.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Rubber banding devalues skill.
  • Physics too complex without onboarding.
  • A track with a single line makes overtaking impossible.
  • The sense of speed comes only from the speedometer.

Sports games

Sports games

A sports sim is the rules of a real game plus seasonal progression. You balance rules and ratings, not characters.

rulesseasonratingsmeta
01 What this genre is

Loop: match → season → transfers → next season. A match lasts 5–15 minutes, a career years. The key is rule fidelity: the player comes for a familiar game. Every simplification must be deliberate and explainable.

Player ratings are data, not design: they are updated from statistics yet affect balance more than any patch. A good practice is to separate rating from role: a high-rated player can be useless in a particular formation, which makes squad selection interesting.

The genre breaks on the meta (one tactic always wins) and on monetisation that breaks competition (pay-to-win in Ultimate Team). Cures: seasonal rule updates, squad limits, “equal conditions” modes and transparent ratings.

Loop
rating ≈ f(statistics, position, context), result = rules + lineup + execution
Ratings must be multidimensional: speed, passing, shooting, defence. A single number makes squad selection trivial.
Sessionmatch 5–15 min
Temposeason 20–40 matches
Key metricwin distribution by tactic
02 How to build it
  1. Define the rules and simplifications, explainable to the player.
  2. Make ratings multidimensional and contextual.
  3. Limit the meta: seasonal updates and squad caps.
  4. Add an “equal conditions” mode for competition.
  5. Verify the rating does not decide the match without the player.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • One tactic always wins.
  • A single-number rating makes selection trivial.
  • Monetisation breaks the competitive mode.
  • Rule simplifications without explanation.

Rhythm games

Rhythm games

A rhythm game is precision and music. Success depends on hit windows, chart difficulty curves and audio latency on the player's device.

timingchartingcalibrationflow
01 What this genre is

Loop: listen → press on the beat → get graded. A track takes 2–5 minutes. The key is the hit windows: Perfect/Great/Good/Miss. Too narrow and hardware punishes the player; too wide and mastery disappears. Standard: Perfect ±25–40 ms, Great ±70–90 ms.

The chart is design, not automation: it must follow musical accents and escalate gradually. Latency calibration is mandatory: without it a player on Bluetooth headphones is playing a different game. The second layer is readability: notes must be visible 1–2 seconds before the hit.

The genre breaks on unfair notes (doubles absent from the music) and on difficulty walls. Cures: several difficulty levels per track, a practice mode with slowdown, accuracy display and honest calibration.

Loop
grade = f(|t_press − t_note|), Perfect ≤ 30 ms, Great ≤ 80 ms
Total latency = audio + input + display latency. Calibration must compensate for the sum, not the parts.
Sessiontrack 2–5 min
Tempowindow 25–90 ms
Key metricPerfect share and calibration drift
02 How to build it
  1. Set hit windows and latency calibration.
  2. Chart to musical accents, not to the grid.
  3. Ensure readability: 1–2 seconds before the hit.
  4. Add several difficulties and practice with slowdown.
  5. Verify every note matches audible sound.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • No calibration: a Bluetooth player plays a different game.
  • Notes that do not match the music.
  • Windows too narrow: hardware punishes the player.
  • A difficulty wall without intermediate levels.
04 Where you can see it in games
Osu!Beat SaberGuitar HeroRhythm Doctor

Collectible card games

Collectible card games

A CCG is a metagame about decks and information. You balance archetypes, not cards: aggro, control and combo must coexist in one metagame.

deck buildingmana curvemetaRNG
01 What this genre is

Loop: build a deck → match → new card → new deck. A match lasts 5–15 minutes, the meta weeks. The key is the mana curve and tempo: aggro wins by turn 5–7, control by turn 10–15. If one archetype is faster and more consistent, the meta collapses.

Card balance is answer balance: every threat needs an answer, and the answer must be available. Randomness is acceptable in draw, not in key effects. The second layer is rarity: cards must not be stronger just because they are rare, or the competitive mode breaks.

The genre breaks on “mandatory” cards (in 90 % of decks) and on combos with no interaction. Cures: seasonal rotations, ban lists, copy limits and healthy randomness: card draw rather than “won on the topdeck”.

Loop
tempo = Σ (mana / turn), P(draw an answer) = 1 − C(n−k, m)/C(n, m)
Hypergeometric distribution: with 3 copies of an answer in 30 cards and 5 cards in hand, the chance is ~42 %. That is what “fair draw” means.
Sessionmatch 5–15 min
Tempometa 2–6 weeks
Key metricshare of cards in 80 %+ of decks
02 How to build it
  1. Define archetypes and their win turn.
  2. Give every threat an available answer.
  3. Limit rarity as a power factor.
  4. Tune rotation and ban lists.
  5. Check the meta: every archetype should sit between 45 % and 55 %.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • Cards stronger because they are rare.
  • Combos with no interaction end the game on turn 4.
  • Mandatory cards in every deck.
  • Randomness decides more often than decisions.

Magic: The GatheringHearthstoneLegends of RuneterraMarvel Snap

Idle and incremental games

Idle and incremental games

An idle game is exponentials and resets. The player optimises numbers; the designer controls how fast they grow and when the wall appears.

exponentialprestigenumbersautomation
01 What this genre is

Loop: accumulate → buy an upgrade → speed up → reset (prestige). A session lasts 5–20 minutes, the game weeks. The key is the exponential curve: income grows, prices grow faster, and the player is always close to the next upgrade. That “just a bit more” feeling is the genre.

Prestige is the main design tool: it wipes progress but grants a multiplier, turning a long session into a series of short ones. Crucially, a reset must be a meaningful choice, not a mandatory ritual after a wall.

The genre breaks on the “dead wall” (numbers grow but nothing happens for hours) and on pointless clicking. Cures: automation, offline income, several currencies, achievements and a prestige tree. And readability is mandatory: the player must see what accelerates growth.

Loop
income = base · Π multipliers, cost(n) = base · 1.15ⁿ, time to buy ≈ cost / income
The classic cost step is 1.10–1.20 per purchase. At 1.15 every next purchase costs 15 % more, which creates the permanent nearness of the next upgrade.
Session5–20 min
Tempocycle 1–60 s
Key metrictime to the next upgrade
02 How to build it
  1. Set the income exponent and the cost step (1.10–1.20).
  2. Make prestige a meaningful choice, not a mandatory ritual.
  3. Add automation and offline income.
  4. Introduce several currencies and an upgrade tree.
  5. Verify there are no dead walls longer than 10–15 minutes.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • A dead wall: nothing happens for hours.
  • Clicking as a mandatory mechanic without automation.
  • Prestige is mandatory and offers no choice.
  • Numbers grow but the player cannot see what affects them.
04 Where you can see it in games
Cookie ClickerAdventure CapitalistMelvor IdleNGU Idle
36
Genre atlas GEN-36 / 36 · part V basic

Party games and social deduction

Party games and social deduction

A party game lives on conversation at the table. Rules must be understood in 60 seconds and rounds must be short enough that the loser wants another.

socialbluffingshort roundsspectators
01 What this genre is

Loop: round → vote/challenge → result → new round. A round takes 1–5 minutes, a session 20–60. The key is simplicity of entry: rules explained in a minute, with depth emerging from player behaviour rather than from mechanics.

Social deduction requires information asymmetry: some know more, some less. It is important that every role has its own game: the traitor needs a plan, not just sabotage. And observing must be possible: an eliminated player should not be bored.

The genre breaks on “dead” elimination (the player waits five minutes) and on toxicity. Cures: short rounds, tasks for eliminated players, discussion before voting, private channels and soft penalties. And fair role randomness: nobody should be the traitor five times in a row.

Loop
round 1–5 min, rules explained ≤ 60 s, eliminated share at any moment ≤ 25 %
Three numbers decide whether people play again: round length, teaching time and the wait for eliminated players.
Sessionround 1–5 min
Tempoteaching 60 s
Key metricshare of players who play again
02 How to build it
  1. Make rules explainable in 60 seconds.
  2. Give every role its own goal, not just sabotage.
  3. Occupy eliminated players: tasks, observation, voting.
  4. Cap rounds at 1–5 minutes.
  5. Verify roles are dealt fairly and do not repeat consecutively.
03 Where the genre breaks
  • An eliminated player is bored for five minutes.
  • Rules take longer than a minute to explain.
  • The traitor has no plan beyond sabotage.
  • One role always wins at equal skill.
04 Where you can see it in games
Among UsJackbox Party PackTown of SalemGoose Goose Duck
Part VI · style atlas and prompt studio

Style and the prompt studio

From dossier to brief

The earlier parts give you mechanics, balance and genres. This part assembles a brief from them: pick a genre, add two or three balance principles, apply a style — and get a prompt you can take to a team or a language model.

47style atoms
6layers
8presets
4formats

A prompt is a budget of attention: the more precisely the numbers and constraints are named, the less room is left for an average result. Empty slots are better left empty than filled with clichés.

Style atlas

six layers that make up the look of a game
01

Look and rendering

10

How the game looks technically: pixels, drawing, low-poly, voxels, photorealism. It is the first decision and it rules out half of the rest.

Low-resolution pixel art 240×135 pixel art, limited palette, visible pixels, 8–12 frame animation
Hand-drawn 2D hand-drawn sprites and backdrops, lively linework, soft shadows, watercolour fills
Stylised 3D stylised 3D with chunky forms, flat materials and readable silhouettes
Photorealism PBR materials, physically based lighting, cinematic optics, honest shadows
PS1-style low-poly low-poly models, affine textures, vertex wobble, fog as fog
Voxels voxel geometry, destructible blocks, chunky volumes, simple materials
Vector flat clean vector shapes, flat colours, geometric grid, minimal texture
Painterly painted backdrops with visible brushwork, atmospheric perspective, light as paint
Anime cel cel shading, crisp outlines, dramatic angles, speed lines
Clay and felt a shot miniature: clay, felt, cardboard, visible texture and seams
02

Palette and light

08

A limited palette sets the mood more strongly than any plot. Warm dusk, neon noir, faded ash, pastel — this is the language of emotion.

Neon noir black base, acid neon, rain and reflections, rim light
Warm cosy amber, terracotta, cream light, soft shadows, evening gold
Desaturated grimness low saturation, grey-green, dust, rare accents of blood and gold
Soft pastel pastels, milky shadows, pink and mint, the feel of paper
Duotone two colours and their shades, high contrast, poster-like graphics
Monochrome ink black-and-white ink, hatching, white paper, a single accent colour
Solarpunk greenery, glass, warm sunlight, copper and moss, optimism
Acid brutalism grey concrete, an acid accent, big typography, hard shadows
03

Camera and space

07

Isometric, side-scrolling, first-person, close third: the camera decides what the player sees and therefore what they play.

Isometric isometric camera, fixed angle, readable tiles, depth through scale
Side-scrolling side camera, one movement vector, parallax layers, a framed stage
First person first-person camera, weapon in frame, wide FOV, head inertia
Close third person over-the-shoulder camera, character in frame, smooth follow, cinematic
Top-down overhead camera, the whole arena in frame, tactical reading of space
Fixed shots fixed shots like old cinema, angle changes between screens
Cinematic smooth cinematic moves, widescreen framing, depth of field
04

Tone and emotion

08

Hope, melancholy, dread, playfulness, epic scale, satire. Tone is the promise a game makes in its first thirty seconds.

Hope a tone of hope and repair: the world is broken but can be mended
Melancholy quiet melancholy, loss, slow time, beauty in emptiness
Eerie quiet dread: something is wrong and cannot be named
Playful playfulness and humour, fast tempo, exaggerated animation
Epic epic scale, vast spaces, solemnity
Satire satire and absurdity, recognisable types, a mean smile
Intimacy intimacy and closeness, small spaces, personal stories
Clinical clinical precision, sterility, bureaucracy, the anxiety of order
05

Sound and music

08

Chiptune, orchestra, industrial, ambient, lo-fi, folk. Sound sets the tempo and is remembered before the graphics.

Chiptune 2–3 channel chiptune, arithmetic waves, noise percussion
Orchestral a live orchestra, leitmotifs, dynamic layers driven by tension
Industrial industrial rhythms, metal, mechanical hum, distortion
Ambient ambient drones, silence as an instrument, rare events
Lo-fi lo-fi beats, warm grit, jazz chords, vinyl
Folk acoustic folk, live instruments, local modes
Synthwave synthwave, analogue pads, gated drums, wide stereo
Diegetic sound sound from the world only: radio, footsteps, wind; almost no score
06

Texture and interface

06

Diegetic HUD, minimal UI, juicy feedback, tactility, documentary dryness. This is what the fingers feel.

Diegetic HUD interface inside the world: gauges, notes, physical scales
Minimal UI minimal interface, information through the world and sound
Heavy juice strong feedback: hitstop, shake, particles, flashes, a sound for every action
Tactility tactile details: dragging, item weight, physical levers and buttons
Documentary calm restrained presentation without effects, long shots, trust in silence
Systemic design every action has a systemic consequence; rules matter more than scripts

          reference
          
Glossary of terms

          
          37 terms
        

        

          Terms that show up both in this text and in job descriptions. Keep them handy during a technical interview.
        

        
A*
Shortest-path search with a heuristic h(n): f(n) = g(n) + h(n). An admissible heuristic never overestimates the remaining cost.
ECS
Entity Component System: entity — an id, components — data, systems — logic. Gives cache locality and composition.
DOD
Data-Oriented Design: lay out memory for the traversal first, code second. The base of fast simulations.
Fixed-point
Fixed-point arithmetic (Q16.16): deterministic across platforms, unlike float.
Lockstep
Clients exchange only commands and simulate the same world; state is never transmitted.
Rollback
Resimulating unconfirmed inputs from a server snapshot; the basis of client-side prediction.
Verlet
Position-based integration: x′ = 2x − x_prev + a·dt². Stable, convenient for constraints.
PBD / XPBD
Position-Based Dynamics: constraints are projected onto positions; XPBD makes stiffness iteration-independent.
SPH
Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics: a fluid as particles with a smoothing kernel and pressure.
BVH
Bounding Volume Hierarchy: an AABB tree for fast culling and raycasts; built with SAH.
SAH
Surface Area Heuristic: a BVH split quality criterion based on bounding surface area.
MCTS / UCT
Monte Carlo Tree Search with the UCT rule: balancing exploration and exploitation in a game tree.
Utility AI
Choosing an action by a weighted sum of normalised factors; an alternative to behaviour trees.
Flow field
A grid of directions towards a goal: cheap pathing for large groups of units.
WFC
Wave Function Collapse: constraint-based generation with propagation and backtracking.
SDF
Signed Distance Field: distance to a surface; convenient for CSG and ray marching.
Marching cubes
Extracting an isosurface from a density grid using a 256-case table.
PBR / BRDF
Physically Based Rendering: energy-conserving materials; the BRDF describes light reflection.
GGX
Microfacet normal distribution model with a long specular tail.
Ambisonics
Encoding 3D audio in spherical harmonics (W, X, Y, Z) and decoding it for headphones or speakers.
HRTF
Head-Related Transfer Function: the filter describing how ears and head colour sound from a direction.
PRD
Pseudo-Random Distribution: the chance grows after failures, reducing streak variance without changing the mean.
Glicko-2 / TrueSkill
Bayesian ratings with uncertainty (RD/σ) updated after a match.
ARIMA
Time-series model: autoregression, differencing and a moving average of errors.
GAN
Generator versus discriminator; WGAN-GP stabilises training via the Wasserstein distance.
FFT
Fast Fourier Transform: O(N log N); used for oceans, texturing and audio.
Perlin / fBm
Gradient noise and its fractal sum of octaves; the base of procedural terrain and materials.
Kepler
T² = 4π²a³/(G(M+m)); the equation M = E − e·sin E links time and position on the orbit.
Draw call
A draw submission: one batch of geometry with one pipeline state. The main unit of CPU render cost.
Compute shader
A program executed as a separate pass over a grid of data; not bound to geometry.
Workgroup
A group of GPU threads working together; a barrier inside the group is nearly free.
Stall
A wait where the CPU or the GPU sits idle waiting for the other. The main enemy of asynchrony.
Hi-Z
A max-depth reduction pyramid of the previous frame; a cheap source of occlusion tests.
False sharing
Two threads write to different fields of one cache line and keep invalidating it for each other.
Temporal reprojection
Reusing last frame's result reprojected along camera motion.
OIT
Order-Independent Transparency: transparency without sorting, via weighted accumulation and division.
A/B test
Comparing two variants on random player cohorts: the only honest way to verify an effect.

      


      

        
Method and limits

        
Formulas use game units rather than SI where that reads better; constants are tuned for gameplay, not for a physics lab. The code is minimal, without optimisations or error handling: its job is to show the structure, not to replace an engine. Complexity figures assume a typical implementation; real numbers depend on platform and compiler.

        
The demos use Canvas 2D and plain maths: no libraries, no CDN, no build step. That is deliberate — the file opens with a double click, works offline and never goes stale with its dependencies.
